en: Preface to the Re-engraved *Commentary on the Examples of the Meaning of Śamatha and Vipaśyanā* The *Examples of the Meaning of Śamatha and Vipaśyanā* composed by the Master of Piling constitutes the grand mainstay for weaving the net of the teachings and the essential pivot for opening and closing the gates of contemplation.
Just as King Yin’s net—when the three [fish] were released and one side was set aside—encompassed the three types of śamatha and vipaśyanā; so too does this work.
They are distinct. To establish one [path], one must unify *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. This is like catching a bird with a cool trap.

Furthermore, it is like the Zhuque Gate (South Gate): three side gates and one main gate; behind them are three equal gates, headed by the single gate of "Non-arising" (*anutpāda*). Only those who have realized the truth, such as Juefan, can pass through this.
I once examined the *Linjian Lu*, which cites this text and uses the analogy of public road earth versus private soil.
It was excavated to form an image. The wise person knew it was a road; the common, ignorant folk said the image had come into being.

Later, when an official wished to travel, he took the image back to fill the road. The image fundamentally neither arose nor perished, and the road likewise has no talk of new or old. As an ancient Buddha’s verse says:
"If it were not for Master Fan’s discerning eye of Dharma, which is perfectly clear, how could one know that the teacher of Piling [was the true one]?"
"Truly, he is an ancient Buddha returned to this world! Furthermore, Song Wen Lu Gong Yanbo was indeed a preeminent scholar of his time.
Having gone to Long’an Temple to hear a monk chant that gāthā, he attained realization and turned toward the Buddha.

He gathered one hundred thousand people for a Pure Land assembly and passed away peacefully while reciting the Buddha’s name at the end of his life; this is recorded in detail in the *Lianzong baojian*. As for Da..."
The lay practitioner Zhong Zhao of Mingtian Gu compiled the *Tianle Mingkong Ji* (Collection of Celestial Music Resounding in the Void). It further cites verses from ancient Buddhas, concluding with:

"The Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future point to the same thing: within the portion of sentient beings, amidst the phenomena of birth and death, everything is entirely the dharma of non-arising.
Why do you not awaken to this, yet instead willingly undergo birth and death? Furthermore, why do you wish to abandon birth and death and seek something else?"
Seeking non-arising only serves to further increase one's delusion and confusion. Thus, this text is not merely for a single school;

it is, in fact, a universal principle for the world at large. My two masters, the Venerable Congyi of Yongjia in Wenzhou and Chuyuan, were brothers in the Dharma who followed in the footsteps of Master Zhong.
While Congyi, with his divine wisdom, compiled the *Essentials* (*Zaoyao*) previously, Yuan served as the *Sengzheng* (Chief Monk).

The commentary on this [text] follows later. Both works enjoy their own excellence and have been widely circulated in the world. However, while their meanings are attached to provisional names, they originally arose from the desire to support the school.
Once the branches were divided, internal strife broke out, and a battle of pen and tongue ensued.
Nevertheless, this commentary has been transmitted throughout Japan (Fusang) for many years; it is considered a difficult text for the Tiantai school’s lecturers and scholars. For this reason—

The difficulties here were none other than those arising from the three instances where "crow" (wū), "bird" (niǎo), and "horse" (mǎ) were miswritten, and the single stroke of the character "field" (tián) being mistaken for "extend" (shēn).

Regarding these discrepancies, as I possess but meager talent, I have collated the text; I did not dare to lightly alter it in cases such as the omission of the month in the phrase "the fifth month of summer" (xià wǔ lòu yuè).
However, errors such as the famous corruption "three pigs crossing the river" (sān shǐ dù hé) have been corrected in their entirety before the work was sent to the printing blocks.
This book was begun by the editor, Cao Gu, on the eighth day of the fifth month of the summer in the year of Eteng Tuntan (1108) during the Chongning era of the Great Song.
He set down his pen on a day of rest in the second month of summer in the following year, Zhanmeng Zujiang (1119).
I, too, happened to begin the collation on the fifteenth day of the fifth month in the first year of the Hōei era (1704), the year of Jiashen, and completed it on that same date.
Now, on this day of the middle decade of the month of Gao in the year of Yiyou, we perform the ritual of pruning the mulberry trees; the years between now and then amount to six hundred and one.
The cycles of the Dharma turn in succession, and the branches and trunk are in perfect accord. Truly, the causal conditions of the Triple Gem are inconceivable.

Imperially Commissioned: A Commentary on the *Zhiguan yili* (Exemplification of the Meaning of Stopping and Contemplation), Written by the Śramaṇa Xiuyun within the Nianfo Temple at Dayuanshan in Shuzhou Pingyan, Based on the *Rongtong miaozong* (The Subtle Pivot of Comprehensive Integration). (Including Preface)
Preface by the Śramaṇa Chuyuan of Yongjia:
The Venerable Jingxi’s *Fuxingji* (Record of Aiding Practice) consists of several million words that explain the text of the *Zhiguan*; its clarity is like the bright sun.
Yet, he constantly feared that later students might not understand the Great Design; therefore, he has set forth its grand framework and grasped its essential pivot.

Essentials. A general outline of one section is presented here in seven categories, so that those who labor in study and practice may further clarify their subtle understanding and establish their sublime conduct;
this is the reason for composing these "Examples of Meaning.

Although such was the intention of the Holy Master, alas, the faculties of people in the final age are clouded and dull, and few are able to know the occasion or attain subtle penetration. This is all that remains.
Examining the text and Fuxing’s records, since they are already not fully clear, the establishment of these categories and examples is likewise applied in vain.
Without an explanation, by what means could the meaning be made manifest? In the past, the Great Master Fazhi of Siming flourished during his time and produced many compositions;
that these writings were not recorded was it not because his conditioned body did not survive long enough [to do so]?
Is this so? Since the Dharma-knowledge has already ceased, there have occasionally been those who have edited and revised the texts;

however, there has never been anyone who has provided an exegesis of this scripture. I have long harbored the aspiration for this task, but due to the necessity of directing the efforts of others in my preaching, I have not had the leisure to attend to it.
Recently, having retired from public life, I have considered taking up the pen beyond my daily devotions to fulfill my long-held ambition. It so happened that—
A fellow practitioner from our same school sent me from afar what he called the *Yili zuanyao* (Essential Compendium of Doctrinal Precedents), requesting that I evaluate its merits and flaws.

Thereupon, I incensed the burner, unrolled the scroll, and read it in detail; before long, I was so absorbed that I did not even realize the time had passed, and I sighed, saying: "Alas! Such a person!"
When interpreting and resolving the text through citations, one may occasionally achieve understanding;

yet, if one does not yet know the great purport of the text, it is like taking the realm of the dharma-nature's virtues in the Initial Vehicle as the realm for the true-thusness principle-observation of the Cultivated Virtue.

Regarding the contemplation of the reality of *vijñapti-mātra*, he pats his own chest in self-aggrandizement, claiming that few people understand it; since this is already mere delusion, what need is there to discuss others?
Furthermore, he breaks the syntax, misinterprets the text, and erroneously alters the characters—this will not be mentioned here, as it shall be seen in the subsequent passages.
Being of dull wit, I have nonetheless undertaken this explanation, and thus I have titled this work *A Commentary on the Examples of the Meaning of *Śamatha* and *Vipaśyanā*.
This work is essentially based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other commentaries on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

Among them, there are passages cited that coincide with those in the *Za* (Compendium); these cited passages are the writings of the Patriarchs, and the writings of the Patriarchs are the common property of the world.
How could it be that they may be cited by others while I am not permitted to use them? Please observe this.
The explanation of the meaning differs from that of the celestial realms.
On the eighth day of the fifth month in the summer of the third year of the Chongning era (Jia-shen) of the Great Song,
this preface to the *Zhiguan yili* was composed at Dongxi Caotang.
The commentary states: This title is abbreviated; in its full form, it should be *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā-yì-lì* (The Meaning and Examples of Great Calm and Insight).
According to the old edition, it should be called *Yuán-dùn-śamatha-vipaśyanā-yì-lì* (The Meaning and Examples of Perfect and Sudden Calm and Insight).

When Zhǎng'ān re-edited it, he removed the term "Perfect and Sudden" and added the designation "Great" (*mahā*). This is because the term *mahā* contains three meanings. Why? Because in the Sanskrit language...
*Mahā*. In the language of China, this means "Great," "Much," and "Supreme. Now, as for "Great": the wondrous virtue of *prajñā* (wisdom) pervades the entire dharma-realm;

it is ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). As for "Much": the wondrous virtue of liberation (*vimukti*) possesses all phenomena; it is inconceivable designation (*acintya-prajñapti*). As for "Supreme":
the wondrous virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is the nature of all phenomena; because it transcends the two extremes, it is the sublime middle (*madhyama*).
This is the Way. These three dharmas are distinguished as three, yet their essence is not three. To take one is to take all three; to take all three is to take one.

Neither three nor one, they are inconceivable. This name is used to head the terms "calm abiding" (śamatha) and "insight" (vipaśyanā), thereby revealing that whether it be calm abiding or insight, both fully possess these three.
Thus, there is a single calm abiding which is threefold calm abiding, and a single insight which is...

The three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) are none other than the secret treasury of the three virtues (*tridharma-guṇa*). Furthermore, one should understand that *śamatha* is not merely stillness and *vipaśyanā* is not merely insight;
although the names of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* differ, their essence is not distinct. Therefore, the two—*śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*—are non-dual.
*Śamatha* is designated as such to remedy the affliction of distraction, while *vipaśyanā* is designated as such to remedy the affliction of dullness. One should know that they are but one.

The *Three Thousand* [Verses] serves merely as a basis for *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. My ancestor, the Dharma Master Zhizhe, heard it from Lingluan, attained realization at Dasu, and expounded it at Yuquan;

this is precisely that dharma-gate of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Zhanran, the Master of Zhang’an, re-edited it and titled it *Mahā-*, in order to manifest the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) and for the convenience of the term *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
The former title, "Perfect and Sudden" (*yuan-dun*), was a general designation. (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. This translation reflects the portion available.)
Because [the teachings] from one, two, three, four, five, up to the immeasurable are all Perfect and Sudden, they do not compare to the *Mahā* which directly reveals the Three Dharmas;
therefore, it was revised. As for what is called the "principle of meaning" (*yili*), the single character "meaning" (*yi*) must not be explained lightly.

It encompasses the five summaries and contains the ten expansions; it includes the wondrous understanding and wondrous practice, the causes and fruits of one's own cultivation, the capacities for transforming others and being transformed by them, and even the ultimate convergence in the secret treasury of the three virtues—only then does the single character "meaning" (*yi*) reach its full significance.

The compiler merely states, "Meaning is the basis of *zhiguan* (calm abiding and insight)," but these words are vague and lack any definitive conclusion. One should know that this was not the intent of the Venerable Jingxi.

To clarify this meaning, I have established seven categories as a model. This enables contemporary practitioners to comprehend the five summaries, the ten expansions, and even the ultimate goal, thereby perfecting wondrous practice and attaining Buddhahood through it. How could such matters be spoken of lightly?
As for what is called a "model" (*li*), this refers to the method used in the *Spring and Autumn Annals* and the *Zuo Zhuan*. These commentaries possess both general models and major models.
Regarding the general principles and so forth: these seven rules in this text constitute the major rules. Liang Su’s *Tongli* (General Rules) constitutes the comprehensive rules.
Below this text, there are many such general principles; for instance, it says: "In listing chapter headings, there are those that correspond, those that open independently, and those that combine."
Regarding "examples" such as "opening and closing for others," the term *lì* (例) refers to categories or analogies.

Here, this entire treatise is organized into seven general categories (*lì*), and within these general categories, there are also many specific sub-examples. Therefore, the explanation of this title must not be undertaken hastily.
The Tiantai śramaṇa Zhànrán composed this commentary and explanation.
"Tiantai" is the name of a mountain; it was the place where he practiced the Way and composed his writings. It is also referred to as the land of Weisāng in Bīlíng.
"Śramaṇa" translates as "diligent and at rest. "Zhànrán" is the name of the Venerable Master. "Composed" (shù) means to write or compile.
The explanations are all as previously stated and will not be further detailed here.
First, the examples of the distinct divisions of the transmitted sections; second, the examples of the authentic teachings upon which they rely;
third, the examples for the exegesis of the text and its meaning; fourth, the examples of the general and specific categories within the major chapters.
The fifth is the example of resolving doubts regarding the mind and its objects; the sixth is the example of the mutual support of understanding and practice;
and the seventh is the example of using parables to resolve doubts and reveal the correct.
The commentary states: Taken collectively, throughout these seven examples, every section is intended to shatter deluded attachments.
They reveal correct principles, achieve sublime understanding, and establish sublime conduct; when distinguished individually, each has its own specific domain.

Therefore, it is said that the transmitted schools are distinct, ranging from "Resolving Doubts" (Yu-ji) to "Revealing the Correct" (Hsien-cheng). One shall see this for oneself upon entering the text.
Regarding the first point, the "examples of the specific lineages transmitted," the commentary states:

This marks the heading. As for the term "transmitted" (*suochuan*), it refers to that which has been passed down through a succession of teachers and disciples rather than being a product of arbitrary speculation;
hence, it is called "transmitted. The present text specifically refers to the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) transmitted by the Great Master Tiantai to Nanyue.
The Middle Way’s Perfect and Sudden [Teaching] is taken as that which is transmitted; it is neither gradual nor indeterminate, and thus is said to be a distinct division.
This collectively refers to one entire division as the great essence of the correct practice of the Perfect and Sudden Buddha Vehicle.

The commentary states: Jingxi’s intention was that he feared readers, upon seeing the teachings of gradual, indeterminate, sudden, and perfect within this section, would assume there were divergent paths.
Therefore, he specifically stated that the entire section as a whole is intended to show the great essence of the correct practice of the Perfect and Sudden Buddha Vehicle.
As for the "Perfect and Sudden Buddha Vehicle," it is the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation and manifestation of the three thousand [realms].
It is the true reality (*dharmatā*). Taking this as one’s practice constitutes correct practice; prior to its revelation, all partial and limited practices are erroneous practices.

Regarding the term "the great body": just as a person has hands, feet, and various limbs, yet the body itself is the great body, so too is the Perfect and Sudden teaching the great body, while the other two [teachings] are merely its limbs. The compiler [states]:...
The "General Outline" (Daigang) explains the general framework; it is loose with respect to the specific meaning.

Although the "General Meaning" (Daiyi) contains several instances at the beginning of the text where the three types of cessation-and-contemplation (san zhiguan) are mentioned as conclusions, these are merely casual references to names used to conclude sections of the argument;
they do not constitute the actual threefold aspects of practice.
The commentary states: This is an explanation intended to resolve a doubt. Fearing that one might suspect:

"If this entire section concerns only the correct practice of the Perfect and Sudden Buddha Vehicle, why are there three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* mentioned in the subsequent text? Therefore, it is explained as follows.

Although there are several instances throughout the initial sections on "Generating the Great Resolve" in the *Dàyìzhāng* where the three types of cessation-and-contemplation (*samatha-vipaśyanā*) are mentioned as concluding statements,

these merely borrow the names of the three cessations-and-contemplations in a general sense to conclude the passages on generating the resolve and so forth, thereby establishing the principle of the three cessations-and-contemplations.
It is not that being "not-as-it-is" constitutes the three types of practice; practitioners should know that even this is not yet the perfected and sudden (yuan-dun) mode of practice.

How much less so the other two? This is because the perfected and sudden mode of practice must fully possess twenty-five factors as its expedient means (*upāya*), for it is only when the characteristics of the cultivation and manifestation of the ten objects and ten vehicles are complete that it is established. Regarding the "number and locations," starting from three...
From the above up to the ninth, all are termed "numbers. The term "fanyer" (汎爾) means "flood-like" or "pervasive" in its general application;

"er" (爾) is a particle. The phrase "not for the sake of" (非為) means "it is not. Master Jingxi’s intention was that these names are borrowed for the sake of general application merely to establish the meaning;
they do not themselves constitute three distinct modes of practice. The compiler points to this as the literal character [of the term].
This is an error. It should instead say "it is not meant to be" (*fei wei*). This is a mistaken emendation. However, it is not only the compiler who considers this an error;

among those who have lectured on this from of old, all those of shallow understanding who fail to properly investigate the underlying principle are likewise so inclined. This is not a new interpretation.

Because the *Dàyì* (Great Meaning) is concise in its phrasing yet expansive in its intent, it employs the "three" and "one" to summarize and condense [the teachings]. One should know that within this section, the intent lies solely in the Sudden (*dùn*).
The commentary states: This passage explains the purpose for employing the three types of cessation-and-contemplation (*zhǐguān*) as used in the "Chapter on Great Meaning. Why are they employed?

The three [sections on] cessation and contemplation conclude the section on the heterodox. By opening the "Chapter on the Great Meaning" (*Dàyì zhāng*) into five summaries (*wǔlüè*), one chapter contains five summaries;

thus, while the text is concise, its meaning is extensive. This is because these five summaries encompass both the causes and fruits of one’s own practice (*zìxíng*) as well as the capacity and object of transforming others (*huàtā*).

All return to the Great Place, subsuming the nine extensive sections below. Because the causes and fruits of one’s own practice and the capacities and objects of transforming others all return to the secret treasury, the meaning is broad.

Master Tiantai feared that readers, in pursuing the various textual features such as the arousal of the mind and great practices, might have many divergent mental conditions and lose their original intent; therefore, he used the "Three and One" to bring them together.
Summary. Although these three are employed, they are merely general; the primary intent of this school lies solely in the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun).
Regarding the "three and one": the "three" refers to the gradual, the indeterminate, and the perfect and sudden; the "one" encompasses the meaning of all three.

One should know that "one" is the universal (tong), while "three" is the particular (bie); it is not that there are separate dharmas apart from this. There are those among the disciples of Jingxi who hold deviant views.
The commentator did not comprehend this meaning and thus claimed that beyond the three [gradual stages], there is yet another "sudden-sudden" single contemplation;

consequently, he referred to the Perfect Sudden as the "Gradual-Sudden" contemplation. This erroneous analogy and its underlying doubts will be clearly refuted in the following text, where the reader shall see for themselves.

As for the phrase "numerous passages," it refers to the fact that within the sections on "arousing the great mind" and "cultivating the great practice," there are respectively numerous textual instances. Arising...
In the mind, he says: "The arousal of the bodhicitta is precisely contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); the cessation of deviant thoughts is precisely tranquility (*śamatha*).

This concludes with a single application of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Furthermore, it is revealed that within this context, regarding the arousal of the mind according to the Four Noble Truths, he says:

"Since what has been explained above is extensive, I shall now conclude by means of the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Moreover, within the Four Great Vows, it says: "If one understands this mind, one may [proceed] at will..."
It leads to the attainment of śamatha and vipaśyanā. That which is without arising and without obstruction is *vipaśyanā*;

that whose nature is quiescent extinction is *śamatha*. This also constitutes the synthesis of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Furthermore, within the fourth samādhi of the Great Practice (*mahācaryā*), there are four sections:
first, regarding all sūtras; second, regarding all wholesome states; third, regarding all unwholesome states; and fourth, regarding all neutral (*avyākṛta*) states. This...
After the four sections, he concludes with the three types of *samatha-vipaśyanā*, stating:

"Furthermore, if one clarifies 'following one's own mind' (*sujanyasvamanasikāra*) based solely on the final [stage], this is the meaning of the gradual approach. 'The final good' refers to the successive comparison up to the Buddha-realm;
this is the conclusion of the gradual process. Moreover, it is said: if both good and evil are clearly understood as following one's own mind, this is the meaning of the sudden approach."

This concludes the section on the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun). Furthermore, it is said: "If one examines the 'folding and unfolding' (zhedie) of the wholesome [practices] according to the 'following one's own mind,' this refers to the 'indeterminate mind.

This employs the indeterminate *śamatha-vipaśyanā* as its conclusion. As for the term "folding and unfolding," it simply means that the former two [methods] use the gradual to trigger the sudden, and the sudden to trigger the gradual;
hence it is called "folding and unfolding. Although the original text contains much more, I have cited only this briefly.

Therefore, the preface states: "The general purport lies in the Single Instant (yùndùn). Since the concise must crown the extensive, they cannot be differentiated. Furthermore, it indicates the intermediate position, stating:
"As for the texts on the Perfect and Sudden (yuándùn), they are as recorded at Yùquán Temple."

The commentary states: This is a citation of scriptural evidence. Its meaning is as follows: Among the ten major chapters, the chapter on the "General Meaning" (Dà-yì) consists of five brief sections followed by nine extensive ones.
Although three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) are employed within the General Meaning, the intent lies solely in the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) approach.

This is because the general encompasses the particular, and the brief encompasses the extensive; they must not be treated as distinct or divergent. As for the phrase "indicating the locus," it refers to...

The "Wen" (Text) refers to the written portion. In the *Preface to the Zhi Guan* by Zhizhe of Zhang’an, it is stated: "The *Cidi Chanmen* (Gradual Gate of Dhyāna) originally comprised thirty fascicles;
today, ten fascicles have been compiled into a formal text. This was privately recorded by Fa Shen as the *Liun Miaomen Chan* (Six Wondrous Gates of Dhyāna).

It involves traversing the twelve dhyānas with an undetermined mind, namely the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and various other dharma-gates such as the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). [This was] during the Chen dynasty... [text fragment ends].
This is the one requested by the Secretariat Director Mao Xi for the Great Master to deliver.

As for the "Text on the Perfect and Sudden," it was expounded at Yǔquán Monastery in Jīngzhōu on the twenty-sixth day of the fourth month of the fourteenth year of the Kāihuáng era of the Great Suí dynasty.

This is what Zhāng'ān himself stated regarding his own record. Since it is called the "Text on the Perfect and Sudden" and was recorded at Yǔquán, we know that this section is exclusively [the teaching] of...
Regarding the "Perfect and Sudden" (yuantun): as for those teachers of biased interpretations who claim it is "gradual-perfect," although the subsequent text mentions the four teachings,
the eight teachings, the conceivable and inconceivable, and the mutually dependent and absolutely independent,
all are intended to reveal the single reality of the Perfect and Sudden.
The commentary states: "The subsequent text" refers to the sections following the introduction. Both the introduction and the main exposition are perfect and sudden (*yuantun*).
Although they involve conceptual thought and relative distinctions, they all serve to lead toward the inconceivable and the absolute non-relation.
If one encounters words in the text concerning relative distinctions and the like, one must not immediately conclude that these constitute gradual or partial contemplation.
Therefore, in the text of the Great Vehicle, concepts such as "the conceivable" and "the relative" serve as the attendants;
the wondrous principle of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) serves as the body of the chariot; untainted sublime contemplation serves as the white ox; and all other dharmas are the ornaments.

The commentary states: The purpose of citing this passage is to demonstrate that the *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Great Calming and Contemplation) is indeed the peerless and exquisite calming and contemplation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which reveals the ultimate reality by opening up the provisional teachings. How could there be a Perfect and Sudden teaching superior to this?

Why, then, do those with biased interpretations claim it to be "gradual-perfect," and separately establish the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*—which they claim combines the distinct and the universal—as the "Sudden-of-the-Sudden" contemplation, asserting that [the *Lotus Sūtra*] refers to the "great vehicle"?
Regarding the "textual passages": each of the ten objects (*daśa-viṣaya*) employs the ten stages of practice (*daśa-yāna*).

At the conclusion of each section on the ten stages, the *Lotus Sūtra*’s parable of the great vehicle (*mahā-yāna*) is cited as proof. The passage concerning the first object, the realm of the aggregates (*skandha*), is the most detailed.

However, the citations and correspondences do not exceed the textual phrases of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Fuxingji* (Sub-commentary). I shall now cite them in full. The *Fuxingji* states: "As for that vehicle..."
Its height and breadth constitute the inconceivable realm. The canopy and parasol, with their precious cords of compassion interlaced, represent the arousal of the bodhicitta.

The placement of the vermilion pillow—with its inner and outer aspects—is as follows: if it is the pillow within the carriage, it represents resting all practices, which is the stage of settling the mind (*anxin*).
If it is the pillow outside the carriage, it represents movement or stillness; movement and stillness are simply the meanings of penetration and obstruction. Its...

Swift as the wind, it immediately shatters ignorance; this refers to the meaning of "shattering" (the *pāramitās*). Beginning with the white ox and ending with levelness and correctness, these refer to the meaning of the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*).
Furthermore, having many attendants refers to the primary and auxiliary practices. Traveling in the four directions refers to the successive stages (*bhūmi*).
Patience and detachment occur at the beginning of these successive stages; patience here simply means enduring the five grades of practice.

The two types of objects—those favorable and those adverse—are made to enter the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). "Detaching from craving" refers specifically to detaching from the craving for phenomena that resemble [the true nature] within these six sense faculties.
Furthermore, as for the "stages and positions," these are merely the steps traversed by practice.

Fearing that practitioners might give rise to confusion, the five grades within the stages and positions are separately set forth as the "purity of the six sense faculties" (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*) to encourage practitioners to detach from hindrances and from craving.
Therefore, we know that the first seven [factors] clearly elucidate the body of the vehicle and its equipment; the latter three are merely what the vehicle traverses.
If there were nothing to traverse, the meaning of "transportation" would not be established. For this reason, these ten factors are collectively termed the Mahāyāna. (Full text)
To say that the wondrous principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) constitutes the body of the chariot refers to the initial vehicle’s contemplation of the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*).
To take the pure, untainted (*anāsrava*) wondrous contemplation as the white oxen refers to the cultivation of the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).

To regard conceptual thought and its counterparts as the servants and attendants refers to the remedial aids for opening [the way]. That all other dharmas are the ornaments means the arousal of the bodhi-mind.
One must focus the mind skillfully to settle it in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, thereby discerning where the path is open and where it is obstructed.

Although the correspondence of the meaning to the text is thus, those who employ *vipaśyanā* skillfully will, in each and every vehicle, fully realize the ten directions as the attainment of the essential principle. Question:

Generally, when citing evidence, one must rely upon the Buddha’s sūtras and various treatises (*śāstra*) in order to engender faith. Why is it that the citations in the present text do not [follow this convention]?
If you merely cite the preface and the main body of the *Zhiguan* as proof for this text, how can it inspire faith in people?
I reply: Generally, there are two types of discourse. The first is when debating with other schools;
in such cases, one must cite the Buddha’s words and the treatises. This is like the *Jingangbei*, which was composed in response to the Xianshou school.
I shall merely cite texts such as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. For now, I will discuss this solely within the framework of our own school and therefore will not cite other sources.
Why? Because the perverse interpretations of biased masters are themselves heterodox;

even those disciples of Jingxi who have long been refined by his teachings would not dare to contradict their own school, let alone [contradict] the Holy Master Zhiyi, who personally heard and personally realized the truth. Thus, I shall proceed according to what was heard...
He practiced; he realized according to what he practiced; he taught according to what he realized. How could one not believe in such magnificent and flourishing transformation?
Therefore, I have cited only the texts he heard as authentic evidence.
Therefore, it is known that this treatise has no other underlying intent.
The commentary states: This is a summary. It refers to the single work, the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation), with its five brief sections and ten extensive sections.
From beginning to end, there is nothing that is not the correct practice of the Perfect and Sudden Buddha Vehicle; beyond this, there is no other intention. This...

○ Second, regarding the examples of the authoritative teachings upon which [this treatise] relies:

the commentary states, "This is the heading. It establishes the basis relied upon (*āśraya*) in order to manifest that which relies upon it (*āśrita*). That which relies upon it consists of the five...

The *Brief* and the *Extensive* are the wondrous *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Their basis consists of the two sutras that reveal the provisional to disclose the real and discuss the eternal while supporting the Vinaya;
these two must be mutually dependent to be called the True Teaching. In the final age, anything other than this is the false teaching.
This serves as one such example.
The various passages cited span an entire lifetime of the Buddha’s teaching; however, the formal style and core intent are centered solely upon two sutras:

first, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which reveals the ultimate reality through the concepts of origin and trace; and second, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, which supports the Vinaya rules to reveal the eternal. This is because these two sutras are both identical to the "ghee" (the highest stage of the five flavors).
The commentary states: This specifically refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* alone regarding śamatha and vipaśyanā.
As for the statement that "scattered citations draw from various texts," this does not mean a process of critical examination, deliberation, or quotation.

Rather, it is our patriarch, the holy master Zhiyi, who has wondrously realized the very source of the Buddhas' transformative guidance; whether expanded or condensed, it resides solely within a single thought-moment. [He] ascended the high seat...
At that time, with a mind of compassion and unimpeded eloquence, he expounded this *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Spontaneously, it perfectly accorded with the Buddha’s five periods and eight teachings, as well as the provisional and ultimate, the partial and the complete, of both the *Hīnayāna* and *Mahāyāna*. Therefore, it is called "scattered citations.
This is unlike the writings of worldly teachers, who, at the time of composition, search through sūtras and śāstras to extract evidence and wield their pens [with laborious effort].
As I approach the paper, my pen moves with a creaking sound as if being drawn out; this serves as a prelude. The term "comprehensive" (*gai*) means to encompass or to interrelate.

"One generation" (*ichidai*) refers to the period beginning from the attainment of the Way until its culmination in *nirvāṇa*; since the affairs of this single cycle are completed, it is called "one generation."

The phrase "the successor offers renewed thanks" refers to the formal expression of gratitude. Regarding the statement that the literary style embodies the correct meaning: this points to the text of the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) as its primary substance;
thus, it is called the "correct body. It exclusively returns to the two sutras of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.

As for the *Lotus Sutra*, it reveals the reality of the three thousand realms within the provisional and ultimate aspects. As for the *Nirvana Sutra*, it emphasizes the application of the precepts and regulations to support and manifest the eternal nature.
This is merely an explanation of the introductory text; it shall be explained again in the subsequent sections.

Thus, the explanation of the names involves the contrast between the provisional and the ultimate, and so on, up to the section on the partial and the perfect, where the three analogies of the lotus are fully cited.

Explanation of the Names: The "Fourfold Unity" of Guangzhai reveals that the essence possesses its functions. That is to say, the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) serves as the primary essence of practice;
moreover, all ten stages of the contemplations regarding various objects take the great vehicle (*mahāyāna*) as their metaphor.

The commentary states: Since the preceding text specified that one should take refuge in only two sutras—the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa*—this current passage first explains the meaning of taking refuge in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* alone.

Thus, in the first chapter, "Explanation of Names," of the ten chapters of the *Mohe Zhiguan*, the names "Cessation" (*śamatha*) and "Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) are explained by means of the two subtleties of the relative and the absolute.
Therefore, it is known that these are precisely the cessation and contemplation that "reveal the real by opening the provisional."

How can such a biased interpretation claim that [the teachings] are "gradually perfected"? In the section on the "Partial and Perfect," the text already cites the three analogies of the lotus to explain the names of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Among all the temporal teachings of a single lifetime, only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* uniquely employs the analogy of the lotus; thus it says: "For the sake of the lotus, there is the flower;
when the flower opens, the lotus appears; when the flower falls, the lotus is formed. This serves as a metaphor for the original purpose of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world.

The provisional is established by means of the real; the provisional is opened to reveal the real; and the provisional is discarded to establish the real. Thus, one knows that there is nothing more sublime than *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Regarding the manifestation of the essence and the inclusion of function—the fourfold "oneness" of Guangzhai: "one" refers to the path of the single reality, which is the three thousandfold real marks (*trisahasra-lakṣaṇa*).
This means that the three thousandfold real marks of the *Lotus Sūtra* constitute the primary essence of practice. How much more so for all other [teachings]!

Regarding the fact that all ten vehicles within the "Ten Objects" (*daśaviṣaya*) are metaphorically likened to a great carriage (*mahāyāna*): this great carriage is an analogy for the ten vehicles of contemplative methods (*daśayāna-dhyāna-dharma*) explained in the *Dharmaparyāya*.
This constitutes the essential meaning of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation) text, which ultimately returns to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Having thus concluded the direct exposition of the textual meaning, I shall next re-cite the text to provide a detailed commentary. Within the second of the ten major chapters, the names of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are explained.
There are four sections: first, the relative; second, the absolute; third, the reconciliation of differences; and fourth, the integration with the three virtues.

Therefore, it is said that the *Shiming* (Discourse on the Explanation of Names) discusses the relative and the absolute. Thus, one knows that *śamatha-vipaśyanā* is the most sublime practice of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Regarding the statement that the names are explained through the three analogies of the lotus found within the sections on the partial and the perfect, this itself consists of five parts.
First, the Great and the Small; second, the Half and the Full; third, the Partial and the Perfect; fourth, the Gradual and the Sudden; fifth, the Provisional and the Real.

Within the category of the Provisional and the Real, the provisional is briefly established with three meanings: first, establishing the provisional for the sake of the real; second, opening the provisional to reveal the real; and third, abolishing the provisional to establish the real.
These correspond to the three analogies of the lotus in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, whereby all Buddhas [act] through this single great matter.

The world-transcending [teaching] originally establishes one true *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) while applying three provisional *śamatha-vipaśyanās*. The provisional is not the primary intent, yet that intent does not lie outside the provisional.
It merely unfolds the three provisional *śamatha-vipaśyanās* to reveal the perfect and sudden one true *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, and so forth;
thus it is said, "the three analogies of the lotus. As for the phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*), the sequence should necessarily involve the mutual inclusion of essence and characteristics.
Regarding the term "Dharma" (法): because it transcends these two categories, the phrase "up to and including" (乃至) is used.

As for the statement "revealing that the essence possesses function, as in the four [meanings] of Guangzhai," this refers back to the third section on the characteristics of the essence (體相). This itself constitutes four parts: first, the characteristics of the teaching (教相); second, the eye and wisdom (眼智).
Third, the objects; fourth, gain and loss. These four are identical in meaning to the four "onenesses. The teaching and its characteristics are one;
the eye, wisdom, and practice are one; the object and principle are one; and gain and loss, and the person, are one.

The reason for citing these four onenesses is to reveal that this *śamatha-vipaśyanā* takes the opening of the provisional and the realization of the true aspect as its essence. According to Guangzhai...
The Master explains the passages on "opening and revealing" (*kaixian*) within the *Lotus Sūtra* by employing the principle of the "Fourfold Identity" (*sishi*).

Since he previously employed the three metaphors of the lotus in his explanation of the title, he now employs the "Fourfold Identity" once again in the passage concerning the essence and characteristics to reveal the essence itself.

Thus, whether regarding the name or the essence, there is nothing that is not the peerless and wondrous *śamatha-vipaśyanā* of the *Lotus Sūtra*. As for what is called "one": the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) stands alone, capable of being one with each and every thing.
Therefore, it is said that they are "one. The designation of the "Four Ones" (sì yī) originally originated with Guǎngzhái. Tiantái harmonized with the old tradition and also employed the Four Ones.
Although the number four is the same, their meanings differ greatly. Guǎngzhái established the One Result, the One Cause, the One Teaching, and the One Person.
Tiantái abolished the term "One Result" and established the "One Principle" (lǐ yī). If there were no principle, then all phenomena...
Without a fundamental basis, it is identical to the work of Māra. Guangzhai established "One Cause," while Tiantai rejected that and established "One Practice.

The discourse on "Cause" is singular and shallow, failing to encompass the "Result"; Tiantai specifically established "One Practice," the meaning of which is profound, because he takes the beginning of practice as the cause and its culmination as the result.
Regarding "One Teaching" and "One Person," their names are the same as those of the old [tradition]. Guangzhai...
Since [you] take the Lotus Sūtra as the convergence of all myriad virtues yet do not speak of the Buddha-nature’s permanence,
your interpretation stands worlds apart from that of Tiantai’s "Fourfold Identity."
Therefore, at the conclusion of the "Arising" chapter, there is a general eulogy which states: "Sought with diligent effort throughout accumulated kalpas, realized at the site of enlightenment;
Śāriputra’s three requests and the threefold teaching through both Dharma and parables—this is precisely what is contained herein."
The commentary states: This passage cites the Buddha’s causes and effects, as well as the praise of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which is supreme and unsurpassed.

"Diligently seeking through accumulated kalpas" refers to the cause of this *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. "Realizing at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)" refers to the fruit of this *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

"Śāriputra’s three requests" refers to the request for this *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. [This concludes] the section on the three cycles of teaching consisting of the Dharma, the Parable, and the Causes and Conditions.
It is said: "To speak of this śamatha and vipaśyanā—this is precisely what is meant by 'it lies herein. This refers to the perfectly sudden, most sublime śamatha and vipaśyanā.
How can one hold a biased interpretation and claim it is gradual? Regarding the phrase 'at the beginning of the text on the ten stages of generating the practice':

within the initial section of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* on the entry into the contemplation of the aggregates (*skandha*), there are two parts: first, the Dharma; second, the analogy. The analogy cites the great chariot. First, the Dharma..."

Within this, there are six sections: first, the listing of the ten dharmas; second, the origination; third, the citation of analogies; fourth, the praise; fifth, the detailed explanation; and sixth, the summary conclusion.
Although the text of the praise occurs after the citation of analogies, it is referred to as being at the end of the section on origination for two reasons:
first, because they are adjacent; and second, because the praise is fundamentally a praise of the ten dharmas, and therefore it is simply called "origination."
This is at the end of the text. Regarding the statement that one has diligently sought [the Way] through accumulated kalpas, there are both near and distant referents.

"Near" refers to the Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Buddha; "distant" refers to the time when he was practicing the bodhisattva path. As for the realization at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), there too are near and distant referents.
"Distant" refers to his attaining Buddhahood in the original Sahā world; "near" refers to today’s site of the nirvana. Since *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are what the Wise One (Zhiyi) taught...
Regarding the practice, it is appropriate that the praise accord with both the fundamental (hon) and the phenomenal (jaku).
Thus we know that the four kinds of samādhi all rely upon the true aspect (shinjitsu-sō). The true aspect is the dharma of peace and bliss;

the four conditions are the practice of peace and bliss. Having realized the true aspect, what is obtained through reliance on names is called the "great fruit. The arising of the teachings is merely...
To cause sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter [the truth], the ultimate goal is simply to return to the wondrous Dharma and secret treasury of the three tracks;
therefore, from beginning to end, everything relies upon the Lotus Sūtra.

The commentary states: In the preceding passage, the ten stages (*daśayāna*) were praised as being based on the sublime *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, using the Buddha’s causes and effects as well as Śāriputra’s request as examples.
Now, it is clarified that the four kinds of samādhi all rely upon the true reality (*dharmatā*), and all cultivate the ten stages to be able to achieve the fruit of Buddhahood;
this explains how cultivating the cause leads to the attainment of the fruit. The phrase "this is known" is a connective term linking what precedes with what follows.
The meaning is that one deduces from the Buddha’s diligent seeking and realization that these four kinds of samādhi can all be cultivated to attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

Regarding the "four kinds of samādhi," these apply generally to the four teachings (*catur-yāna*), but here they specifically refer to the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*) and do not extend to the others.

The "constant walking" (*caṅkrama*) is based on the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra*’s practice of standing while contemplating the Buddha; the "constant sitting" (*niṣadyā*) is based on what was taught by Mañjuśrī.

Question: Regarding the contemplation of the three paths: the "half-walking, half-sitting" practice involves reciting sutras and maintaining mantras according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the Vaipulya [sūtras];

the "neither-walking-nor-sitting" practice involves examining good, evil, and neutral states according to the *Caturvidha-karma-viniścaya* (The Examination of the Four Kinds of Karma). Although these four practices differ, there is no distinction in their true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, it is said that they all rely upon the true reality. Nevertheless, one should understand that although the text mentions them collectively, [the distinctions remain].
Regarding the four kinds of samādhi, the intent of the present text is simply to establish the wondrous practice of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Question:

In the present *Mohe zhiguan*, the ten vehicles and ten objects begin with the contemplation of the aggregates and sense bases (*skandha-āyatana*), which relies exclusively on the constant sitting posture for a period of ninety days.
How can this be identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* samādhi? Answer: There are two points to consider. First, according to the [opening of the]...
Because it reveals [the truth], there is no dharma that is not the Lotus Sūtra.

Second, the Great Master Tiantai employed the wondrous essence of the three thousand realms (*sanqian miaoti*)—which opens up the provisional to reveal the real—within the practice of constant sitting (*changzuo*). Thus, he caused constant sitting to become the practice of the Lotus Sūtra.

It is like a sage king who governs all under heaven; wherever he goes, there is none who does not regard him as supreme, and none who does not acknowledge him as their lord. Take this as a proximate analogy.
This may be compared to resolving a doubt. To say that the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the dharma of peace and bliss:
the term "true aspect" necessarily encompasses the three truths. Thus, the *Anantamukha-sādhaka-nirdeśa Sūtra* states: "To speak of the true aspect is to speak of signlessness (*animitta*).
It is without the signs of birth-and-death, and without the signs of nirvāṇa. Even 'signlessness' is non-existent; therefore it is called signless. It is without arising.
Death is the absence of marks (*animitta*). If there were no nirvāṇa, there would be no absence of marks. To negate both extremes simultaneously is the Middle Way.
That even the absence of marks is absent is also the Middle Way. To illuminate both extremes simultaneously is the absence of a middle way.
The perfect fusion of these three is the Secret Treasury; it is called Great Nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is said to be the Dharma of peace and bliss. [In] Sanskrit...
Nirvana; this translates as "peaceful bliss" (*an-akuśala*). This dharma of peaceful bliss is the sublime principle that is the object of contemplation.
The four conditions are the practices for attaining peaceful bliss; these are the sublime practices that constitute the subject of contemplation.
Beginning from the initial stage of the "name," one diligently cultivates them until one enters the five ranks and the six faculties—all of which are practices for attaining peaceful bliss. This...

Through the perfection of practice, one enters the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), which is called "realizing the true mark" (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*). Having realized the true mark, one partially attains the three bodies (*trikāya*); this is the transformation of the primary retribution (*vipāka*).
The supporting environment (*niśraya-vipāka*) thus obtained—the land of true retribution—is also termed the "great fruit. Body and land are non-dual, and both are called the great fruit.
This is explained in terms of receiving retribution through the *dharma-body* (*dharmakāya*); it does not refer to the birth-body (*janmakāya*) attaining patience (*kṣānti*).
It is also the Bodhisattva. Therefore, the five summaries are called the "Great Fruit," and the great chapters are called the "Fruit.
Having completed the great fruit of retribution, there must necessarily be the capacity of those who can strike the responsive trigger;

in response, the teachings of the five periods arise, even to the point of enabling sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The five summaries are called "Tearing the Net," and the great chapters are called...

The purpose of initiating this teaching is that both self-cultivation and the transformation of others ultimately converge in the Secret Treasury; thus it is said, "they all return to the three tracks," and so forth.
The five summaries are called the "Great Sections," and the Great Chapters are called the "Ultimate Return. From beginning to end, everything is none other than the Lotus Sūtra.
How can one hold such a biased interpretation as to claim it is merely a gradual and incomplete contemplation? Is this not to suppress and belittle the Dharma?
Is this not the teaching that transcends the eight [vehicles]?
This is precisely the wondrous practice of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
The commentary states: This concludes that the entire treatise on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* ultimately converges upon the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as its sole reliance. It says:

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* refers to ascending to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). As for "wondrous practice" (*miaoxing*), it refers to the five grades of the name-stage (*mingzi*) and the ten stages of faith (*shixin*).
The intent of this entire treatise is solely to guide the practitioner into the "Pool of Coolness," which is the first stage;
from this point onward, it is not that one does not cultivate contemplation, but rather that once this level is reached, one flows into it spontaneously and no further effort is required.
Thus it is said.

Next, regarding the application of *nirvāṇa*: although all [teachings] rely on the *Lotus Sūtra* and ultimately converge upon the single reality (*eka-tattva*), the faculties of beings in the final age are dull;
if they lack assistance, their correct practice will collapse. Only when the primary and auxiliary practices are combined can one proceed far along the path.
The commentary states: This clarifies that this entire treatise on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* ultimately relies upon the intent of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Although it accords with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in its universal return to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), the defilements in this land are turbid and evil, the spiritual faculties of beings are dull and obscured, and their views and afflictions are heavy.
Having heard the words from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that reveal the reality, they immediately claim that everything is nothing other than the true path.
They ask: "What is there of observing the precepts or violating them? What is there of good paths or evil paths?

Upon seeing those who observe the precepts, they point at them and laugh, regarding them as followers of the Hīnayāna; yet upon seeing those who violate the precepts, they honor and revere them, regarding them as having attained the highest realization. Thus they fall into ruin.
Regarding the Dharma-body: if one loses the life of wisdom, and if one does not rely upon the Vinaya, one will lose even the bodies of humans and devas;
how then can the unsurpassed path of the Buddha be expected? Therefore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the bestowal of the precepts is emphasized without the slightest laxity;

their utility in providing support is of the greatest merit. Thus, these two sūtras share the same flavor. Furthermore, it should be understood that this is for the purpose of accomplishing contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
One should simply adopt the common points. Since they are explained in the *Wenju ji* (Record of Textual Phrases), they are analyzed in detail.

Although there are sixteen phrases that differ from the *Lotus Sūtra*, one must understand their respective applications and orientations; one must not use those [differences] to obstruct this present text.
If even the Buddha’s transformation-body takes *nirvāṇa* as its life-span, how much more so for those practicing in the final age, who cannot advance without assistance?
Therefore, by upholding the Vinaya and proclaiming the permanence [of the Buddha], one reveals the true mark (*dharmatā*). One should attribute this merit to that [upholding of the Vinaya].
The commentary states: This passage uses an analogy to clarify the purpose of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Even while the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, was in the world, amidst those gathered for the grand assembly of his flourishing transformation, there were still those who clung to reality and were deluded regarding skillful means. Therefore, as he approached the end of his life, he once again bestowed the precepts to rescue their lives of wisdom;
thus it is said, "for the sake of longevity. How much more so after his parinirvāṇa, when the faculties of sentient beings have become increasingly dull?
Seeing that [the teachings] were flourishing, if one did not employ auxiliary means, how could the single true Way be practiced?
Therefore, he correctly utilized the Lotus Sūtra, intending to demonstrate that the two sūtras—the Perfect and the Constant—are equal.
The commentary states: Since it is said that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is used as the primary [teaching], we know that the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* is used as a secondary support for the path.
If the support were itself the primary path, how could there be a distinction between the secondary and the primary? This is explained from the perspective of those with dull faculties;

for those who employ the supporting teachings, there is the matter of supplementing the secondary with the primary. That "the two sūtras are equal" means they are simultaneous and of the same flavor. This...
This section concludes the entire treatise on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Its literary form and primary intent both ultimately return to the two sutras.
○ Regarding the third point, the "Method for Explaining the Text and Meaning," the commentary states:
"Text" refers to the expressive words of the entire treatise on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. "Meaning" refers to that which is expressed by those words.

This is why it is so. It refers to the meaning of the five summaries, the ten expansions, the ten objects, and the ten vehicles. In this context, the two characters "text" (wen) and "meaning" (yi) are that which is explained (*so-shih*).
The three characters "to dissolve and explain by way of analogy" (*hsiao-shih li zhi*) are that which explains (*neng-shih*).

As for "dissolving and explaining" (*hsiao-shih*), it is like the sun melting ice until it dissolves and disperses; hence, it is called "dissolving and explaining. "By way of analogy" (*li*) has already been explained above.

Furthermore, it is divided into two parts: first, a detailed investigation of the meaning of the text; second, an elucidation of its structural form. The first part [of the first division] is further divided into two:
first, a detailed investigation of the meaning of the text; second, a detailed investigation of the textual characteristics.
The commentary states: Regarding "thorough investigation" (*parīkṣā*): "thorough" (*pari*) means the sense of being meticulous and detailed;
"investigation" (*īkṣā*) means the sense of probing to the root and exploring to the limit. As for "structural form" (*śarīra*): each section of a text has its own structural form.
Although they all ultimately converge upon the perfect reality (*pariniṣpanna*), the various passages cited therein each possess their own structural form, such as when citing texts of the Hīnayāna.
Their essential nature and manifestation naturally belong to the Small Vehicle; this can be understood by applying it to the examples of the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect [vehicles].
As for examining the textual characteristics in detail, each section of the text also possesses its own specific features; one should investigate them thoroughly.

The first consists of ten examples. First is the citation of evidence regarding the universal and the specific. For instance, when citing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to demonstrate that there is only one reality (*ekayāna*), the text describes the former teachings as that which is to be opened up;
thus, the passages within that section contain both the provisional and the real. If the evidence were restricted to the single reality, one would cite only the passages concerning the real;
if the evidence were intended to be universal regarding the skillful means (*upāya*), one would cite the former meanings alongside them. This is as in the citation from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
"Gradual" and "indeterminate. The same applies to the scope of the four flavors of texts cited and the various sections [of the *Mohe zhiguan*].

The commentary states: These examples are drawn from the Preface; Zhiyi cites evidence for the three types of cessation-and-contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) and, within a single section, cites evidence that is both universal and restricted.
"Universal" means being without fixed direction and unobstructed; "restricted" means being confined and definitively fixed.
Regarding the statement, "The words 'like a guide,' 'the *Lotus Sūtra* section,' 'the sole reality,' and so forth":
if one does not describe the coarseness of the past [teachings], how can one manifest the subtlety of this present sūtra? Therefore, the Chapter on the Five Buddhas states:
"The Buddhas of the past, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and expressions, have expounded all dharmas; these dharmas are all for..."
Because there is but the One Buddha Vehicle. This first recounts the former coarseness and subsequently reveals the sublime. This applies to all five Buddhas;
therefore, within these sections, there are both the provisional and the real. Regarding the statement that citing the texts of the Real leads to the realization of the One Reality, the Sūtra says:
"Directly abandoning the provisional means and teaching only the unsurpassed Way" refers to this.

If one says that "proving the provisional means" also involves citing the meaning of the past [teachings], this serves as proof for the gradual and the indeterminate [vehicles]. Regarding the proof of the gradual vehicle, the scripture states:
"Such persons should enter the Buddha’s wisdom through this Dharma gradually. Jingxi said: "Since these are not people taught by the *Avataṃsaka* school, nor..."

All teachings that enter [the path] suddenly originate from the Deer Park; because they subsequently traverse the two flavors in between, they are called "gradual. The *Aniyata-sūtra* (Scripture on the Indefinite) provides scriptural evidence, stating:
"If there are sentient beings who do not believe or accept [this teaching], one should instruct, benefit, and gladden them with other profound dharmas of the Tathāgata.
This means that those who do not believe or accept—that is, those who do not believe in the Perfect and Sudden—should for the time being be transformed through other profound dharmas.

The Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is profound and not otherwise; the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings (Zang and Tong) are otherwise and not profound. Because the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) is sequential, it belongs to the "otherwise" category;
yet because it speaks of the Middle Way, it is profound. Since it is either "otherwise" or "profound," the realization [of the fruit] is indeterminate.

As for the statement that the texts and divisions cited from the four flavors (*catasro rasāḥ*) regarding their scope and limitation are likewise so: for instance, citing the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as the "milk flavor," if the scope is limited, it serves as a proof...
The sudden [teaching] penetrates all three; the "milk" flavor at the Deer Park, the "two butters" of the Vaipulya and Prajñā, and the "curd" [of the Nirvāṇa Sūtra].

If one restricts the perspective, the realization [of the sudden teaching] penetrates all three, for these three flavors are all teachings of gradual progression. Therefore, it is said that their pervasiveness and restriction are likewise so.

Second is the general citation of scriptural categories, which refers to citing teachings to prove [the validity of] contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and so forth. For example: citing the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding "first illuminating the high mountains"; the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* regarding "initially sitting beneath the Bodhi tree";
the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* regarding "milk coming from the cow"; and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* regarding "extraordinary skillful means.

These are cited to prove the meaning of the three types of cessation-and-contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*). Therefore, one should know that while the names of the gradual stages in the teachings and contemplations may be identical, their meanings are fundamentally different. That text judges [them as such].
The Teaching. Now, because they are of a similar category, I have borrowed from them here.

The commentary states: This passage is also a citation from the introductory section concerning the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. The present text refers to it as "broadly citing related categories.
The intention is to prevent readers from becoming bogged down by the literal wording; therefore, this example is provided so that they may understand the introductory text.
The cited evidence merely borrows from the teachings to illustrate the contemplation. To say that the *Avataṃsaka* first illuminates the high mountains is proof of the Sudden [teaching].
Next, it illuminates the deep valleys; this is proof of the Gradual [teaching]. Finally, it illuminates the level plains; this is proof of the Indeterminate [teaching].
Because the five destinies and other realms illuminate sentient capacities in a diverse and indeterminate manner, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks only of three illuminations.

Tiantai, however, opens up the "level ground" illumination to constitute three periods, correlating them with the five flavors of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, such as milk and so forth, thereby judging the teachings of a single lifetime;
this has profound significance. As for the phrase "initially sitting at the Bodhi tree," this serves as proof of the gradual [teaching]. The Buddha, by means of one...
The manifestation of sounds to preach the Dharma, whereby sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind, proves that [the teaching] is indeterminate.

That the preaching of the Dharma is neither existent nor non-existent proves that it is sudden. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* describes the sequence from milk produced by a cow to the subsequent stages of cream and so forth, proving that it is gradual.
Placing poison in the milk such that it kills a person proves that it is indeterminate. On the Snowy Mountains there is a grass; if a cow [eats it]...

Consuming it immediately yields *sarpis* (clarified butter). This realizes the sudden [teaching]. Regarding the phrase in the *Lotus Sūtra*, "by means of various skillful means," the teachings of the four periods and three vehicles are the "various skillful means";
these represent the gradual and the indeterminate. Revealing the primary truth (*paramārtha*) realizes the sudden.

Some say that the five periods and eight teachings constitute the "various" [means], as distinguished in the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning). Such explanations are all citations of the teachings used as proof.

Contemplation. To broadly cite these analogies is not to say they are entirely identical; one should know that within the Eight Teachings, three [aspects] and the three forms of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* differ eternally in their essence.
Among the Eight Teachings, the "Sudden" refers specifically to the *Avataṃsaka*, while the "Gradual" and "Indeterminate" are applied to the teachings of the four periods.
Now, these three texts are all Mahāyāna and equally take the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) as their object; how could they be the same? Question: Regarding the Gradual...
Next, you ask: "How can the *Nirvāṇa* school, the *Avalokiteśvara* of the Indeterminate school, and the *Lotus Sūtra* of the Perfect and Sudden school be the same?
I reply: Since the *Nirvāṇa* and the *Lotus* were taught at the same time and share the same flavor, they are the same.

Although the *Avalokiteśvara* belongs to the Vaipulya (Vaipulya/Pratyutpanna) section, from the perspective of its perfect reality and because it has already been revealed [as such], it is therefore the same. Furthermore, one should...
Knowing that the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* correspond to the three root-natures (*indriya*), there arise three distinct divisions.

In the Perfect and Sudden (*yuantun*) approach, both understanding and practice are sudden. In the Gradual (*jianci*) approach, understanding is sudden while practice is gradual. In the Indeterminate (*buding*) approach, understanding is sudden while practice may be either sudden or gradual.

All of these are persons of the Perfect [Teaching] and are not different from one another. As for the statement regarding the classification of teachings (*panjiao*) in that text, it refers to the *Xuanyiwen*.

The *Dafahua jing* is categorized according to the fivefold, eightfold, and other systems; this constitutes a case of "similarity of type. Therefore, the names "gradual," "sudden," and "indeterminate" are borrowed [from the *Mohe zhiguan*] merely to classify the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Third is "borrowing names to express meanings," which means borrowing provisional names to express ultimate meanings.

For example, by citing the names used in the Vaipulya (fangděng) sutras to denigrate [the Lesser Vehicle], one expresses the present teaching’s meaning of opening up the provisional and severing all dependencies. It can be understood that other periods follow this pattern:
what constitutes "combined," "exclusive," "confrontational," and so forth in those [earlier] contexts, becomes "opening," "abandoning," "harmonizing," and so forth in the present context.

The commentary states: This section on "borrowing names to explain meanings" and so forth appears at the end of the chapter "Pervasive Destruction of Phenomena by Entering Emptiness from the Conventional" in the sixth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
It then cites the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "Although various paths are taught, in reality they constitute a single vehicle," and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*:
"Furthermore, there is one practice, which is the practice of the Tathāgata," as well as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "The knowledge of all modes knows all things."

The *Dharmapada* (or *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka*) states that upon entering a *campaka* grove, one does not smell other fragrances; the *Avataṃsaka* refers to this as the "equality of the dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*).
What is now called the "name of expulsion and seizure" is actually the passage from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* in which the celestial maidens within Vimalakīrti’s chamber rebuke Śāriputra.
Therefore, it says: "Upon entering a *campaka* grove, one does not smell other fragrances. The Great Master Tiantai utilized this...
This title serves to expound the wondrous contemplation that reveals the provisional through the *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Thus it is said: "It expounds the present meaning of absolute non-reliance.
What constitutes a refutation and rejection of the Lesser Vehicle in that context becomes, in the present context, the opening, the abolishing, and the harmonizing.

Quoting the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to manifest the wondrous *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, what constitutes integration and refinement in that context becomes, in the present context, the opening, the abolishing, and the harmonizing.
Indeed. That the single practice of the Great Sūtra possesses the same timing and the same flavor can be known by oneself.

While the *Huayan* Dharma-realm’s manifestation of wondrous *śamatha-vipaśyanā* constituted a combination with the Separate [Vehicle] and a separation from the Partial [Vehicle], in the present context, it constitutes the opening, the abolishing, and the harmonizing.

Furthermore, citing various sutras to clarify the sublime *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, it says: "Those who borrow provisional names" refers to relying on the teachings of the past, and thus they are called "provisional names.
If one relies on the revelation of the ultimate truth (*kaishin*), wherein all things are real, what provisionality could there be?
As for the statement that "the other three periods are cited," the Deer Park [period] is not included; this is merely because the textual flow proceeds in such a manner.

Fourth is the metaphorical transference of analogy. For example, in treatises such as the *Sūkarikhaṇḍa-sūtra*, patience and other virtues are illustrated by analogies such as a pig rubbing against a golden mountain;

here, analogies for śamatha and vipaśyanā are borrowed from worldly categories and applied according to their specific meanings. Why restrict ourselves to the literal text? Take the single entity of fire:

in various sūtras, it is sometimes used as an analogy for anger and sometimes for wisdom; it is employed for its function of illuminating or its function of burning, depending on its form or its nature.

Whether in terms of essence or function, the same applies to the analogies of earth, water, wind, and so forth. Therefore, one should not restrict the meaning to the literal text alone. The commentary states:
this passage serves as a model for the entirety of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* treatise and other texts; indeed, all the use of metaphors follows this principle.
As for the statement, "The pig rubbing against a golden mountain is discussed as a metaphor for patience," etc., this is from the *Mahāyāna-śāstra*. Treatise.

This is an analogy for the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). It is said: "If a person inflicts harm upon one, it is like a pig rubbing against a mountain of gold; the essence of the gold becomes even more refined.
This now serves as a metaphor for how the three obstacles and four māras are pacified through endurance, such that clarity and stillness flourish ever more intensely.

As for the question of why these are analogies drawn from worldly things yet applied according to their underlying meaning rather than being restricted to the literal text: the *I Ching* (Book of Changes) says, "Take what is near from within oneself; take what is distant from the external world."
Regarding "things": from the heavens and earth, the rivers and seas, the sun, moon, stars, and constellations, to wind and clouds—all these are capable of serving as metaphors.
Even empty space and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) may be used as analogies, let alone other objects.

This is intended for people to understand that the application of metaphors depends on the appropriateness of the occasion and must not be restricted to a single one; hence it is so stated. The compiler has included the character "以" (*yi*) here.
This is an error. It should be the character "yi" (已). Now, I say that this is not merely a mistaken alteration of the characters;
it is also a violation of the syntactic reading (*pò jù dú wén*). It should be read as: "The metaphor refers to worldly categories of things, which are applied according to their shifting meanings.
How can one violate the syntax and further err in altering the text? When fire is cited as an analogy, as well as earth, water, and wind, the logic of the passage is clearly evident, is it not?
Furthermore, [the text] continues as follows.

Fifth is the "Citing Related Passages to Distinguish Differences. This refers to instances where various texts employ the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā) or the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* to provide scriptural evidence for the gradual [attainment of the path], the initial [stages], or the partial and small [vehicles].

In such cases, both the terminology and the underlying meaning are borrowed. For example, in the opening of the section on the two types of practitioners—the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*)—it is stated that the five aggregates, the king, and the number [of factors] arise simultaneously.
"Other times," etc., serves merely to distinguish differences; it does not borrow the meaning of the term.

The commentary states: This passage is also an example cited from the single work on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, serving as a general principle for citing and distinguishing differences found throughout various texts below.
Regarding the statement "using the *Abhidharma* and *Tattvasiddhi* [to explain] up to the borrowing of names and meanings": the *Abhidharma*...
The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* is a treatise on the gate of existence; the *Śūnyatāsaptati* is a treatise on the gate of emptiness.

In the sixth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, the refutation of the provisional within the middle clarifies the sixteen moments of mind, which precisely constitute the stage of the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) for the first fruit. The repeated contemplation of the ultimate truth constitutes the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

The *Yōmon* (Gate of Existence) school’s various treatises clarify that fifteen moments of mind constitute the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), while sixteen moments of mind constitute the stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
