Therefore, the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Seeing) says: "What has been explained thus far is merely the contemplation of the consciousness aggregate (*vijñānaskandha*) spoken in this manner; [it applies to] the other four..."

The aggregates (*skandha*) are likewise; the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are likewise. These three categories are all dharmas that are results of retribution (*vipākadharmas*).

As for the remaining "factors" (*anuśaya*): they arise from volitional deliberation (*cetanā-vicāra*). They are called "factors" (*anuśaya*) because greed, hatred, delusion, and false views can drive and enslave a person.
Generally speaking, they are categorized as afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). "Factor" (*anuśaya*) here refers to a class. Regarding their connection to the realms (*dhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)...
The categories of affliction (*kleśa*) differ: across the three realms and nine stages, with nine grades in each stage, there are eighty-one grades.

This generally pertains to the afflictions of thought (*vicikitsā-āsrava*). However, speaking in general terms, both the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*) and those of thought are termed "proclivities" (*anuśaya*).
This refers, for example, to the ninety-eight *anuśayas*. Furthermore, the delusions of insight (*darśana-heya*) may also be collectively termed "categories" (*pakṣa*).

For instance, there are eighty-eight [delusions] regarding the view of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*), and likewise eighty-eight regarding the view of non-existence (*vibhava-dṛṣṭi*) up to the "neither-nor" view (*ubhayānta-rahita-dṛṣṭi*).

Because the number of categories differs for existence, non-existence, and so forth, they are also called "categories. Regarding the phrase "following the first category," this also refers to the text concerning the provisional nature of the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). First...
Since this chapter employs the method of the three stages and four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) for investigation, all subsequent chapters follow this same pattern.
Thus it is said: "By taking the first chapter as a model, the destruction of the eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) is likewise accomplished.

Once the views have been destroyed using the three types of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) and the four propositions to dismantle the single and combined four propositions of the eighty-eight latent tendencies, even the "beyond-words" [latent tendencies] are treated in the same way. This is the refutation.
The refutation of the "aggregates" (*skandha*) and the "predispositions" (*anuśaya*) is mentioned as an illustration, with further details omitted.

Regarding the statement that the "continuum" (*saṃtati*) and "mutual dependence" (*apekṣā*) are established by analogy with the "cause" (*hetu*), this is also a provisional text for the purpose of refuting [the notion of] establishment through causes. Within the refutation of establishment through causes, one employs the fourfold logical analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) to either suppress or sever [the opponent's position];
the same applies to the continuum and mutual dependence. Among these three types of conventional designations (*prajñapti*), examples are cited while other details are omitted.
Regarding the instruction to "carefully examine the extensive meaning to explain the remaining texts" and "to first contemplate the principles before the intent becomes obscure":
this was Jingxi’s admonition for both readers and lecturers that they must carefully examine the meaning of the extensive texts to explain the concise ones;

furthermore, they must first investigate and contemplate the *dharmapada*, the inclusion of phenomena (*dharmasaṃgraha*), and even the three types of provisional designations (*trividha-prajñapti*) before [proceeding]. Only then will they not be obscured in their understanding.

This is a failure to grasp the intent of the abbreviated text. As for the statement that "the ten dharmas for accomplishing contemplation" merely involve a detailed understanding of the roots and causes within the aggregates (skandhas) and bases (āyatanas), this too refers to citing an example to indicate brevity.
When first setting one's mind to practice contemplation, one contemplates only the aggregates and bases.
The true reality of the three thousand realms encompasses the three types of spiritual capacities; therefore, there are ten vehicles.

Since the ten vehicles have been explained in detail regarding the objective realm of the aggregates (*skandha*), one has thereby recognized the root of contemplative methods and the primary source for entering the Way. As for the remaining nine realms, contemplation can only be applied once they have manifested;
thus, within these nine realms, one merely distinguishes their objective aspects. Once the characteristics of these distinguished objective aspects are clear, [contemplation may proceed].

Once this has been established, the ten contemplations regarding the objects [of perception] below are not analyzed in detail; however, as for those who turn their illumination toward the objects according to the circumstances, they simply employ the previously mentioned ten vehicles of contemplating the aggregates (*skandha*) to shift their contemplation and bring forth the objects. This can be understood by itself.
Commentary on the Examples of the Meaning of *Śamatha* and *Vipaśyanā*, Scroll One;
Commentary on the Examples of the Meaning of *Śamatha* and *Vipaśyanā*, Scroll Two.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chuyuan of Yongjia.

Next, the explanation of the structural patterns (*śarīra*) is divided into two parts: first, the structural pattern of the text (*vyañjana-śarīra*), and second, the structural pattern of the meaning (*artha-śarīra*).
Regarding the first, the structural pattern of the text, there are also ten categories.
The commentary states: This is the structural outline of the text. Within the method of explaining the meaning of the third section, there are two parts:
first, a detailed investigation of the textual meaning; second, an explanation of its structural force. The first part has already been concluded; now follows the second, hence the word "next."

First, regarding the expansion and contraction of the Dharma and the analogy: if the Dharma is concise while the analogy is extensive, one should expand the Dharma-text so that it corresponds with the analogy, rather than adhering strictly to the concise Dharma and thereby obstructing the textual flow of the analogy.

Alternatively, if the Dharma is extensive while the analogy is concise, one may condense the Dharma to correspond with the analogy, or expand the analogy to correspond with the Dharma—as in the analogy of the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) for the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), and so forth. Or, the Dharma may be specific while the analogy is general, as when...
When the great vehicle is used as a metaphor for ten dharmas, one must expand that general metaphor to correspond to those ten dharmas.
If, however, it is used as a metaphor for a well-painted, magnificent hall, there is no need for expansion or correspondence; it is sufficient to simply synthesize them briefly.

When both the dharma and the metaphor are general, such as using space as a metaphor for the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they are treated as such. When both the dharma and the metaphor are specific, they may be understood through the meaning by correlating them according to the text.

The commentary states: This passage serves as a model for the entire work on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, as well as for all other texts. Generally, whenever a simile is employed, none appear beyond those listed above.
This is also intended to instruct students of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, as well as lecturers, to apply their attention in this manner when encountering similes in the text.

Regarding the statement, "If the phenomenon (*dharma*) is brief and the simile is extensive, up to the point where the simile becomes obstructive," it means that the phenomenon is brief while the simile is... [the simile].

Broadly speaking, as in the "Chapter on the Medicine King" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the ten similes that praise the teaching constitute the broad exposition, while the single summary constitutes the concise version.
As for the principle that the words unfold the Dharma so that the text and the similes correspond, it is as stated in the first simile:
"For example, among all the flowing streams, rivers, and waters, the ocean is foremost. This is the simile. This Dharma...

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is likewise so. It is a synthesis. Among all the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgatas, it is the most profound and vast (this is the expansion of the Dharma to correspond with the metaphor).
This continues up to the tenth [chapter], such as the "Pure Cool Pond" and others; each is thus.

This is the brief exposition of the Dharma expanded upon the Dharma itself to accord with the metaphor. Regarding the statement that "the Dharma is extensive while the metaphor is brief," it is like the Five Buddhas.
"Revealing the provisional to manifest the real" refers to the extensiveness of the Dharma. "Like the Udumbara flower" is a metaphor for brevity.

To consolidate the extensiveness of the teachings bestowed by the five Buddhas and treat them as a whole under the metaphor of the rare Udumbara flower is precisely to gather together extensive teachings and follow them with a brief metaphor.
As for the statement that "alternatively, the metaphor may be opened up to correspond to the Dharma like the wish-fulfilling jewel," this refers to the contemplation method of the Initial Vehicle.
At the end of the section on the "Contemplable Realm" (*siyi jing*), it says: "It is like the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), a supreme treasure of the heavens.

Though its form is as small as a mustard seed, it possesses great functional power. Pure and wondrous objects of the five desires, the seven treasures, and *linglang* gems do not come from within its store nor enter from without;

they are not premeditated in sequence, nor are they selected for quantity. They are neither coarse nor exquisite, yet they provide abundance or scarcity according to one's wishes. It rains down in profusion without ceasing."

"It cannot be fully filled. This shows that even material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) can be thus; how much more so for the spirit and mind, which are subtle and wondrous—how could they not possess all dharmas?
(Full text). Now, it is said that this single metaphor serves as a general illustration for the three realms within the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*).
"Resembling a mustard seed" illustrates a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*). "Possessing great functional power" praises that single thought-moment. "Pure" [is the third realm].
The "wondrous five desires" and the "seven treasures" [such as those mentioned by] Lin and others clarify what is possessed. This is a metaphor for the realm of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*);

it is not stored within, nor is it self-originated. It does not enter from without, nor is it caused by another. That it is neither common nor uncaused can be understood through this. This is a metaphor for the realm of cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*).
The phrase "pouring down a profusion of rain" and so forth is a metaphor for the realm of transforming others. Is this not indeed an opening of the metaphors?

This concerns the Abhidharma. Furthermore, it should be understood that although there are three types of inconceivable objects (*acintya-viṣaya*), the contemplative method of the primary vehicle (*ekayāna*) pertains precisely to the object of nature (*dharmatā-viṣaya*).
Cultivating merit for the sake of transforming others serves to perfect this object of nature.

How can the compiler then take the inconceivable object of cultivated merit to be the contemplation of the phenomena of consciousness (*vijñaptimātra-vastu*)? He has, moreover, caused [the practitioner] to practice constant sitting (*nitya-prahāṇa*).
If a practitioner were to thus abandon themselves to the three natures, it would be utterly improper and most laughable.

In this world, there are those who take the objects of cultivated virtue to be the subject of contemplation; they are still unwilling to regard this as the contemplation of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), let alone those with correct vision.
If one were to judge the merits and faults of these two positions, both would be like people who have lost their way while searching for a stray sheep—how could they be fit for discussion?

Yes. It is said that sometimes the individual dharmas are the metaphors and the whole is the subject being illustrated. For example, when the great carriage (*mahā-yāna*) is used as a metaphor for the ten vehicles (*daśa-yāna*), this total metaphor is applied to the ten dharmas;

specifically, at the end of the text on the Ten Vehicle Contemplation Methods (*Daśa-yāna-guan-fa*), the great carriage is cited as a whole to illustrate the ten dharmas—this is a case where the metaphor is total.
If one were to expand the total metaphor to correspond to each of the ten dharmas individually, it would be as when it says, "That carriage is high and broad."
This is the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*). The canopy and so forth represent the arousal of the bodhicitta.

Placing the red pillow inside represents the skillful settling of the myriad practices through internal rest. The external pillow represents the variability of movement and stillness, as well as penetration and obstruction.

This extends even to traveling in the four directions, representing patience, detachment from craving, and so on. Thus, the general metaphor is opened up to correspond with these ten dharmas, as has already been seen above.

The text does not quote this in full. Regarding the statement that if one uses the analogy of a magnificent hall skillfully painted, there is no need for detailed correspondence but only a brief synthesis:
the fourth fascicle of the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation), following the section on the arising of the ten vehicles, offers an analogy, saying:
"It is like Viśvakarman constructing a magnificent hall, which is neither too sparse nor too dense, with no gaps large enough to admit a thread. This is not [the case here].

It is like the measurements that a skilled craftsman can calculate; or like a master painter who delineates the outlines and renders a portrait so realistically that it is not something a mere colorist could add by hand.

To apply the analogy: these ten successive methods of contemplation are comprehensive and refined in both their horizontal and vertical arrangements, so subtle and exquisite that they escort the practitioner to *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge)—a feat impossible for a "blind" meditation master.
This can be understood from what Master Songwen has explained. When both the dharma and the metaphor are general, it is like using empty space as a metaphor for the dharma-realm;
this is self-evident. If both the dharma and the metaphor are specific, it is like using a ladder as a metaphor for gradual progression.

Observing a vajra-jewel placed in the midst of the sun is a metaphor for indeterminate contemplation (*aniyata-vipaśyanā*). One who attains mastery soars through the air, which is a metaphor for the perfect and sudden contemplation (*yuganaddha-avivarta-vipaśyanā*);
this is clearly evident. The citations of texts used to explain the meanings above have merely been summarized to highlight the essentials;
were they expanded upon, they would become excessively prolix. Therefore, I shall conclude here.

Second, the combination of the dharma and the analogy. Third, their mutual presence or absence. These are established and applied according to what is appropriate, with their inclusion or omission suited to the occasion.

The commentary states: There are cases where there is the dharma but no analogy for its combination; this is because the principle and meaning are already manifest, and because the faculties and dispositions [of the listeners] are sharp.

There are cases where there is both the dharma and the analogy for its combination; this is because the dharma is difficult to understand, so an analogy is raised to clarify it, thereby clarifying the dharma through the analogy.

Because [the meaning] has not yet been made manifest, one employs the *upanaya* (application) to unify it. There may be cases where there is the *pakṣa* (subject), the *hetu* (reason), and the *dṛṣṭānta* (example), yet no *upanaya*;

this is because the *dharma* (the principle) has already been made manifest by the example, and thus an application is unnecessary—such as when three parables are cited to manifest the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Conversely, there has never been a case where there is an application but no example. Whether these elements are present or omitted depends entirely on the requirements of the specific occasion; this is all there is to it.

Third is the opening and closing of self and others. Generally, when enumerating chapter headings, there are three types: first, opening and closing in relation to oneself, such as the five concise [teachings] in relation to the ten extensive ones;

second, opening and closing in relation to others, such as the ten extensive [teachings] in relation to the five layers of profound meaning (*wǔzhòng xuányì*); and third, opening and closing through mutual inclusion.

As with "opening above and closing below," there is a sense in which "opening and closing" is established, such as in the *Saṃgraha* and other works where six items are opened and four are opened, etc.;

these do not go beyond [discussing] the causes and effects of self and others, wherein the phrasing may expand or contract according to the occasion, yet the subsequent enumeration must invariably reach ten.
From the perspective of meaning, however, expansion or contraction follows what is appropriate.
The commentary states: "Regarding the opening and closing of 'self' and 'others,' and the general arrangement of chapter headings," this refers to the general rules of exposition.
"Opening and closing in relation to self," such as the five summaries and ten expansions, means that the five summaries are contained within the single [section] of the ten expansions;

by opening the chapter on the General Meaning (*mahā-artha*) into the five summaries, these five summaries are then contrasted with the nine subsequent expansions, all of which pertain to the causes and effects of one's own practice (*sva-caryā*).

The transformation of the "other" (the object) and the "self" (the subject) involves only differences of expansion and brevity; this refers to the opening and closing [of categories] in relation to the self.

If one correlates the tenfold expansion with the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-vidha-gambhīrārtha*) of the *Miaoxuan*, this refers to the opening and closing in relation to the other. In the *Zhiguan* [text], the section on "Explaining Names" (*shiming*) corresponds to explaining names.

The section on "Characteristics" (*tixiang*) corresponds to discerning the essence (*ti*). The "Inclusion of Dharmas" (*shefa*) refers precisely to the dharmas included within that essence. As for the "Method" (*fangbian*)...

Thus, the correct contemplation of karmic retribution belongs to the "Essential Doctrine" (the primary school). The partial and perfect ways of initiating the teaching belong to the "Characteristics of the Teaching.

The former involves discussing the profound mysteries to explain the sutras, which exclusively pertains to "Understanding" (*jñāna*); the latter, however, relies on the sutras to perform contemplation, and thus pertains to "Practice" (*caryā*).

Regarding the mutual inclusion and exclusion of these characteristics—as when opening the upper and closing the lower—it is first distinguished within the "Arousing of the Bodhi-mind" section of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (First Fascicle).
Regarding "their non-existence": this means that nine are bound and one is liberated; thus, all ten are non-existent. Jingxi said:
"Whether it be the mind or the Way, those that are non-existent are very many; I have merely mentioned ten as examples. As for "opening the upper and closing the lower":

if the two vehicles are counted as two, then the asuras are subsumed within the realms of ghosts and animals, resulting in only five paths. This is "opening the upper and closing the lower. If one were to combine the two...
Taking the vehicles as a single expedient means constitutes one path; opening them up, with the asuras as a separate path, constitutes the six destinies (*ṣadgati*).

Although there are such differences in the expansion and contraction of these higher and lower realms, the numerical principle must be ten. Regarding the establishment of these expansions and contractions in terms of both word and meaning, they are like the *saṃgrahavastu* (articles of attraction) and other such categories.
"Opening into six, opening into four, and even down to the mind being only one": Opening into six means encompassing all principles, delusions, wisdom, practices, stages, and teachings.
Opening into four refers to these same six as consisting of the two aspects of one's own practice—cause and fruit—and the two aspects of benefiting others—means and ends.
Thus, it is called "four. This is the meaning of the four textual sections and the two underlying principles.
"Only in one" means that because there are two aspects of cause and effect, while the four textual sections are merely cause and effect, it is said that "the meaning is twofold.
However, since the intent is that they are subsumed within the single reality of śamatha and vipaśyanā, it is said to be "in one. The Compiler (Zuǎnzhě) remarked: "The text is likely erroneous."
"It should be six characters. This is also not the case. Since those [sections] encompassing the dharmas already open up six categories, it says "six texts," and so forth.
Here, since it speaks of opening into six and opening into four, and even regarding their opening and closing, they refer solely to the causes and effects of self and others;
therefore, there are four. One should know that while in that context one must speak of six, here one must...
The phrase "four" [in the original text] is not a scribal error. As for the textual form—whether expanding or contracting, whether more or less—it is adjusted according to the occasion.
The subsequent count must necessarily reach ten; this expansion and contraction is merely a matter of opening and closing. Expansion is opening; contraction is closing.
Whether there is more or less is also determined by the occasion, but upon reaching the final summation, the number must necessarily reach ten. This is because ten is the [complete] number.
This is the Dharma. It does not forget the fundamental principle of the great chapters. The compiler says that the character "後" (hou) is an error and should be "從" (cong).

This, too, is a groundless and forced interpretation. To say that "following the meaning" means that the length is adjusted according to what is appropriate implies that while the number must necessarily reach ten, the meaning values being flexible and lacks fixed constraints.
Fourth, regarding the phrase "notes (chū) such as [this]": if the preceding text already contains it in full, or if it exists extensively in other sections, repeating it would result in prolixity;
or if the extensive text is not essential, then in order to provide an explanation, one must precisely indicate the location by summarizing and pointing it out.
Furthermore, if there are omissions in the transcription, they must be filled in.
The commentary states: Regarding the meaning of "and so forth," the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) has already explained it based on the *Guangya* and the *Shuowen*.

Since the meaning is evident, it is not cited again here. As for the phrase "that which was already fully set forth above," this refers to the fivefold concise presentation of the sequence of arising in the "General Meaning" chapter, intended to clarify the tenfold extensive sequence of arising.
Since the fivefold concise version is already complete, the sequence is not written out again when reaching the tenfold extensive version.
"First: Therefore, the commentary says 'and so forth. This has already been fully set forth in the preceding text. Regarding 'or as extensively preserved in other sections':
for example, in the first fascicle of the *Zhiguan*, the fourfold Four Noble Truths are correlated with the lands both horizontally and vertically.

The phrase 'the commentary says 'and so forth'' below that passage refers to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* and various texts of our own school that clarify the lands; this current text is brief, while the extensive versions exist there."
If these two passages were to be expanded further, the text would become overly prolix; hence the commentary states "and so forth" (*yathā-prabhṛti*).

Alternatively, when extensive textual citations are not essential—such as in the section on the arousal of the great mind (*mahācittotpāda*), where ten types of arousal are listed beginning from "inference through reasoning" (*tarkānumāna*) and ending with "seeing others undergo suffering"—the meaning is already sufficiently summarized.
If one were to cite even more extensively from various sūtras and śāstras regarding the arousal [of the mind]...
The phrasing of the *Xinwen* (Text on the Mind) is not essential to its meaning; therefore, I have merely provided annotations as appropriate.

As for the requirement that an explanation must be specific and precise, rather than vague or general—since this is the teaching of Jingxi transmitted by his masters—it is necessary to point out each detail and extract the essentials of the text to demonstrate them, as has been done above.

The text has already fully indicated the five [categories]; the remaining sections are preserved extensively in works such as the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā*. The extensive texts are not essential here.
Apart from the ten types of generating the mind (*cittotpāda*), there are omissions in the transmitted manuscripts that must be filled in.

For example, regarding the passage on "at one time" within the five matters preceding the commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the text is explained according to the contemplation of a single [aspect], yet the annotation is missing below the text.
...and so forth. Jingxi said: "Under the section 'Contemplating the Mind' (Guānxīn), one should have added the characters 'yúnyún' (and so forth).

This omission must be filled in. Fifth is the matter of refutation and establishment, preservation and abandonment. For instance, when refuting ancient masters or refuting heterodox views, once their doctrines have been dismantled, there is no need to preserve them further;
even if their names are retained, their meanings are not employed. Alternatively, if there is even a slight impropriety, there will be both rejection and acceptance.

"If one refutes [the former], one refutes it specifically and partially; having refuted oneself, one must establish [a new position] to form a unique school of inconceivable principle, in order to accommodate the inconceivable transformation of the One Vehicle," etc.

The commentary states: "Refuting and establishing, preserving and discarding" means that one refutes the ancients to establish the present, preserving the name while discarding the meaning. Refuting the ancients...

The Master [Zhiyi] has already refuted such heterodox and deviant views, as he did when criticizing the erroneous interpretations of the *Sui ziyi* (Following One’s Own Intent) and the claim in the *Wuxing jing* (Scripture on Non-action) that "sexual desire is itself the Way. Such unrestrained violation of precepts is like the example of grasping a snake without restraint.
Tiantai has diligently refuted these doctrines; since they have already been destroyed, there is no need to preserve them further, even if they still persist.
One may preserve its name, but its meaning can no longer be employed. If there is even the slightest inconsistency, there must be rejection and selection.

For example, regarding the *Four Ones* (si-yi) of the Guangzhai school which interprets the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Tiantai adopted the names of those "four ones," yet rejected their meanings—specifically the "one cause" and "one fruit"—and established his own system of "one principle, one practice, one teaching, and one person. Relying upon this...

Although it employs [the terminology of] those [schools], its underlying principle is eternally distinct from them. As for "refuting the partiality of the Lesser Vehicle," this refers to refuting the biased texts of their doctrines.

As for "refuting [others] while necessarily establishing [one's own]," why stop at merely refuting the four periods and three teachings of the Lesser Vehicle? Everything is refuted so that nothing remains;
this is done to establish the inconceivable principle of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. It is by means of the coarse that the subtle is revealed, and for this reason, [these teachings] are established.

Furthermore, this is established in order to perfect the inconceivable transformation throughout a single lifetime. Within the guidance provided during this one period, there are provisional and real teachings, as well as small and great ones;

the intention is for these to ultimately converge in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Only when they are neither provisional nor real, neither small nor great, does the inconceivable transformation truly come to fruition. Therefore, it is established.

Sixth, there are differences in length. Whether it concerns the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) in their broad or narrow aspects, the interrogation and scrutiny through questions and answers, the correspondence between principles and analogies, or the opening and closing of topical sections, one may explain and resolve them according to the text itself without needing to seek elsewhere.

However, regarding such works as the *Niusiyijing* (The Inconceivable Realm) and the *Pofa bian* (The Universal Destruction of Dharmas), one must necessarily examine the beginning and end to seek out the middle. One may either condense the long into the short or expand the short to [the long].
This being so, it is necessary to first expand upon the literary momentum before proceeding to a detailed analysis.

Once the text is clarified through such analysis, one must then integrate these fragments into a whole, ensuring that the logic and phrasing flow smoothly, so that the path of practice within this school has a clear point of convergence. Furthermore, when employing both general and specific expositions, the general serves as a heading for the specific;
if the meaning of a specific exposition is extensive, one should subsume the specific back into the general.
The commentary states: Regarding "length and brevity being different," that which is extended and unfolded is called long; that which is rolled up and condensed is called short.
As for the characteristics of phenomena, whether large or small, such that there is no need to seek them far away—this follows the standard method of explaining meanings used by our school.

We simply take those textual expressions that are clear and manifest, where the meaning accords with the purport of the teaching, and the principle is free from error or deviation, so that it may be capable [of conveying the truth].
Regarding this, it is already sufficient from the perspective of principle and there is no need to seek it elsewhere.

As for such passages as the "Inconceivable Realm" and the "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas," the intent is to clarify that the meaning of these texts cannot be interpreted or explained in a haphazard manner.

For instance, in the "First Inconceivable Realm" and the "Contemplation Method of the One Vehicle," one must contemplate the beginning and the end to seek the middle; only then can [the meaning be understood].
One may grasp [the principle] and thereby give rise to understanding; once understanding is established, contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is formed. The same applies to benefiting others. Why?

Because, having begun with the inconceivable realm by specifically discerning the aggregates (*skandha*), one cultivates contemplation through the mind and thus realizes that a single thought-moment is itself the three thousand realms, and the three thousand realms are themselves a single thought-moment.

This is the realm of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*). If one does not enter into this contemplation, four types of conceptual calculations (*catur-vikalpa*) will suddenly arise; therefore, one employs [this method].
Investigating by means of the four propositions is the sphere of cultivating virtue (*bhāvanā-gocara*). Because one gives rise to further attachments through this investigation, one might ask:
"If all phenomena do not arise from self, other, or even without cause, why do the sūtras and śāstras speak of self, other, and cause?
This doubt concerns the sphere of transforming others (*parārtha-gocara*). To refute this notion, it is said: "All..."
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have themselves already abandoned the four faults; in transforming others, they are unimpeded in their fourfold teaching.
This constitutes a profound contemplation of emptiness that shatters the objects of transformation for others. Next, this self and other are synthesized to establish the three truths.
Next, three parables are presented to illustrate the wondrous realm. Next, the functional power of this wondrous realm is clarified. Finally, all phenomena are subsumed.
Thus, the three truths are established. Therefore, these seven categories, from the beginning to the end, constitute the contemplative method of the One Vehicle’s inconceivable realm.
Consequently, one must cause this contemplation to traverse from the beginning to the end to seek the middle; only by extending the momentum of the text can it be analyzed and explained in detail.
It is said that "sometimes the long is condensed into the short, and the short is expanded into the long," because of the inconceivable.
Within the objective realm (*viṣaya*), the non-sequential is first revealed by means of the sequential; thus, this demonstration exists. What is it?

First, one points to how a single mind gives rise to the ten realms, beginning with the hell realm and ending with the Buddha realm. Within each individual realm, the causes, conditions, fruits, and retributions are demonstrated.

This unfolds the brevity of the single mind, differentiating the various dharmas of cause and effect within the ten realms. The single mind— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the content up to that point.)
When these are suddenly brought together, they constitute the wondrous realm; thus it is said that "one extends the long by means of the short.

Regarding the phrase "the inconceivable realm and so forth," the word "and so forth" (等) refers to the awakening of the bodhicitta and the skillful application of the two vehicles' contemplative methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Therefore, the text below immediately states: "and the universal shattering of dharmas. The compiler erroneously points to the preceding six chapters [as being included in this category].
"Based on the sūtras, one opens up a wondrous understanding; 'equal' refers to what precedes.

Although the phrase "equal to what precedes" occurs in the subsequent text, it is not applicable here because that current passage uses the word "equal" to mean that the contemplative methods of the two vehicles [Hīnayāna] are equal to those that follow.
I shall now set this forth in full: within the arousal of the bodhicitta, one expands the brief into the long.

Within a single mind, one can give rise to the nine fetters; by means of a single liberation, one fulfills the ten non-conditions, and can also fully manifest the four types of bodhicitta and the four kinds of "is.
If one extends the long and condenses the short, whether it be "is" or "is not," all is gathered back into a single thought-moment.
When "is" and "is not" are identical as such, there is neither dharma nor non-dharma—this is the true bodhicitta, the Dharma-realm.
However, although the act of "discarding" (揀) does not explicitly indicate "affirming" (顯), since Jingxi has already directed that the force of the text be extended further, how could this not be so?

Furthermore, since in the preceding passage concerning the extensive, the abbreviated, and the non-existent, it was stated that using the five abbreviated [precepts] to arouse the great mind constitutes the manifestation of the numerical and textual characteristics of the extensive;
and that within the abbreviated arousal of the great mind, the textual characteristics are extensively manifested while the numbers are abbreviated—then [the same logic applies here].
These extensive and concise aspects manifest together to form a single intent; so why should there be any doubt?

In the *Qiaonan zhiguan* (Convenient Arrangement of Stopping and Contemplation), one mind of non-dual stopping and contemplation is opened out into sixty-four variations, and further into one hundred and twenty-eight variations.

To expand the brief so as to make it long, one summarizes the one hundred and twenty-eight cycles as nothing other than the sudden and perfect *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) within a single thought-moment;

this serves to condense the long into the brief. Within the "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas" (*Pó fǎ biàn*), non-dual *śamatha-vipaśyanā*—which is neither horizontal nor vertical—is likewise taken as the brief.
If one were to expand the brief so as to make it long, then it becomes vertical, it becomes horizontal, and it becomes...

It is neither horizontal nor vertical. If one takes the long and joins it with the short, they both converge within a single thought-moment into the inconceivable *śamatha-vipaśyanā* that is neither horizontal nor vertical, yet is both horizontal and vertical.
Such is the meaning of the text; yet the compiler did not perceive this.
To erroneously cite the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practices) as stating: "The text of the 'Inconceivable Realm' differs while the meaning is one;

'neither identical nor different' serves to conclude the long by means of the short. 'Opening toward the three truths' and 'cultivation, nature, self, and other' serve to expand the short into the long"—this is not the meaning of concluding the long and expanding the short.
These [principles] naturally exist beneath each of the ten vehicles; this [citation] is a deluded and confused attribution. It is not [correct].
How can this be erroneous? In the "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas" (*Pó fǎ biàn*), the long [passages] are condensed into the short; these are for the most part false and erroneous.

I cannot cite them all in full. To summarize the specific by means of the general, or to subsume the specific within the general, as stated in various texts, may also be seen therein, though I cannot record it all in detail.
Seventh is the concealment and manifestation of the dharma and the metaphor. If the dharma is concealed and the metaphor is manifest, one seeks the meaning of the metaphor to dissolve the dharma.

If the dharma is manifest and the metaphor is concealed, one seeks the meaning of the dharma to dissolve the metaphor. This principle applies similarly to whether the metaphor is concealed or manifest in relation to the application (*upanaya*).
In this way, the intent of the text is not lost, and the preceding and succeeding sections support one another.

The commentary states: This section of the text concerns the teachings of Jingxi [Zhiyi] regarding those who study *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. In the application of the dharma and its metaphor (*dṛṣṭānta*), there are instances where one is hidden and the other is manifest;

this must be investigated in detail. When it is said that the dharma is hidden while the metaphor is manifest, and one seeks the meaning of the metaphor to dissolve the dharma, such examples are numerous.
For now, I shall cite one: for instance, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is difficult to comprehend, whereas raising a metaphor makes it easy to clarify. Therefore...
Regarding the two gates of the original and the trace—the opening, the abolishing, the merging, and the reconciling—this Dharma is profound and hidden, difficult for people to comprehend.
For this reason, the Tathāgata employed the analogy of the lotus. Master Tiantai personally received this intent on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; therefore, he explained it as follows:

The lotus exists for the sake of the flower; when the flower blooms, the lotus appears; when the flower falls, the lotus is perfected. This serves as a metaphor for the three stages of giving, opening, and discarding.
Both the "Original" (hon) and "Trace" (jaku) gates possess these three meanings; this is what is meant by using metaphors to elucidate the Dharma.

If one seeks the intent of the Dharma by making the metaphor implicit while manifesting the Dharma to explain the metaphor, it is as stated in the fourth fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*: "It is like a pig rubbing against gold."

The mountain and the various rivers flowing into the ocean—these two metaphors illustrate *śamatha* (calm abiding). Since the literal meaning of these metaphors is obscure, one should seek the underlying intent of the Dharma to clarify them, so that the metaphor follows the meaning of calm abiding.
Furthermore, firewood burning in a blaze and wind fanning a bellows—these two metaphors illustrate *vipaśyanā* (insight).
Since the meaning of the analogy is obscured, one should seek the intended meaning of the Dharma to clarify the analogy, so that the analogy follows from contemplation.

It is the same whether the analogy is obscure or manifest in relation to the application (*upanaya*). That is to say, when the analogy is manifest while the application is obscure, one seeks the meaning of the analogy to dissolve the application;

when the analogy is obscure while the application is manifest, one seeks the meaning of the application to dissolve the analogy. One should apply this principle of the obscuration and manifestation of the Dharma and the analogy accordingly.
This is merely to avoid prolixity.
Eighth is the inquiry and response regarding delusion and understanding. If one is deluded in the question but not in the answer, one formulates the question by seeking the intent of the answer.
If one is deluded in the answer but not in the question, one completes the answer by investigating the text of the question. Sometimes the question arises from the answer; or...

Standing alone, it dispels hindrances. Sometimes it proceeds by way of answering; sometimes it proceeds by way of posing a challenge based on the answer; sometimes the answer accords with the question;
sometimes the answer contradicts the question; sometimes the answer blocks the question; and sometimes the answer opens up the line of inquiry.

The commentary states: Regarding the question posed by one who is deluded and the answer given by one who is not, it is as stated in the "Analysis" following the first section on the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*:
Question: Previously, you distinguished what is not [the case] and spoke of it as "not"; now you reveal what is [the case]. Why do you speak of it as "both" being so? Answer:

That which is spoken of as "both being so" refers to that which is neither bound nor liberated; therefore, it is said to be "both. To say they are "both" means that both seek the supreme [enlightenment].
To transform those below. Therefore, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes the *Zhiji* (Record of Compilation), where a person of former times explained this question-and-answer session as follows:

"Regarding the question-and-answer here, the question asks whether the previous judgment belongs to the 'neither' category. This is not so. If one were to formulate the question based on that [previous case], it should have been:
'Since the previous was neither-affirmative-nor-negative, is the present both-affirmative-and-negative? Based on the intent of the current answer, the meaning is entirely..."
This is so. The intent of the answer is merely to affirm that the three types of bodhisattvas are indeed [bodhisattvas]. When has it ever been said that "both 'is' and 'is not' are both 'is'"?
Therefore, in the question, it is stated generally that "both are not," rather than saying "both 'is' and 'is not' are both 'not'.

In the answer, it is simply stated that "the bodhisattvas are both 'is'," rather than stating that "the nine 'nots' are both 'is'. This is because, according to the other's intention, even the nine "nots" must also be "both 'is'."

Now, it is said that although the text of Tiantai’s questions is obscure, the text of his answers is very clear; therefore, one may seek the intent of the answers and apply them to the questions, whereby the questions themselves become manifest.
If one were to follow the interpretation of others cited by Jingxi, not only would they be confused regarding the questions, but they would also be confused regarding the answers.
If one were confused about the answers but not the questions, it would be as the question in the Preface states: [The text continues with the specific question from the Preface.]

The names of the teaching and the object are the same, yet they differ instantaneously. The teaching is the same as the Perfect Teaching (Enkyō), and the object is the same as the True Aspect (Jissō), yet their aspects differ instantaneously.
There are three types of differences, such as gradual progression; this question can be seen [in the text], and thus there is no confusion.

In the answer, it says: "Yet they are the same while not the same; they are not the same while being the same. Within the gradual progression, the six wholesome and unwholesome [factors] each have three. There is none...

The outflows (*āsrava*) comprise three categories in total, which, when categorized among ordinary beings, amount to twelve distinct types; hence they are said to be "indeterminate. Regarding the statement that there are twelve or thirteen distinctions, the explanation is as follows:
first, one cultivates taking refuge and precepts, which are the three [remedies for] fire, blood, and weapons;

second, one attains the three good destinies; third, the single stage of the untainted (*anāsrava*) constitutes the two vehicles of the two teachings, making four; these added to the preceding [categories] complete [the count].
Tenth: (1) *śamatha* (meditative concentration) stops desire and distraction; (2) *maitrī-karuṇā* (compassion) stops [the mind from] pervading space;
(3) *nitya-sthiti* (constant abiding) stops the two extremes. These three do not open or close, yet they form thirteen distinct points.

Since "constant abiding" is the true reality (*dharmatā*) that serves as the object of focus (*ālambana*), it should not be counted as a limit of distinctness; therefore, it is said there are twelve distinct points. Its...

Regarding the "one phrase of the three" within the general category of the untainted (*anāsrava*), many people do not understand it. In the past, some explained it through the lens of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*):

asserting that "untainted" refers to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), "general" (*sāmānya*) to the contemplation of the conventional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), and "middle" (*madhya*) to the contemplation of the middle way (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*). Others have said that "untainted, general, and middle" refers to the generalization of the three realms (*traidhātuka*).
Such interpretations are truly laughable; they fail to realize that this— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The full passage would likely continue with the correct explanation of the term.)

The general heading encompasses the opening and includes both the three stages and the three [aspects]. Therefore, it is said that within the general category of the untainted (anāsrava), there are these three.
As for the term "indeterminate" (aniyata), because indeterminate śamatha and vipaśyanā have no distinct stages, they are merely appended at the conclusion of the gradual [path].
The question arises from the answer; as it was asked in the introduction: "This chapter is identical to the Mahāyāna, identical to the true nature (dharmatā), and identical to..."

This is called "Cessation and Contemplation" (śamatha-vipaśyanā). Why is it called "Discriminating Differences"? The Record states: Because the preceding answers were different, one anticipates a different question based on those same [principles];

thus it is said that "the question arises from the answer. Alternatively, it may be used to resolve isolated difficulties, as in the "Examination at the End of the Section on the Pervasiveness of Refuting Dharmas," which says:
Question: The *Ratnavali* (Yingluo jing) states that when the third contemplation is perfected, the first stage (*bhūmi*) manifests.

Why then do you now say it is the eighth stage, or perhaps the first dwelling (*vihāra*)? Answer: These are established through the mutual borrowing of meanings. It is said to be the eighth stage because one borrows the superior to establish the inferior;

it is said to be the first dwelling because one borrows the inferior to establish the superior. This is simply because the *Ratnavali Sutra* clarifies the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (*bypakya*). Alternatively...

Regarding the reason for answering that they are "both": as stated in the first chapter of the *Wenzi* (Private Exegesis) of the *Fahua Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), in the section consisting of sixteen points of private analysis, it says:
"If that is so, afflictions (*kleśa*) are also the root of all phenomena; since they are originally intended to be treated, they are also the starting point of contemplation.

Furthermore, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the diseased body are also the basis of phenomena; since they are originally intended to be treated, they are also the starting point of contemplation. Why is this?"

The meaning of "not being attained" (意不得) is both general and specific; this passage serves as the response by treating them as simultaneous. Alternatively, it proceeds from the response to a raised objection:
[The objection asks], "In the first chapter on Stopping and Contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), it was stated that even the teachings of the Hīnayāna are the Buddha’s word.

For what reason do you say they are not? If you say they are not, then one should not speak of 'gradual' [attainment]. The response is: Since the distinction between Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna has been made, the Hīnayāna is not the subject under discussion here. What is currently being discussed is the "gradual" [attainment] within the Mahāyāna context.

This is merely a gradual progression from the subtle to the manifest. As for the gradual approach of the Hīnayāna, since they are unaware of the true reality (*dharmatā*) both at the beginning and at the end, it is not truly gradual.

This constitutes an answer that addresses an objection. Alternatively, there are answers that accord with the question, which follow the conventional path and do not require the citation of further evidence;
and there are answers that contradict the question, such as the subsequent analysis of the question regarding the realm of demonic activity (*mārakarman*), where the demons cause agitation.

[The preceding section] concludes. [Question: "The Good Dharma has arrived. Is it as if winter has passed and spring has come? [Answer: "Not necessarily so. This is an answer that contradicts the question.
It is also like those answers found in various texts where the initial response states, "This interpretation is not correct," and so forth; all such cases are answers that contradict the question.

Alternatively, there are answers that block the question, which means they preempt the difficulty being raised. For example, in the third fascicle of the *Zhiguan*, there is a question... [text continues].
The initial contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional has both a destructive and a constructive aspect, and is thus called the "contemplation of the two truths.

The second contemplation likewise possesses both a destructive and a constructive aspect; why is it not also called the "contemplation of the two truths"? Answer: The previous contemplation has already received the name "two truths";

now, this one receives a name based on its superior quality, namely, the "contemplation of equality. Question again: The third contemplation also possesses both a destructive and a constructive aspect.
"Why not instead receive its name from its superior function? Answer: "The first two contemplations involve obstructions; therefore, they are further refuted and their functions are further employed.
The third contemplation is free of obstructions and thus receives its name solely from its function. It cannot be treated as an identical case. This answer closes off the question.
The answer opens the inquiry, as in the second passage of this text; however, there are many other passages as well that cannot be cited in full.

Ninth is the method of citing examples to explain the text, such as in the passage on the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). Sometimes the phrasing contains multiple implications, which should be determined by the specific teaching so that the six passages form a single category.
Whether it concerns the truths (*satya*) or the conditions (*pratyaya*), all dharmas are likewise treated.

The commentary states: The textual basis for śamatha and vipaśyanā frequently cites the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) of the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā). Here, I shall briefly cite one or two instances.

For example, in the sections on "Acting According to One’s Own Intent" (*Sui-zi-i*) throughout the various virtues, as well as in "Counteracting Aids to Opening" (*Dui-zhi-zhu-kai*), the phrasing used to clarify the six perfections contains implicit meanings that should be definitively established by the teachings.
Now, I maintain that these refer solely to the meaning of the perfections as phenomena subject to arising and ceasing within the Tripitaka.
It is not inclusive. From the Vaipulya (fangděng) and Prajñāpāramitā (bōrě) onwards, the meanings encompass both the Shared (tōngjiào) and the higher teachings.
Regarding this inclusivity: there are the six [perfections] where cause and effect are both shared; there are the six where the Distinct (bié) and Perfect (yuán) enter into the Shared;

and there are the six where one relies on the Shared for guidance. Although the names of the six perfections are identical, the contemplation of their emptiness is likewise identical in meaning; it is not by—

Regarding the classification by teaching (*śāsana-vyavasthāna*): to what do these meanings ultimately refer? By means of these three meanings, they are distinguished. The initial mind of a Bodhisattva in the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*) employs emptiness in the same manner as the Shared Teaching (*sāmānya-śāsana*);
however, they differ in that their mental aspiration (*citta-praṇidhāna*) is directed toward the Middle Way. Yet, within the Separate Teaching there is no separate division;

it also includes those who encompass the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-śāsana*), which is likewise determined by meaning, so that the Dharma remains undisturbed. The initial mind of a person of the Perfect Teaching employs ultimate [emptiness].
To practice the Dharma of the six perfections in vain is for these six dharmas to be nothing other than the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
From this, one comes to know the six perfections of arising and ceasing, non-arising, the immeasurable, and the unconditioned. Thus, these six textual expressions constitute a single category.

It is not that giving arises and ceases while the other five [perfections] are non-arising; rather, the Four Noble Truths and Dependent Origination differ only in their opening and closing [of exposition].
This may be understood by comparing their respective translations.

Tenth, regarding the establishment of the Dharma through teaching: all [teachings] establish their doctrinal tenets according to the essence of their respective teachings; thus, while some names are partial, their underlying intent is complete.
"Establishing by means of the substance.

The commentary states: "By means of the teaching, one establishes the dharmas," etc. "Dharmas" refers to the dharmas such as the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Perfections.

To establish these dharmas by means of the teaching means [to distinguish] from the Tripitaka’s *saṃvṛti* (arising and ceasing) up to the Perfect Teaching’s *anabhisaṃskāra* (non-action). Thus it is said.

"All follow their respective doctrinal essences" means that the *pitakas* follow the essence of arising and ceasing, up to and including the Perfect [Teaching], which follows the essence of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

"Establishing the tenet of the doctrine" refers to the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) of that specific teaching. Alternatively, it is called "the partial intent within the perfect," as it is determined by way of the essence.
For example, the *Vimalakīrti* is specifically designated by the name "liberation," while the *Prajñāpāramitā* is specifically designated by the title "emptiness and quiescence.

The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* specifically highlights "stopping" (*śamatha*), whereas the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* specifically highlights "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*). In all these cases, although the names are partial, the wondrous essence is complete and integrated.
Question: How does this differ from the ninth [chapter]? Answer: Because the preceding [section] clarifies that the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and so forth are mutually inclusive. Therefore...
This establishes it through the teaching. This merely clarifies the method of establishing [the meaning] by means of the teaching; it is not without differences.
Second, the "essential nature and force of the meaning" (*artha-svabhāva-vega*) also constitutes ten examples.

The commentary states: Since the initial passage spoke of the "essential nature and force of the text," which refers to the *vyañjaka* (the signifier), the present passage speaks of the "essential nature and force of the meaning," which refers to the *vyaṅgya* (the signified).
Furthermore, it is not that the text lacks meaning, nor that the meaning lacks the text; these are merely spoken of according to their predominant aspect.
First is the fundamental intent of the body of the treatise: whenever one wishes to explain a meaning, one must first contemplate the category of the text.

For example, in the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), although the "contemplation of the mind" (*guanxin*) is established under every section of meaning, the fundamental intent of the text is to clarify that the fivefold profound meaning (*wuzhong xuanyi*) transcends all other teachings.

Thus, the teaching of "contemplating the primary through the secondary" (*zhèngguān bàng*) relies on phenomena to give rise to contemplation; within this teaching on the contemplation of the mind, the provisional and the real, as well as the original and the manifested, are taken as the primary focus.
One constantly uses the five flavors and eight teachings to distinguish the provisional, and employs the world-systems and their atomic particles to distinguish the manifested.
If the original and the manifested were to become intermingled, or if the teachings and flavors were neglected, there would be no means to reveal the two subtleties of the relative and the ultimate.

The remaining flavors and remaining sections may be understood by seeking them through analogy. As for the present *zhiguan* (calm abiding and insight), although various teachings are employed, the intent lies in the ten dharmas to accomplish wondrous contemplation.
Thus, while the primary teaching is the contemplation itself, the ancillary elements serve to reveal the true principle;
the ancillary elements extend to various teachings to further generate faith, and the ancillary elements cite various sutras as references.

The commentary states: Regarding "first, the categories of sections," this refers to the period beginning from the *Avataṃsaka* and ending with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa*, each of which was compiled into its own collection according to its own thematic affinity; hence they are called "categories of sections.

As for the statement that "under the various meanings in the *Fahua xuanyi*, 'contemplation of the mind' (*guanxin*) and so forth are established," this means that beneath these various texts, contemplation is initiated based on specific events, and the principle of "contemplation of the mind" is thereby established.
The primary intention lies in judging and interpreting the *Lotus Sūtra* as surpassing all other teachings; therefore, it is said that the teaching is primary while contemplation is secondary.
Regarding the phrase "within the teaching": since there are two paths—teaching and contemplation—it specifically points to the teaching, hence the expression "within the teaching."

Regarding the statement that "taking the provisional and the real, as well as the trace and the fundamental, as the primary focus": the opening of the provisional to reveal the real and the opening of the trace to reveal the fundamental constitute the main theme of this sutra.
To manifest the subtlety of the fundamental and the trace, Tiantai Master employed the five flavors and eight teachings for both vertical classification and horizontal explanation.

He did so desiring to lead people to recognize that among the flavors, the ultimate is the *tīrthaṅkara* (clarified butter), and that among the teachings, it is peerless among all scriptures. For this reason, he was earnest and diligent in his efforts.

The pointing with the hand indicates this Gate of the Trace (*jìmén*). To say that one uses the number of dust motes in a world to distinguish the trace refers to the revelation of the fundamental through the opening of the trace.
The Sūtra provides an analogy, saying: "Suppose five hundred thousand million *nayuta* *asaṃkhyeya* trichiliocosms were all ground into dust;
having passed beyond the eastern direction [by as many worlds as there are dust motes]..."
Take a single mote of dust from among hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeyas of trichiliocosms.
Then, proceeding eastward, pass as many lands as that and drop another mote of dust. Continue traveling east in this manner until all those motes of dust have been dropped.
Furthermore, take all the lands where dust was dropped as well as the lands where no dust was dropped, and reduce them all to motes of dust. One.
"One kalpa of dust. Since [the Buddha] actually attained Buddhahood in his original ground, the time has further exceeded this number by immeasurable and boundless amounts;

this reveals the reality of his original attainment. If the original and the manifested were intermingled without distinction, the flavor of the teaching would become discordant, remote, and incomplete.
"The two mysteries of the provisional and the ultimate, and the two subtleties of the relative and the absolute, cannot be manifested without these two gates of origin and trace.

One may understand this by seeking it through analogy with the remaining flavors and remaining sections. For example, the *Avataṃsaka* (Huayan) sudden section is assigned to the first "milk" flavor; it takes both the Shared and Distinct [teachings] as its primary focus.

Within this [Lotus Sūtra], one cannot take the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as the primary focus, because it possesses its own distinct orientation. As for the Vaipulya (Fangdeng) and Prajñāpāramitā...

If it is so, then up to the Vaipulya section, which corresponds to the middle flavor of gradual practice, *sarpis* (fresh butter) is assigned; its primary function is to refute and reject [erroneous views].

The Prajñā section, corresponding to the final flavor of gradual practice, is assigned *ghṛta* (matured butter); its primary function is to undergo refinement through further distillation. Thus it is said:

"The remaining flavors and remaining sections may be understood by seeking them through their respective analogies. As for the statement, "If now, even when employing various [methods] in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*..."
The intent of the teaching lies in the ten dharmas; when one achieves wondrous contemplation (*myōkan*) through them, the contemplation is primary while the teachings are secondary.
This is to reveal the true principle of the three thousand realms as the fundamental substance of the contemplative method. Therefore, it extends peripherally to all other teachings.

Although it is said to extend peripherally, the merit of its function in establishing wondrous contemplation is by no means shallow. It is for the sake of causing those who hear and practice it to give rise to deep faith; therefore—
First, citing various sutras and treatises from the side;
second, examining the similarities and differences among the teachings. Since the *Lotus Sūtra* is the basis, there must be eight teachings.

Although there are eight teachings, the four—sudden, gradual, secret, and indeterminate—are the Buddha’s methods of transformation (*vyañjana*), while the four—*piṭaka*, *tripiṭaka*, *vaipulya*, and *nikāya*—are the Buddha’s methods of transformation (*dharma*). Based on these dharmas, one gives rise to contemplation; as for this contemplation:

There are four [vehicles]. Since the gradual [vehicle] differs from the others, an indeterminate [vehicle] is further added; thus, when observing the teachings, there are six. By opening up the provisional and revealing the real, the three [vehicles] such as the Tripitaka are unified.
Because the gradual and the indeterminate fundamentally know the ultimate perfection, the Buddha’s original intent is that only the Buddha-vehicle exists.
Now, although the texts follow the teachings—whether they be eightfold or fourfold—their fundamental intent is solely to establish the One Buddha Vehicle.

The commentary states: "Regarding the observation of the similarities and differences of the teachings," this means that while the names of the teachings are the same, their essential natures are eternally different; hence, they are called "similar and different."
Regarding the sudden, gradual, and indeterminate teachings, they are situated within four periods: the Sudden teaching is in the *Avataṃsaka*; the Gradual teaching is in the three flavors;
and the Indeterminate teaching is interspersed throughout the four periods. Although these three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* share the same names, their essential natures differ.

Nevertheless, as for the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* discussed here, generally they all take the *Lotus Sūtra* as their ultimate source, while specifically each has its own particular lineage (as already seen above). For now, we shall follow the general perspective.
Thus it is said. Therefore, it is stated that since one relies upon the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there must be eight teachings (*aṣṭa-śāsana*). As for why there must be eight teachings:

As for the phrase "according to the teachings" in this passage, it refers to this *Mohe zhiguan*. Although there are the eight teachings and the four teachings, they are categorized as such because they are coarse...

It reveals the wondrous. By means of the conceivable, it reveals the inconceivable. The purport of this section is solely to establish the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekayāna*) through the three thousandfold wondrous contemplations.

Third, regarding the rules for the gates of contemplation: although four gates are established to accommodate various capacities and objects, the essence and measure of the teaching is non-arising (*anutpāda*).

For those afflicted by the disease of attachment to emptiness, they teach *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as the medicine to cure that emptiness.

the "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas" (*Fapobian*) in the *Zhiguan* first enumerates four gates and subsequently relies upon non-arising (*anutpāda*) for pervasive destruction.

If one is to interpret the characteristics of the dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) in order to establish practice and understanding, those who study the *Zhiguan* should know that this scriptural teaching— when interpreting the characteristics of the four gates— should be understood as follows.
The three teachings and four gates are coarse and provisional; only the four gates of the Perfect [Teaching] are subtle and real.

By providing detailed analysis and interpretation, one establishes the understanding of perfect practice; hence the term "practice and understanding. Regarding the expressions "rejection and supersession" and "comparison and decision":

using existence to reject non-existence, and using non-existence to reject existence; the same applies to both being and neither being nor non-being. As for comparison and decision, emptiness is superior.

Regarding "existence," and so forth, up to "the excellence of the neither-nor over the both-and": "above" refers to the gates [of existence, non-existence, both, and neither], while "below" refers to the neither-nor.

By synthesizing them in this way, they finally converge upon the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the three thousand worlds within the One Vehicle.
Fourth is "harmonizing differences and examining similarities. If all diverse names enter equally into a single reality, it is called "universal harmonization" (*tonghui*).

The meaning is as follows. Furthermore, that which breaks through pervasive categories and enters [the truth] is called a "General Assembly" (tonghui); that which pertains to a specific teaching or specific gate is called a "Specific Assembly" (biehui). Regarding the examination of similarities:

for instance, in the names established throughout the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras, although the volumes and sections differ, the names and their defining characteristics are not distinct.

How can one allow the Dharma to be treated as a single uniform whole simply because the names are the same? One must certainly use principle to discern and differentiate them. As with the various non-Buddhists...
Even humans still establish the names of the three bodies for Maheśvara; how could these three names be identical in essence as the ultimate goal of our own school?
Therefore, it is said that one must not seek a distinct essence by following the common name, and thus uses characteristics to distinguish them.

Consequently, one examines what is the same to bring out what is different, and considers what is different to bring together what is the same. Whether different or the same, they all enter the single ultimate.
The commentary states: "Harmonizing differences and examining similarities" means to harmonize differences so they become identical, and to examine similarities so their distinctions emerge.

This text consists of two parts: first, harmonizing differences; second, examining similarities. Harmonizing differences also has two parts: first, general harmonization; second, specific harmonization. Regarding general harmonization:

"However, while the four 'accordances' (*sui*) differ in name, they are identical in meaning. The four accordances are the great compassion that responds to what is beneficial; the four 'universals' (*si*) are the pervasive pity."
"Bestowal" (dāna) and "covering" (chāyā) differ only in their relative positions. For example, consider a single object: if a person stands to the east of the object, they call it "right";

The four [applications of] the four [types of] universal suitability (catuḥ-saṃvṛti) are likewise so. Furthermore, the *Dhyāna Sūtra* calls them the "teachings according to desire," which refers to the cultivation of causes. (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*)
This is called "worldly language," which refers to the receiving of retribution; these two differ only in terms of cause and effect.

The *Dhyāna Sūtra* calls this "selecting the Dharma according to what is convenient to adapt to individuals. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calls this "observing people for the sake of others to accommodate them with the Dharma";
these two differ only in their manner of joyful engagement. These are the names used in the sūtras and śāstras for "remedial means" (*pratipakṣa*) and "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*).
Because they are identical, there is no need for reconciliation; this reconciliation is the entry into totality (*sarvatraga*). Regarding the alternative names for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*:

as found in various sutras and treatises, they may be called "detachment," "non-abiding," or "non-attachment"; they are also termed "unconditioned," "quiescent extinction," and "non-discriminative meditative concentration.
These are the alternative names for *śamatha*. Alternatively, they are called "knowledge and vision," "clear cognition," "the eye," "awakening," or "wisdom."
"Prajñā-illumination," "clarity," and so forth are alternative names for this contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Since Prajñā is a single dharma that the Buddha has taught under various names, all these diverse names are unified under the single name of "contemplation. The same applies to liberation (*vimukti*);

because it has many names, all these diverse names are unified under the single name of "quiescence" (*śamatha*). Therefore, it is said that both the general and specific categories are subsumed [within these two].
The Dharma is exhausted; this exhausts the logical force of the "One Family" (Ekayāna) doctrine, yet the subsumption of all dharmas is inexhaustible.

As for the statement that even the "Dharma-gates" (dharmamukha) possess the meaning of both the general and specific assemblies, it means that not only do the [practices of] following, cessation, and contemplation possess them, but even all dharma-gates likewise possess the two assemblies of the general and the specific.
What are these dharma-gates? They are the Four Truths, the Four Mindfulnesses, and so on, up to the Eightfold Path.
The right [concentration], the three samādhis, the twelve links of dependent origination, the six perfections, and so forth—therefore they are called "Dharma-gates.

Furthermore, to break through all [gates] and enter [the ultimate] is called a "Universal Assembly" (tonghui). To accord with a specific teaching and a specific gate is called a "Distinctive Assembly" (biehui).

Because one uses the ten-vehicle contemplation method of the Gate of Non-arising to enter other gates, without distinguishing between the differences of gates and teachings, it is called a "Universal Assembly. When...

Regarding the designation of "distinct assemblies" (*bieh-hui*) for the respective teachings and gates: although *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calming and insight) establishes three teachings and four gates, we here provisionally rely on the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

This constitutes the "appropriate teaching. Among the three gates, sometimes the gate of "existence" (*you*) is the appropriate gate for entry; even up to the point where the gate of "neither emptiness nor existence" (*fei kong fei you*) serves as the appropriate gate for entry.

Furthermore, within these specific [categories], there are both general and specific aspects. Regarding the "examination of similarities":

whenever names are established in the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras, although their volumes and sections differ, their names and characteristics are not distinct. How can one allow the Dharma to be treated as a uniform whole simply because the names are identical?

One must certainly distinguish the Dharma through its underlying principles. As for "Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras," setting aside the Mahāyāna treatises, consider the Hīnayāna ones, such as the *Madhyama Āgama*.
The bhikṣus praised what Śāriputra had said as the most sublime among the sublime. Furthermore, they said: "The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

Departing from these two extremes, there is the Middle Way. One should know that this most sublime of the sublime is not to be regarded as inconceivable."
The term "subtle" (*miao*) refers merely to Śāriputra’s explanation of the skillful means of the patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*), which does not harm the objects of others.
This middle way (*madhyamā pratipad*) cannot be taken as the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*). This middle way is simply that which is free from suffering and free from pleasure;

Regarding the names of the three bodies (*trikāya*), the *Ji* (Record) of the fourth fascicle states: "The ash-smearing heretics (*pāśupata*) also reckon that Maheśvara possesses three bodies;

Therefore, it is said that one cannot seek a distinct essence by following the general name; thus, one uses characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) to distinguish them.

By means of the teachings, one differentiates between the heterodox and the orthodox, the Great and the Small, and the partial and the perfect. Only the Perfect [Teaching] can be called truly possessing reality.
Thus, one examines similarities to reveal their differences, and reconciles differences so that all may become identical. This concludes the two preceding sections. Whether they are different...

Regarding "entering together into the single ultimate": when the preceding notions of identity and difference are both subsumed as being neither identical nor different, one then returns to the single ultimate.
This "single ultimate" is the three thousand realms of reality (sanqian shixiang).

Fifth, using one case as an illustration for all: just as with the two paths of teaching and realization, or the qualities possessed by a single mind, one does not—unlike worldly people who grasp at a single moment of conceivable objects and establish it as the Buddha-dharma-realm—take what was previously explained as conceivable and subsequently explain it as inconceivable and so forth.

The commentary states: This section of text consists of five parts. It is intended to clarify that when the Great Master Tiantai expounded the Dharma, although the text may appear in a single location, its meaning runs through from beginning to end.

"If poison is placed in milk, the milk will kill a person. This milk is a metaphor for the teaching of the sudden exposition of the *Huáyán*; therefore, it is said: [as follows].
