Karma, demons, dhyāna, and the two vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha) are the karma-obstruction (*karmāvaraṇa*). Since the correlations are thus established, the underlying meaning may also be seen.

The aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) are precisely the signs of the activity of the *māra* of the aggregates. The meditative concentrations of the followers of the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas constitute the *māra* of the formations aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Afflictions, views, pride, and so forth are the *māra* of afflictions. Illness is the *māra* of death, for illness is the cause of death.
The "work of Māra" refers to the celestial Māra (devaputra-māra). If one explains the meaning [of the text], this can also be seen there.

I maintain that this passage discusses "separation" from a horizontal perspective; for among the ten objects (*daśa-viṣaya*), each has its own sequence or lack thereof, extending even to the distinctions between "further" and "not further," the three obstructions (*trividha-āvaraṇa*), and the four Māras. It is for this reason that it is so stated.
Furthermore, as for the "ten objects" (*daśa-viṣaya*), they are also presented in their entirety for the purpose of establishing the number ten.

The commentary states: This corresponds to the second [section], which discusses detachment (*viveka*) in terms of vertical progression. The text is arranged according to the sequence of arising to clarify the ten objects;
that is, the meaning of discussing detachment vertically exists within the number ten, hence it is so stated.
Therefore, the subsequent chapter poses the question: "If dharmas are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, why is the object fixed at ten?
The commentary states: This corresponds to the third [section], which cites evidence to show that the object must necessarily be ten.

The purpose of citing this passage is to clarify that when establishing the objects of contemplation for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, they must reach the number ten; for if they were too extensive, it would cause the intellect to regress, yet if they were too brief, the meaning would not be complete.
"Zhou" (ten) is used because it occupies the central position; therefore, it stops at ten. Moreover, ten is the number representing the generative and transformative processes of Heaven and Earth;
for this reason, when constructing halls or establishing gates, one invariably reaches the number ten. The phrase "the following are the...

refers to the passage in Zhiyi’s *Ten Objects of Contemplation* (*Shi-jing*) concerning the formal exposition of the ten objects. Jingxi [Zhanran] points out that these correspond to the sixteen sections within Chan’an’s private compendium, the *Liao-jian*.
The first question among the series of questions and answers asks: why are there only ten objects (*viṣaya*) in total? The current text does not cite the specific answer.
If, within these ten, one were further to combine them—merging those of the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas into a single "object of skillful means" (*upāya-viṣaya*)—then...
There are only nine [categories]. If one includes the afflictions within the six obscurations as the characteristics of the causal conditions for habituation, there are only eight.
If one takes the afflictions, karma, and the aggregates (*skandhas*) as the objects of the three paths (*trivartman*), there are only seven.

Alternatively, based on the previous eight, if one further includes pride (*māna*) within the category of the afflictions, it likewise results in only seven. If one includes views (*dṛṣṭi*) and pride within worldly dhyāna...
If subsumed [into categories], there are only six. Furthermore, if the affliction of illness is included within the aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*), there are only five.
Regarding "four" and "three": these are like the four Māras and the three obstacles (*āvaraṇa*). If one considers only the contrast between their arising and non-arising, they constitute only two.

If one speaks only of a single object of observation, there is only one. Although such are the ways of opening and closing [the categories], what is clarified here is the nature and class of the characteristics of their arising.

The same applies here; thus, there are ten. By correlating the aggregates (*skandha*) with the nine [categories], the aggregates are not "arisen-attained" (*utpādita-prāpta*). Therefore, the two vehicles and the Bodhisattvas are established separately.

Although their skillful means (*upāya*) are the same, because their resolve (*cittotpāda*) differs, the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*) is heavy while the causal seeds of habituation (*vāsanā-hetu*) are slight.

Because they mutually interpenetrate one another, it is called the "Path" (*mārga*). In all these cases of "arisen-attainment," all three manifest simultaneously. Regarding pride (*māna*) and the afflictions, there is both overlap and non-overlap.
They are distinct. Within dhyāna, visions do not necessarily arise in every case. Although illness may be a manifestation of the *skandhas*, the *skandhas* are not necessarily illness.

Although illness may involve karma, it is not necessarily the manifestation of karmic signs. Although illness may involve māras, it already belongs to the realm of māras. The manifestations of the second, third, and fourth [stages] are somewhat differentiated;
how much more so when they are treated as a single category, which is most general and diffuse.

The commentary states: The answer is that the extraordinary and the ordinary can be unified. Regarding "the causes for the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*) are heavy while the causes for their habitual cultivation are light":

as for "afflictions," generally speaking, these are greed, hatred, and delusion. The *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation) says: "Though one may have been prone to anger since birth, one understands when admonished;
yet what is now aroused is a raging fury, terrifying to behold. While the inverted perceptions of one's life have arisen and ceased only momentarily, what is now..."
That which has arisen remains heavy and does not depart. Since birth, one’s greed for sensory forms may have been suppressed and brought to rest;
yet that which has now arisen makes no distinction between a dead horse and its living counterpart. This is the arising of heavy afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding the causes of light habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the *Zhiguan* states: "Inner mental pain is the habit of killing; inner mental heaviness is the habit of stealing; inner mental vexation..."
Restlessness is the habituation of lust. Since its causal habituation is so slight, how could it possibly be combined with the afflictions (*kleśa*) to form a single entity?

Because they mutually interact and permeate one another, they are called "paths" (*mārga*). Regarding the statement that these various "arising-attainments" (*utpatti-prāpti*) all manifest simultaneously:

this clarifies that the afflictions, karma, and the aggregates (*skandha*) cannot be combined into a single "threefold path-object. As for the phrase "these various arising-attainments," it refers to...

[This refers to] affliction (*kleśa*) and karma (*karman*). The objects of the three paths constantly manifest before one. Because they are "manifestly arising" (*samudācāra*), and "manifestly arising" means "active functioning" (*pravṛtti*).
This is not like afflictions and so forth, which are obtained through contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Therefore, it says: "These various obtainments (*pratilambha*)—all three—are manifestly arising.
Since they cannot be conflated, the compiler, not understanding the meaning of the text, instead claims that "all three are manifestly arising" [refers to something else].
How erroneous is [the claim regarding] the karma of affliction (*nāman-karma*) and so forth! As for the confusion between pride (*māna*) and the afflictions (*kleśa*):

the previous explanation stated that, based on the first eight [categories], pride is further included within the afflictions; therefore, the present explanation says that pride is confused with and distinct from the afflictions.
There are eight types of pride; seven of them are minor, while the eighth, the pride of superiority (*abhimāna*), is grave. Because it is distinct, it constitutes a separate object.

If pride regarding the Dharma were subsumed under the afflictions (*kleśa*), it would then overlap with the distinct category of "pride of superiority" (*abhimāna*); therefore, they cannot be combined.
As for the statement that "in dhyāna, views do not necessarily arise," this explains that views and pride are included within mundane dhyāna.
Indeed, when one cultivates and attains the *anāgamya* concentration or the four dhyānas with a mind seeking fame and profit, these states frequently give rise to views or to pride of superiority.

If one cultivates and attains the *anāgamya* (unattained) and other concentrations with a truly correct mind, one will not necessarily give rise to the pride of seeing (*dṛṣṭi-māna*) or higher forms of pride.
Therefore, the objects of such views and pride cannot be subsumed within worldly dhyāna. Although illness is indeed an aggregate (*skandha*), the aggregate is not necessarily illness.

This explains how the aforementioned "sickness" is subsumed within the aggregates and the sense-bases (*āyatana*). Why is this? Because there are those who remain free from illness throughout their entire existence within the aggregates.
For instance, the Venerable Bakula was free even from the ailment of a headache throughout his entire life, let alone other diseases.
Therefore, it is said that the *āyatanas* (bases) are not necessarily diseased; thus, one cannot conflate disease with the *āyatana-dhātus*.

Regarding the statement that "although there is karma in disease, it is not the manifestation of the characteristics of karma": as for what is called "disease," there are indeed diseases resulting from evil karma. Although these are termed "karma," they are not [the manifestation of the characteristics of karma].
Just as various karmas manifest within the objective sphere of the characteristics of karma, although illness may involve Māra, it already belongs to the realm of Māra.
If it belongs to the realm of Māra, one must necessarily be wary and alert toward Māra. If it does not fall under these three [categories], it does not belong to the affairs of Māra.

Regarding the discernment of karma and Māra within illness, these two are introduced here for the sake of convenience; they are not part of the aforementioned classification and synthesis. [This applies to] the second, third, and fourth [cases].
The characteristics of arousal are already somewhat distinguished; how much more so when considering that which is merely singular and even more pervasive?
This explains the preceding passage regarding arousal and non-arousal as having only two objects. What constitutes arousal? What constitutes non-arousal?

The three obstacles and four māras are simply a comprehensive categorization of the ten objects. If something is not among the three obstacles, it is then one of the four māras; this is merely stated in general terms. If...
However, regarding that which is to be observed as a single object: for what great practice (*mahācaryā*) is this a target? What is its standard?
Therefore, it is said that "the characteristics of their arising are somewhat distinguished. The character "頗" (*po*) is likely an error; it should be "叵" (*po*), meaning "not possible" (*na śakya*).

Thus, one knows that although previously [the ten objects] were permitted to accord with the general principle, they are now individually refuted and returned to the opening [of the teaching], thereby preserving the ten objects (*daśaviṣaya*).
The number serves as the definitive standard.
Therefore, the "conformity to characteristics" (*anulakṣaṇa*) must necessarily be opened up into ten.
The commentary states: This refers to the third point, that there must be ten; it means that for each of the ten objects, there are their respective characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Characteristic...
Since their characteristics are distinct, they must not be conflated; is it not here that the Holy Master established [this teaching]?
Next, I shall clarify the intent behind the formulation of the Ten Vehicles.

The commentary states: The third section clarifies the intent behind establishing the ten vehicles, which is divided into two parts. First, the heading of the text is evident. Second, the explanation has four sub-sections:

first, citing the text to provide the foundation for establishing the intent; second, "Now, exploring... and below, the actual explanation; third, "Now, searching... and below, clarifying the intent of establishing examples based on the text;
fourth, the formal establishment of the examples, which is further divided into two.
The subsequent passage states: "Transversely and vertically encompassing all, the ten contemplations are complete.
The commentary explains: This citation of the subsequent passage serves as the foundation for establishing the present intent.

Although the current text is precisely clarifying the intent of the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*), it refers to the "subsequent passage" because Master Jingxi, having already provided an exegesis of this *Mohe Zhiguan* text, applies that which is capable of explaining [the intent] to explain [it].

Regarding the "subject of exposition" (*vyākhyeya*), the commentator therefore points to that subject as the "subsequent text. The compiler states: "The text concerning the combination and separation of the ten objects concludes, and immediately thereafter the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*) are clarified;
hence it is called 'the subsequent text. Now, I say: the thematic headings for the ten vehicles have already been established at the outset.

One should not, however, consider the combination and separation of the ten objects (*daśaviṣaya*) as superior; this text treats them as subordinate. Regarding the term "establishing the foundation" (*zhāngběn*):

it means that these five expositions serve as the fundamental basis. Therefore, from the general and specific expositions up to the "eternal difference," they do not go beyond the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*) in their horizontal and vertical dimensions;
hence, it is called "establishing the foundation."

Now, examining the meaning of the text, it is explained in five ways: first, a general explanation; second, a specific explanation; third, an explanation by means of the four propositions of horizontal and vertical relations;

fourth, an explanation of the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) according to the underlying intent of the text; and fifth, an explanation that is eternally distinct from those established by others.
The commentary states: This constitutes the second section, the formal explanation consisting of three parts, which outlines the intent and divides the categories.

These five categories were extracted by the Venerable Jingxi from the meaning of the *Ten Contemplations* (*Shi guan*), such that nothing therein exceeds these five; they are fully contained within the *Commentary* (*Ji wen*).

Therefore, I shall now cite the relevant passages from that *Commentary* one by one and briefly provide an explanation. Regarding the term "general explanation," it refers to [the explanation] found in each respective stage.
The ten [realms] viewed in relation to one another are called "horizontal" (*tiryak*). Each one, taken individually according to its own category, has its own height and depth;
this is called "vertical" (*ūrdhva*). This is the first general explanation of the horizontal and vertical. As for the specific explanation:

as stated in the *Inconceivable Realm* (Acintya-viṣaya), "reaching the bottom of the true reality" (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) is called vertical, while "encompassing the ten dharma-realms" is called horizontal. Regarding the "Arousing of the Mind" (*Cittotpāda*), it says: "Seeking the higher is called vertical; seeking the lower..."

The horizontal is named "crossing over" (gyō). Furthermore, seeking the upper while relying on the lower is named "vertical" (shuku). Vowing based on the object is named "horizontal"; settling the mind to penetrate the principle is named "vertical.
The sixty-four stages are named "horizontal," up to the entry and abiding in non-attachment, which is named "vertical. Departing from the three semblances of phenomena is named "horizontal.
This is the second section, the detailed explanation of horizontal and vertical. Regarding the four propositions of horizontal and vertical: by means of...

The ten vehicles of the partial teachings are called "horizontal" and "vertical" when viewed from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching. This is also like using "horizontal" and "vertical" to manifest that which is neither horizontal nor vertical.

If the inconceivable, which is neither horizontal nor vertical, can produce the horizontal and vertical while being described as horizontal and vertical, this constitutes the third fourfold interpretation of the horizontal and vertical.
There are two types of explanation: the collective and the individual; there are four permutations regarding the horizontal and vertical dimensions, as fully detailed in the *Commentary* (*Ji*).
The commentary states: "This constitutes the second section, the correct explanation. A brief reference to the text of the *Commentary* is provided here.
These three topical divisions are already complete in the *Commentary* and will not be presented again; they are briefly as cited in the present text."

Regarding the appended text: the ten dharmas arising is also termed "vertical" (*ūrdhva*). Within each individual dharma, there are various meanings contained therein, which is also termed "horizontal" (*tiryak*).
As for their arising, as expressed in the text, each contains multiple meanings; these are explained in detail according to their respective meanings in the main body of the work.

The commentary states: This constitutes the third section, which sets forth the explanation currently being provided. Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of the dharmas arising in accordance with the text":

this refers to the sequential order of the dharmas that arise in accordance with the text of the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*). Each possesses its own specific characteristics, and is thus termed "vertical" (*ūrdhva*).

Furthermore, because each of these ten vertical dharmas contains multiple meanings, they are also termed "horizontal" (*tiryak*). Therefore, it is said that the vertical is established in relation to the horizontal.
Regarding the discussion of the vertical: to speak of the horizontal is to discuss the horizontal in relation to the vertical.

As for the phrase "the manner of arising is as in the text," this refers to the main body of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Calming and Contemplation); hence it says "as in the text. That text states: "Having personally realized the wondrous realm, one immediately gives rise to vows of compassion for others.
Next, one performs practices to fulfill those vows. Since these vows and practices are skillful, there is nothing they do not pervade. Within this pervasive penetration, [one applies] refinement..."

One discerns what is obstructed and what is unobstructed, causing the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) to progress. Furthermore, one employs this to assist in opening the Way. Within the stages of the Way, one discerns both oneself and others;
one remains equanimous toward internal and external honor and disgrace, and does not cling to the "dharma-love" (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) of the Middle Way.

Thus, one swiftly enters the rank of a Bodhisattva. This is precisely the passage that brings forth the meaning according to the text; it is a discussion of the vertical progression based on the horizontal [classification].
The statement that "each and every dharma contains multiple meanings, which is also called 'horizontal' (*tieng*)," refers to the discussion of the horizontal in relation to the vertical.

That each possesses multiple meanings is fully detailed in the main text; regarding the separate explanations according to their respective meanings, for example, the text on the "First Inconceivable Realm" contains seven sections:
(1) the realm of innate virtue (*xingde*), (2) the realm of cultivated virtue (*xiude*), (3) the realm of transforming others, and (4)... [text continues].

The matters and principles of self and others are synthesized to establish the three truths. Fifth, the analogies of the wish-fulfilling jewel and so forth are presented. Sixth, the functional capacity is clarified.
Seventh, the integration into the single mind is clarified as the overall object of contemplation.

Within this initial vehicle, the topics from the arousal of the bodhicitta up to the departure from craving are explained individually according to their respective meanings; each contains multiple layers of significance, as detailed in the original text.
The texts cannot be cited in full here; this is a case of discussing the horizontal based on the vertical.

Now, by searching the intent of the texts and grasping the concise to know the extensive, although there are minor differences in quantity, I have now categorized each of the ten dharmas into five examples;
thus, these ten are established.
The commentary states: This constitutes the third correct explanation, clarifying the intention behind establishing examples based on the text.
To say "now searching through the text" means that one is searching for the horizontal and vertical meanings within the text-based examples; hence, it says "now searching."

Regarding "comprehending the broad by means of the concise": this refers to causing those who study *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to grasp the conciseness of the five categories while knowing the breadth of the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*).

Although there are slight differences in the number [of items] here and there, Master Jingxi’s intention was that the text of the current five categories and the original text of the ten vehicles are not without slight discrepancies in their number; therefore, each of the ten dharmas is divided into five.

For example, these five examples are employed merely to support the ten vehicles. Fourth, the formal establishment of the examples has two parts: first, establishing five examples for each of the ten vehicles;
second, clarifying below that what has been established differs from the various other schools. The first part [of the second section] also has two sub-parts.
Initially, each of the ten vehicles has five [aspects]. Second, regarding the conclusion of the ten examples, there are five meanings that encompass both the provisional and the ultimate.

As for the five aspects of the wondrous object: first, to demonstrate that the three thousand realms are contained within a single thought-moment; second, to demonstrate that the ultimate principle differs from the subsequent vehicles;
third, because one wishes to reveal and clarify the conceivable object; and fourth, so that those of sharp faculties may attain awakening to the principle.
The fifth is because it serves as the basis for the nine dharmas below.

The commentary states: these five categories are established based on the wondrous object. Regarding the statement that "the three thousand [realms] reside within a single thought-moment," the word "reside" (zai) is a term used for indication.
Since it is said that the three thousand are identical to a single thought-moment, [it follows that] a single thought-moment...

This refers precisely to the three thousand [realms]. How could there be any distinction between "that which is capable" and "the place where it resides"? It is shown that there is nothing by which to represent the locus of the wondrous realm of the three thousand;
therefore, it is said that the three thousand exist within a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*).

Furthermore, one should understand that the present text demonstrates that the three thousand exist within a single thought-moment because it seeks to establish the method of contemplating the mind (*cittāvalokana*) in the *Mohe zhiguan*. If one were to discuss...
Phenomena and phenomena mutually contain and mutually lead to one another. How could it be that the three thousand realms exist only within a single thought-moment?

Thus, whether it be form, fragrance, flavor, or touch; whether self or other, birth or Buddha, the conditioned or the unconditioned—each and every one without exception contains the three thousand realms.
It is simply that they manifest according to the capacity of the practitioner. Within contemplation and outside of contemplation, the three thousand realms are wondrous.

This applies to all objects everywhere; students should understand this. The three thousand wonderful objects are the pivotal essence of this entire treatise and the structural backbone of the ten vehicles.
When practicing contemplation, this alone is the method. Thus it is said: "First taking the true reality as the object, one creates the realm; therein, there is nothing that is not the Middle.
Therefore, one should know that the three thousand [objects] are precisely the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way. As one...

The function encompasses both the extremes of emptiness and the provisional, because the Middle Way takes the simultaneous negation of these two as its essence and their simultaneous illumination as its function.

Furthermore, the *Jinbi* (Golden Needle) states: "These three thousand realms are, in their nature, the Middle Way; they do not belong to existence or non-existence, for existence and non-existence are simply as they are.
The intention of the Patriarch—both the text and its meaning—is as clear as the bright sun. How could it be that the compiler [of this work]...?

The difficulty lies in asserting that the three thousand [realms] definitively reside within the provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*) while being absent from the true nature (*tathatā*) within emptiness; these two would then be inherently incompatible.
Therefore, in explaining the passage stating that "the three thousand reside in a single thought-moment," one extensively cites various texts to justify one's own view.

Yet, the desire to insist that the three thousand definitively reside in the provisional can never be established. As the *I Ching* says: "When there is doubt in the heart, the words become rambling."
To cite [the text] at random and offer a mere exegesis of one's own is surely insufficient to prevent the errors of one’s past; how could such an attempt possibly succeed?
Furthermore, this misinterpretation originated with Master Yue of Jiahe, whose teachings were inherited by Master Zhan.

The compiler then appended his own views to those of Master Zhan. This is what is meant by the saying: "If learning does not take An as its teacher, and words do not hit the mark, it will lead to difficulty. Although...
He has produced many writings. Who would believe such a perverse doctrine? I too have carefully examined the compiler’s intent and clearly know it for myself;
it is not out of pride that I stubbornly refuse to change my mind.

Rather, it is because I wish to obstruct the ears and eyes of future generations that I speak thus. In the world to come, how could the retribution for the sin of slandering the Dharma ever be avoided?

[This section] has been liberated. As the preceding text has already refuted [the opposing views], I shall not cite them in full. Second, to demonstrate that the ultimate principle differs from the later vehicles:

the ultimate principle is precisely the wondrous realm of the three thousand [realms]. That it differs from the later vehicles means that, from the moment of first generating the bodhicitta onward, it is explained in terms of the gate of cultivation.
It involves few practical applications; rather, it takes the wondrous object itself as the very nature of mind to serve as the observing subject.

This is like the explanation in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* by Tiantai: merely hearing these words causes illness to be immediately cured. This serves as the contemplative method for those of the initial vehicle (*ādikarmika-yāna*).

It is like reaching an elder’s place to have medicinal decoctions prepared; this corresponds to the nine successive vehicles (*navayāna*) beginning from the arousal of the bodhicitta (*cittotpāda*) onwards. Thus one should know.

To take the ultimate principle as the object of contemplation is what distinguishes it from the later vehicles. The compiler, however, maintained that the "three thousand [realms]" are definitively the conventional realm of differentiation;

thus, in his commentary on this passage, his mind was deceived and his speech was obstructed. Consequently, he did not dare to state that the wondrous realm of the three thousand is the ultimate principle.
Instead, he sought to conceal his error and carelessly pointed to the passage concerning the "three turnings" and the "ten dharma realms."

Yet these are taken as the Three Truths, which are regarded as the ultimate principle. If one uses the Three Truths as the ultimate principle to explain the sutras prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, how has it ever not been explained by means of the Three Truths?
How could it be that all such explanations represent the final and ultimate teaching?
The Compiler further states: "The 'three thousand [realms] in a single thought' (ichinen-sangyō) is a conventional dharma of differentiated multiplicity.
Now, let us inquire into this: I wonder whether this conventionality is itself inconceivable (*acintya*) or not. If it is inconceivable, how does it differ from the Real?
If so, why must one wait until the Middle and the Real are unified within a single thought as a totality before it can serve as a guiding principle? If that were the case, then the three thousand...
This is not a guide; it must wait for the "immediate middle" (*jìzhōng*) to serve as a guide. This contradicts the texts on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* and the records of Jingxi in their very essence.
Truly, this belongs to those who merely parrot words; their minds have attained nothing, and they preach while being ignorant of the delusions.
They are to be blamed, truly to be blamed. Third, regarding the phrase "in order to reveal and clarify the conceivable realm": this is because of [the practice of] contemplation (*guan*).
The mind is the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*). This realm is difficult to explain and difficult to understand; therefore, one first clarifies the conceivable realm (*cintya-viṣaya*).
Once the conceivable has been contemplated, the conceivable is opened up to become the inconceivable. One should know that the entirety of the conceivable is the inconceivable Dharma;

by manifesting the arising [of the conceivable], it fully reveals the possession [of the inconceivable], and thus there is nothing surpassing this subtlety. Fourth, it is for the sake of awakening those of sharp faculties.
Regarding "by way of principle": those of superior faculties may, through a single contemplation, ascend to the First Abode or reach the stages of the Inner or Outer Ordinary Beings;
thus, the inconceivable realm is for those of superior faculties. From the arousal of the bodhicitta up to the assistance in opening [the realization], it is for those of middling faculties.

The successive stages, patient endurance, and detachment from craving are for those of inferior faculties. Regarding "opening the awakening to principle": this refers to opening the awakening to the principle of the three thousand real marks. This...

Regarding this awakening, one should know that there are three types of fivefold stages: awakening through the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), awakening through the similarity of the six sense faculties, and awakening through the partial realization of the true nature at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).
As for the statement that "the first [stage] serves as the basis for the nine subsequent dharmas":

since the contemplative method of the initial vehicle takes the three thousand realms (*trisahasra*) as the essence of its contemplation, the nine subsequent vehicles are no different from this. Therefore...
The arousal of the mind relies on the three thousand [realms] for its arousal; skillful placement in śamatha and vipaśyanā relies on the three thousand for its placement;
even detachment from craving relies on the three thousand for its detachment. Taking the three thousand as the guiding compass—this statement is indeed correct. The compiler explains this as follows:
Thus, they did not dare to say that the "three thousand" constitute the basis upon which the teaching relies; instead, they spoke only of the "wondrous realm of the three truths.
How can such a deceitful mind be so? *Zhiguan yili suishi*, Fascicle Two.
An Exegesis Following the *Yi-li* on the Meaning of Stopping and Contemplation, Scroll Three.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chuyuan of Yongjia.
An Explanation Following the Exposition of the Intent of the Ten Vehicles.

There are five reasons for the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*): first, because even those who have understood the principle still require a vow; second, to clarify that the arousal of the mind encompasses all phenomena universally;
third, to distinguish it from various partial and inferior [vehicles]; fourth, to clarify that those of middling faculties awaken only when they arouse the mind;
and fifth, to serve as the beginning of the practice for the eight dharmas of the lower [stage].
The commentary states: "First, those who seek to understand the principle must still cultivate vows" refers to individuals of middling capacity entering the Path.
Since they have gained nothing from practicing the Initial Vehicle, it is because they have not yet resolved their minds upon the Dharma-realm to seek enlightenment above and transform beings below.
Therefore, relying on the wondrous principle of the three thousand worlds and the unconditioned Four Noble Truths, they give rise to the Four Great Vows.

Now, saving sentient beings and severing delusions is the realm of downward transformation; it takes compassion as its essence. Studying the Dharma to achieve Buddhahood is the realm of upward seeking;
it takes kindness as its essence. Kindness is able to bestow happiness: the happiness of one is the happiness of all, and the three thousand worlds constitute the essence of this happiness.
Compassion is able to extract suffering: the suffering of one is the suffering of all, and the three thousand worlds constitute the essence of this suffering. This is therefore...
Outside of suffering there is no pleasure; outside of pleasure there is no suffering. This is called uprooting the suffering of the nature-virtue and [attaining] the pleasure of the nature-virtue.

In this suffering and this pleasure, suffering lacks the characteristic of suffering and pleasure lacks the characteristic of pleasure; there is nothing that is not the true reality (*dharmatā*). Now, let me further demonstrate this:

"downward transformation" refers to the two truths of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-satya* and *samudaya-satya*). Suffering refers to the retributive fruits of the ten realms, while the origin refers to the ten...

The realms, afflictions, karma, and birth-and-death are themselves nirvana; this is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Afflictions are themselves bodhi; this is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

This is the Perfect and Real Four Noble Truths. When suffering and its origin are themselves the path and cessation, and the path and cessation are themselves suffering and its origin, then the point where the causes and effects of the ten realms and hundred realms are fused is itself called the "Path.
That their very substance is quiescent and absolute is itself called "Cessation. Therefore, it is said: "Suffering..."
The accumulation [of suffering] is itself the path and cessation; the path and cessation are themselves the accumulation of suffering. To state it briefly:
it is simply that the practitioner of contemplation relies upon this wondrous object, and through the intense pain [arising from] regarding self and others, accomplishes the wondrous contemplation.

Therefore, it is said that even for one who seeks to understand the principle, one must still make a vow. Furthermore, it should be understood that this generation of the mind is that which is generated within meditative concentration (*samādhi*). If...
Before practicing meditation, it is not that the arousal of the resolve (bodhicitta) is absent; this is as in the "Arousing of the Great Resolve" within the Five Brevities.

Although what is aroused is the same, there is no lack of distinction between that which occurs within meditative concentration and that which occurs outside of it. Second, it is for the purpose of clarifying that the arousal of the resolve encompasses all phenomena universally.
Since the arousal of the mind relies upon the three thousand wondrous realms, this is precisely the unconditioned Four Noble Truths within a single thought-moment.

Arousing the mind by taking these unconditioned Four Noble Truths as its object exhausts the three truths vertically and encompasses the Dharma-realm horizontally; there is no encompassing of phenomena that exceeds this.
Third, regarding the phrase "in order to distinguish it from various partial and small [vehicles]": this refers to the object of the present Perfect (or Complete) arousal of the mind.
The arising of the four great vows from the truth of non-action is therefore called the truly correct generation of the mind (*samyak-cittotpāda*).
This distinguishes it from the bodhisattvas of the three teachings, the two vehicles of the two teachings, and the nine non-minds; all of these are not truly correct. Thus it is said:

"To distinguish [it] from the various partial and small [vehicles]. In the text, the character *bian* (to distinguish) has been corrupted through transcription into *bian* (to divide); this is because in the Zhou dynasty, [the character for] skin...

It is called a *biàn* (弁) because it is for the purpose of a crown; this is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*). It is also called *biàn* (辨), meaning "to distinguish"; this is pronounced with the entering tone (*shàngshēng*).

Both the characters and their pronunciations are incorrect and must be corrected. The same applies to the following examples. Regarding the fourth point, "to clarify that those of middling faculties awaken only when [the method] is applied":
if one practices the contemplative methods of the initial vehicle for a long time without attaining entry, what should be done? For this reason, only then—
The teacher instructs them, or they recognize for themselves what is to be advanced and what is to be abandoned; therefore, one generates the bodhicitta based on the object.

It is through this generation that one awakens, and its efficacy arises from the vow. As for the statement "the fifth is the beginning of the eight lower practices," the vow constitutes the commencement of practice.

"Beginning" (*shi*) means "root" (*hon*). When the root is established, practice arises; therefore, it is said that one "initiates the *saṃnāha* (armoring) at the initial mind," and "concludes with great compassion in responding to hardships.
Thus, from the initial settling of the mind (*anjin*) through to the primary and auxiliary practices, they are collectively termed "fulfilling the vow.

Although the latter three stages are not themselves contemplative methods (*kanpō*), they are collectively termed "contemplation" (*kan*) by virtue of the power of contemplation. Contemplation is itself practice (*gyō*). Therefore—
It is known that the arousal of the bodhicitta is the beginning of practice.

Regarding the five ways of settling the mind: first, it is to clarify that although there is an aspiration, one must still engage in practice; second, it is to distinguish those of middling faculties who find it difficult to settle their minds;
third, it is to show that while the Dharma is the same, its application varies according to the individual; fourth, it is to show how ordinary beings bring peace to both themselves and others.
The fifth is for the purpose of demonstrating the opening of the general [category] and the establishment of the specific.
The commentary states: "First, because even those with aspirations must still practice. This means that to have aspirations without practice is called "frantic aspiration" (*unmattapraṇidhāna*).
When practice fulfills one's vows and vows accord with practice, the Buddha-way can be expected. This is also explained from the perspective of the arising of a single period [of teaching].

If one has already entered [the path] previously, would this [practice] still be necessary? Second, regarding the purpose of distinguishing those of middling faculties who find it difficult to settle their minds:
Now, there are generally two types of settling the mind. First, general settling; second, specific settling. General settling...

It consists solely of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). Thus it is said: "The quiescence of the *dharmatā* is called *śamatha*; being quiescent while constantly illuminating is called *vipaśyanā*.
Since the capacities of sentient beings follow many paths and cannot be standardized, one follows their inclinations and establishes them in peace according to what they desire.
By employing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* through the four *siddhāntas*, there are sixty-four permutations. It is like a single net that contains a thousand [meshes].
The eyes: ultimately, the one who catches the fish relies on only a single eye. Although it is caught by one eye, it must necessarily depend upon all the eyes;
only when these sixty-four [eyes] are combined can it be seen. Regarding the third point, "to show that while the Dharma is the same, it varies according to the person":

"Dharma" refers to the three thousandfold [worlds] of wondrous stillness and wondrous contemplation. Their essence is fundamentally the same and cannot be different. "Varying according to the person" means that, in general...

There are distinctions among the various types of peace (*an*). Because their root natures (*indriya-gotra*) differ, there are those who possess emptiness (*śūnyatā*), those who possess existence (*bhava*), those who possess both, and those who possess neither.

Through these four gates, there are the four *siddhi* (the fourfold means of universal salvation), as well as the faith-practice (*śraddhā-carita*) and dharma-practice (*dharma-carita*) lineages; these mutually support one another, revolving and differing according to circumstances.

Thus, one should know that while the Dharma is but a single thought-moment, the three thousand realms manifest differently according to specific conditions. Yet for one who awakens and enters [this truth], what distinction can there be between sameness and difference? IV.

Regarding the phrase "to demonstrate the peace of both self and others for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*)," "ordinary persons" refers to ordinary teachers. Those in the five stages (*pañca-vastu*) and the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are called ordinary teachers; only when one has shattered the delusions of ignorance (*avidyā-kleśa*) is one called a holy teacher (*ārya-ācārya*). Thus, we know that a teacher is difficult to find. Today, base individuals are everywhere; can those who hold such a position avoid error? As for "the peace of self and others": [the text continues as follows: The Master said: "If you wish to establish the peace of self and others, you must first seek the Way within yourself. If you do not seek the Way within yourself, how can you establish the peace of others? Therefore, the Tathāgata taught: 'If you wish to save all sentient beings, you must first subdue your own mind. This is because the mind is the root of all dharmas. If the mind is not subdued, one cannot even benefit oneself, let alone others. For this reason, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. He further said: "The precepts are the foundation of the Way. Without the precepts, there is no Way. Without the Way, there is no Bodhi. Without Bodhi, there is no Nirvana. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. If one upholds the precepts purely, one will naturally attain the Way. If one attains the Way, one will naturally attain Bodhi. If one attains Bodhi, one will naturally attain Nirvana. For this reason, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. He further said: "The precepts are the gate to the Dharma. Without the precepts, there is no Dharma. Without the Dharma, there is no Sangha. Without the Sangha, there is no Triple Gem. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. If one upholds the precepts purely, one will naturally enter the Dharma-gate. If one enters the Dharma-gate, one will naturally join the Sangha. If one joins the Sangha, one will naturally honor the Triple Gem. For this reason, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. He further said: "The precepts are the armor of the Bodhisattva. Without the precepts, there is no armor. Without armor, one cannot withstand the afflictions (*kleśa*). Without withstanding the afflictions, one cannot transcend the world. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. If one upholds the precepts purely, one will naturally don the armor of the Bodhisattva. If one dons the armor of the Bodhisattva, one will naturally withstand the afflictions. If one withstands the afflictions, one will naturally transcend the world. For this reason, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. He further said: "The precepts are the boat of the Dharma. Without the precepts, there is no boat. Without a boat, one cannot cross the river of birth and death. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. If one upholds the precepts purely, one will naturally board the boat of the Dharma. If one boards the boat of the Dharma, one will naturally cross the river of birth and death. For this reason, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. He further said: "The precepts are the medicine of the Dharma. Without the precepts, there is no medicine. Without medicine, one cannot cure the disease of the afflictions. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. If one upholds the precepts purely, one will naturally take the medicine of the Dharma. If one takes the medicine of the Dharma, one will naturally cure the disease of the afflictions. For this reason, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. He further said: "The precepts are the light of the Dharma. Without the precepts, there is no light. Without light, one cannot dispel the darkness of ignorance. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. If one upholds the precepts purely, one will naturally obtain the light of the Dharma. If one obtains the light of the Dharma, one will naturally dispel the darkness of ignorance. For this reason, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. He further said: "The precepts are the treasure of the Dharma. Without the precepts, there is no treasure. Without treasure, one cannot satisfy the hunger and thirst of craving. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. If one upholds the precepts purely, one will naturally obtain the treasure of the Dharma. If one obtains the treasure of the Dharma, one will naturally satisfy the hunger and thirst of craving. For this reason, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. He further said: "The precepts are the king of all dharmas. Without the precepts, there is no king. Without a king, there is no order. Without order, there is chaos. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. If one upholds the precepts purely, one will naturally become the king of the Dharma. If one becomes the king of the Dharma, one will naturally bring about order. For this reason, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. He further said: "The precepts are the mother of all Buddhas. Without the precepts, there are no Buddhas. Without Buddhas, there is no Dharma. Without the Dharma, there is no Sangha. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. If one upholds the precepts purely, one will naturally give birth to the Buddhas. If one gives birth to the Buddhas, the Dharma and Sangha will naturally follow. For this reason, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. He further said: "The precepts are the source of all virtues. Without the precepts, there are no virtues. Without virtues, there is no merit. Without merit, there is no liberation. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. If one upholds the precepts purely, one will naturally produce all virtues. If one produces all virtues, one will naturally gain merit. If one gains merit, one will naturally attain liberation. For this reason, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. He further said: "The precepts are the ladder to the heavens. Without the precepts, there is no ladder. Without a ladder, one cannot ascend to the heavens. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. If one upholds the precepts purely, one will naturally climb the ladder to the heavens. If one climbs the ladder to the heavens, one will naturally enjoy celestial bliss. For this reason, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. He further said: "The precepts are the path to Nirvana. Without the precepts, there is no path. Without a path, one cannot reach Nirvana. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. If one upholds the precepts purely, one will naturally walk the path to Nirvana. If one walks the path to Nirvana, one will naturally reach Nirvana. For this reason, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. He further said: "The precepts are the mirror of the Dharma. Without the precepts, there is no mirror. Without a mirror, one cannot see one's own faults. Without seeing one's own faults, one cannot reform them. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. If one upholds the precepts purely, one will naturally possess the mirror of the Dharma. If one possesses the mirror of the Dharma, one will naturally see one's own faults. If one sees one's own faults, one will naturally reform them. For this reason, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. He further said: "The precepts are the sword of the Dharma. Without the precepts, there is no sword. Without a sword, one cannot sever the fetters of the afflictions. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. If one upholds the precepts purely, one will naturally wield the sword of the Dharma. If one wields the sword of the Dharma, one will naturally sever the fetters of the afflictions. For this reason, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. He further said: "The precepts are the shield of the Dharma. Without the precepts, there is no shield. Without a shield, one cannot protect oneself from the arrows of the afflictions. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. If one upholds the precepts purely, one will naturally hold the shield of the Dharma. If one holds the shield of the Dharma, one will naturally protect oneself from the arrows of the afflictions. For this reason, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. He further said: "The precepts are the chariot of the Dharma. Without the precepts, there is no chariot. Without a chariot, one cannot travel the path of the Bodhisattva. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts is foremost. If one upholds
In general, there are thirty-two cycles for the master’s own practice and thirty-two cycles for teaching others. Regarding these thirty-two:
for instance, within the Gate of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), there are both calming (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), each having four *siddhāntas* (perspectives), which makes eight cycles.

Since there are eight cycles for this single gate of calming and insight, there are thirty-two cycles across the four gates. This being the case for one's own practice, it is likewise for transforming others.
It is likewise so; thus there are sixty-four methods of settling the mind (*anxin*). Therefore, it is said that "ordinary beings settle themselves and others.
Regarding the fifth point, "to demonstrate the opening of the general [method] to produce the specific settling":

since one has already settled [the mind] generally through the wondrous cessation (*śamatha*) and wondrous contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) of the Dharma-nature, the distracted and agitated mind will only further increase its darkness and movement. Therefore, it is necessary to open up the general method into the specific, settling [the mind] individually. Thus...
These four gates and four *siddhāntas* [result in] sixty-four combinations regarding self and others.
Regarding the fifth point, the "pervasiveness of the four methods of refuting dharmas": first, it is to distinguish that this gate specifically employs wisdom (*prajñā*);

second, it is because each individual gate pervades both horizontally and vertically; third, it is for the sake of beginners who rely upon the gates of the teaching; and fourth, it is to show beginners how to rely on the absence of...
Because they arise; because the five [aspects] and three truths are perfectly interfused, thereby shattering [delusion] universally.
Within these five meanings, the latter three apply specifically to the present text, while the former two apply generally to both the beginning and the end.
The commentary states: The medicines used to treat the illnesses of sentient beings vary; it is not possible to cure all ailments with a single medicine.

Regarding the establishment of the mind above [the lower realms], because sentient beings have many scattered afflictions, the method of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is employed. This is concentration endowed with wisdom (*prajñā*).
For those who have already attained realization, no further medicine is required; yet for those who have not yet realized it, the power of the medicine is ineffective.

Merit. Therefore, it is necessary to transform the medicine to treat this ailment. For this reason, this gate specifically employs wisdom (*prajñā*). Wisdom as medicine treats the disease of delusion.
This refers precisely to the application of wisdom conjoined with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) according to the occasion; this is what is meant.
Second, regarding the "gate of employing one according to circumstances," because it is applied horizontally or vertically, it is partial; within the four circular gates, it employs one accordingly.

A single gate—namely, emptiness, existence, and so forth up to neither emptiness nor existence—is like using the gate of emptiness to enter from the conventional into emptiness, from emptiness into the conventional, and from the conventional into the Middle.
This is the vertical progression within the gate of emptiness.

Within this single gate, there is also a horizontal discussion of the Four Truths, Dependent Origination, the Six Perfections, and other such dharmas. Since it is thus for one gate, it is likewise for all gates.

Therefore, it is said that whichever gate one employs, it pervades both horizontally and vertically. Regarding the third point, "for the sake of beginners relying on the gates of the teachings," the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:
"Furthermore, the destruction of dharmas must rely upon gates. The sūtras speak of different gates, namely:

the gate of teaching (*śāsana*), the gate of practice (*caryā*), the gate of wisdom (*jñāna*), and the gate of principle (*tattva*). Now, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* relies solely on the gate of teaching, for the teaching is able to lead one through to [realization]."

Because it proceeds according to the principle of wisdom, it further distinguishes the three [vehicles] within the teachings; it specifically addresses the universal refutation of dharmas (*dharmaparyāpti*) in the context of the Perfect Gate (*pariniṣpanna-mukha*).
One should know that what is employed here as one gate of the teaching is precisely the four gates mentioned above, such as emptiness (*śūnya*) and existence (*bhāva*).

Regarding the fourth point, "showing the beginner's reliance on non-arising (*anutpāda*)," this correctly clarifies that the intent of the section on Calm Abiding and Insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) is solely...
Based on non-arising, one knows that the correct cultivation of the ten vehicles of contemplation is entirely non-arising.
If one’s cultivation does not enter [this state], only then does one pass through the other three gates. Regarding "the fivefold perfect fusion of the three truths breaks [delusion] universally":

because within this universal breaking there is the vertical, the horizontal, and that which is neither horizontal nor vertical; this is explained by resorting to the sequential contemplation as a provisional means.

Regarding the mode of practice: as explained in the *Treatise on the Pervasiveness of the Destruction of Dharmas* (Zhiguan fapian lun) in the initial contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), if these three contemplations were not employed within a single moment of mind, the destruction would not be pervasive.
As it is with the contemplation of emptiness, so it is with the contemplations of the provisional and the middle. Therefore, the text indicates the "wondrous" through six points.

This is precisely the point. Regarding the five meanings herein, as for why the latter three meanings are specifically found in the current text, it is because the intent is to refute dharmas so that they may become universal;

this has already been explained above. As for the reason why the former two meanings apply throughout both the beginning and the end, it means that from the initial contemplation of the wondrous object until the final departure from attachment to the semblance of dharmas, there is nothing that does not employ wisdom stabilized by meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, one may employ any single gate—whether horizontal or vertical—to shatter delusions. However, this is merely a general explanation for the duration of a single lifetime.

If, as in the aforementioned "settling the mind," one has already attained wisdom-concentration (*samādhi-prajñā*) or has already entered into realization, why would it be necessary to further employ wisdom-concentration?
This statement is made solely from the perspective of those who have not yet realized.
The five points regarding the fivefold penetration and obstruction are as follows: first, to demonstrate that the examination and verification are not merely partial;

second, to demonstrate that while there is horizontal and vertical penetration, there is still obstruction; third, to demonstrate that even within a single mind there is still obstruction; fourth, to demonstrate that the "jeweled island" is that which is penetrated;
and fifth, to simultaneously resolve the scriptural passage exceeding five hundred [verses].

The commentary states: Regarding "penetration and obstruction," there are generally two types. First, penetration and obstruction in the general sense; second, penetration and obstruction in the specific sense.
As for penetration and obstruction in the general sense: first, in the vertical perspective, the three delusions constitute obstruction, while the three contemplations constitute penetration.

Second, in the horizontal perspective, the twelve links of dependent origination—consisting of suffering, its origin, ignorance, and the six obscurations—constitute obstruction, while the [paths of] cessation and... [the path] constitute penetration.

The extinction of the twelve links of dependent origination through ignorance and the six perfections serve as the common path. Regarding the distinctions between the three transgressions and the common versus the obstructed paths, *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* quotes the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, stating:
"There are bodhisattvas who, upon first generating the mind of enlightenment, are in accord with emptiness. It further states:

"There are bodhisattvas who, upon first generating the mind of enlightenment, sport in supernatural powers. And it also states: "There are bodhisattvas who, upon first generating the mind of enlightenment, immediately sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). These are identical.

The initial arousal of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*) is horizontal; its division among three types of persons is distinct. Regarding the discussion of what is "open" (*tong*) and what is "obstructed" (*se*): viewed from the perspective of what follows, it is open;

viewed from the perspective of what precedes, it is obstructed—this can be seen by reflecting upon it. Fourth, regarding the openness and obstruction of the single mind: the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:

"If, with respect to each and every phenomenon, each and every subject and each and every object are all immediately empty, provisional, and middle, fully possessing the [Four] Truths, the [Twelve] Conditions, and the [Six] Perfections, this is..."
It is called "unobstructed" because it illuminates both obstruction and non-obstruction simultaneously. If one has even the slightest attachment to this Dharma, it is called "obstruction.

Where there is obstruction, there is no penetration. Regarding the statement that "examination is not a single stage," within these four [categories], to investigate each one by means of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) is itself "examination"; there is no separate examination. If, throughout the four penetrations...

Regarding the arising of obstructions: one must break through the obstructions to preserve the flow of penetration. It is like employing troops where the general defeats the enemy. If the general becomes the enemy, then the enemy is likewise defeated;
if the enemy becomes the general, then the general likewise provides protection. The three contemplations act as the general, and the three delusions act as the enemy.
If the general becomes the enemy, it is merely because one gives rise to obstruction within that which is penetrating. At every stage...
This can be understood by examining the methods [of analysis]. Second, regarding "demonstrating that horizontal and vertical [perspectives] are both penetrating and obstructed":

this refers to analyzing them in relation to one another through successive stages. For example, when emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is able to refute existence (*bhāva*), it is called "penetrating" (*tong*). When the provisional (*prajñapti*) is able to refute emptiness, it is called "penetrating.
However, when emptiness is refuted by the provisional, emptiness itself becomes "obstructed" (*se*). Although the provisional may surpass emptiness, it is still designated as "penetrating."

If one looks toward the Middle Way, it is also called "obstructed" (*saṃvṛta*). Because the Middle excels the two extremes, it is termed "penetrating" (*vyavahāra*). It is "obstructed" because it is separated from the Lesser [Vehicle].

This discussion of penetration as being still obstructed is based on a vertical perspective. If, from a horizontal perspective, the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) are penetrating yet still obstructed, it is as cited above from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*:
the three types of persons' arousal of the mind are the same, while the three contemplations are distinct, each within its own respective domain.

"Passage" refers to not obstructing one another; "obstruction" refers to being confined. The depth and shallowness of the characteristics of phenomena naturally possess their own passage and obstruction.

How much more so when, within them, one gives rise to suffering, its origin, ignorance, obscurations, and the like—would these not be obstructions? Third, regarding the demonstration that even within the single mind there is still obstruction:
the threefold contemplation within the single mind is fundamentally without passage or obstruction. As the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "If, within the unobstructed..."

Regarding those whose ignorance obscures the arising of suffering and its accumulation such that they lack supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): they not only lose their supernormal powers, but also lose their "horse-step" (*aśvagati*).

The terms "supernormal powers" and "horse-step" appear in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. These three original metaphors are used to distinguish the three contemplations (*vipaśyanā*) horizontally: supernormal powers, [horse-step], and... [text fragment].

"Middle" (*zhong*) refers to the contemplation of the conventional (*jia-guan*); "horse" (*ma*) refers to the contemplation of the conventional; "step" (*bu*) refers to the contemplation of emptiness (*kong-guan*).

If one gives rise to attachment even toward the single mind, one already loses the [contemplation of] emptiness, let alone the middle. Thus, all three contemplations are lost. This is the obstruction caused by the distinct characteristics (*bie-xiang*) of the single mind.
To break this obstruction and allow for passage, one must employ the investigation of the four propositions (*si-ju*). Therefore, it is said: "To demonstrate that the single mind still exists..."

Because it is an obstruction. Fourth, "to show that the jewel island is that which is reached" means that the term "jewel island" (*ratnadvīpa*) appears in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, while the term "jewel place" (*ratnasthāna*) appears in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Although the metaphors are identical, the terminology differs; both use the island and the place as metaphors for the realization of the principle.

There are degrees of depth and fullness in this realization of the principle: the partial [realization] occurs at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), while the deep and full [realization] occurs at... [the final stage].
Regarding the ultimate [meaning], the intent of the present text concerns only the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).

As for the fifth point—“simultaneously resolving the scriptural passage because it exceeds five hundred”—the scripture clearly states that in order to extinguish the illusory city and proceed toward the treasure site, one must pass through the perilous barriers of five hundred *yojana*s before reaching the thoroughfare.
Regarding the term “five hundred *yojana*s,” there are three meanings. First, concerning...
First, regarding the places of birth and death as karmic retribution; second, regarding the delusions of afflictions as the causes of birth; and third, regarding contemplative wisdom.
As for "being able to transcend five hundred places of birth and death": the three realms constitute three hundred; the land of expedient means constitutes four hundred;

and the land of true recompense constitutes five hundred. Regarding the afflictions that serve as the cause of birth: the delusions of view constitute one hundred, and the five lower fetters [constitute another hundred].
Two hundred refers to the [first] two fetters; five upper-tier fetters refer to three hundred; the sands and dust of afflictions refer to four hundred; and ignorance refers to five hundred.

As for those who can transcend these through contemplative wisdom: the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) can transcend three hundred; the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya*) can transcend four hundred;

and the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) can transcend five hundred. One should know that this is all but a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*); within the ten realms and the hundred realms, cause and effect are non-dual.
This is precisely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. A mere snap of the fingers can traverse five hundred yojanas; there is no obstruction to be broken, nor any penetration to be guarded.
This is the true meaning of penetration and obstruction.
The fifth section, "The Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment" (Ṣaḍdhātuvarga), has five purposes: first, to demonstrate that the factors of enlightenment must be employed for cultivation;

second, to demonstrate that this balanced cultivation differs from the partial or limited approaches of the Lesser Vehicle; third, to demonstrate that the foundations of mindfulness have the aggregates as their objective domain; fourth, to demonstrate that the factors of enlightenment encompass all practices;
and fifth, to demonstrate that following each chapter there must necessarily be a gateway.
The commentary states: First, regarding "for the sake of harmonizing the factors of the path" (*mārgāṅga*), there are four types of factors of the path:

first, mutual generation; second, their respective divisions; third, mutual inclusion; and fourth, correspondence to stages. Here, it is clarified that for the purpose of harmonization, only the category of mutual generation is relevant;
the other three are not forms of harmonious adjustment. As for why this harmonization is necessary: although the preceding section has refuted [the notion of] pervasiveness...

Furthermore, one must discern what is obstructed and what is unobstructed. If the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*) are not balanced and regulated, how could one quickly attain correspondence with the true Dharma?

Therefore, by regulating and balancing the two sets of three, the two sets of five, the single seven, and the single eight, one reaches the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) and enters into ultimate truth.
This merit arises from regulation; for those who have already entered via the aforementioned five vehicles, this is not required. Thus it is said.

First, it is because one must cultivate the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) for the sake of harmonization. Second, it is to demonstrate that this balanced cultivation differs from the partiality of the Lesser Vehicle.
As the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "The thirty-seven factors of the various paths and truths are not recorded here in full;

rather, only the thirty-seven factors of the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) path-truth are clarified, in order to establish the principle of the three contemplations within a single mind. Since it says, "only clarifying the unconditioned," [it follows that...]

In this chapter, the distinction from the partial and limited meanings [of the Lesser Vehicle] can be seen therein. Third, regarding the statement "to show that the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) have the aggregates (skandha) as their object":
the perfect aggregate-object is itself the inconceivable; it is also termed the aggregates and bases (āyatana).

Therefore, in the text concerning the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness, it first demonstrates that the arising of a single thought-moment is inconceivable, which is precisely the aggregates and bases of the ten realms.
These [factors] mutually obstruct one another. This is a reiteration of the first inconceivable realm as the object of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

Since the previous general contemplation of the aggregates (*skandha*) did not lead to awakening and entry, one therefore departs from the general to produce the specific, taking the four objects of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena (*dharma*) to bring them into balance.
Thus, it is known that the preceding five vehicles all contemplate the aggregates; therefore, this serves as an illustration following the subsequent refutation of pervasiveness.
As for the remaining aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*), they serve as the fundamental basis for the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) regarding penetration and obstruction.

Thus, one should know that after the universal contemplation of the self has been dismantled, the factors of enlightenment such as penetration and obstruction all involve the complete contemplation of the five aggregates. Therefore, it is said:

"To demonstrate that the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) have the aggregates as their object. Fourth, "to demonstrate that the factors of enlightenment encompass all practices" refers to the four teachings.
Regarding the statement that "practice does not transcend the factors of enlightenment," as cited from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*:
"The thirty-seven factors are causes for nirvāṇa, but not causes for Great Nirvāṇa. This refers to the practices of the three preceding teachings subsumed within the thirty-seven factors.
Furthermore, it is said that the immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are the cause of Great Nirvāṇa;

these are the thirty-seven factors of the path according to the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*). Moreover, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The factors of the path are good spiritual friends; by means of them, one achieves perfect enlightenment.

These factors of the path encompass both cause and effect. Furthermore, if one were to categorize all phenomena separately by means of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), [they would likewise be included].

This means that while it is said that the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) encompass all phenomena within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), here it is specifically this single dharma of the four foundations of mindfulness that encompasses all phenomena.
Furthermore, regarding the mutual inclusion of the seven categories: for example, by citing the single dharma of the foundations of mindfulness, the remaining six categories are subsumed;
likewise, even by citing the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), everything is subsumed. This is what is meant by "mutual inclusion" (*parasparasaṃgraha*).
Because the *mārga-varga* (factors of the path) universally encompass the practices of the four teachings, it is said that "the factors of the path subsume all practices.

Fifth, regarding the statement that the section following the *varga* must necessarily have a "gate" (*mukha*): this clarifies that when the thirty-seven factors are about to reach the city of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there are three gates to that city.
If one enters these gates, one immediately attains the realization of truth; these are the so-called gates of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
It is also called the three samādhis; these are brought about through the functional power of the actual factors of the path (mārga-aṅga).

Regarding the seven correct [factors] and the five aids: first, it is to show that those with heavy obscurations must necessarily rely on aids; second, it is to show that the perfections (pāramitās) of the phenomenal level can treat such obscurations;
third, it is to show that the dharmas subsumed within the aids to the path are all-encompassing; fourth, it is to show the combined practice of the correct and the aids.
Because of their characteristics. Fifth, it is to show that the three teachings are all aids. The commentary states:

Regarding "primary and auxiliary," they are the aids to the primary [teaching]; thus they are called "primary and auxiliary. Because one does not enter through the cultivation of the prior primary contemplation, one must rely on the path of auxiliaries.
It is like washing clothes in the world with water; if the stains do not come away, one must...
Just as one uses ash and soap to assist clear water so that grime may finally be removed, it is said that when there is a single heavy obscuration, an auxiliary must necessarily be employed.

"Obscuration" refers to the six obscurations (*ṣaḍ-āvaraṇa*), which block the gates of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); hence they are called "obscurations. First is the obscuration of stinginess, which obscures the gate of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).

Second is the obscuration of greed, which obscures the gate of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). Third is the obscuration of anger, which obscures the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Because they defile the gates of the perfections (*pāramitā*): even down to the obscuration of ignorance, which obscures the gate of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).

These six obscurations are present in all people; there is only a difference in their degree of lightness or heaviness. Now, it is explained that the aids to the path (*mārga-parikarman*) are intended to treat those that are heavy.

Therefore, they are distinguished by means of the four propositions of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. The first is: when the faculties are sharp and there are no obstructions, one easily enters the cool pond [of nirvāṇa] and requires no further effort.

First, those with sharp faculties who encounter obstacles; because they are focused solely on the three gates of liberation, they do not require external aids. Second, those with dull faculties who encounter no obstacles;
by employing the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) to bring about balance and adaptability, they transform their dullness into sharpness, and likewise do not require remedies.
Third, those with dull faculties who encounter heavy obstacles; these pull apart and destroy the contemplative mind. Because of this specific root-nature, a remedy is required. Therefore it is said:
Those who are heavily obscured must necessarily receive assistance. Second, regarding the point that the *pāramitās* can treat these obscurations by demonstrating their function:
taking obstruction as "blocked" and the *pāramitās* as "penetrating," since this now clarifies the application of antidotes, they should be employed accordingly.
Because these six serve as remedies (*pratipakṣa*), they are employed for that purpose. However, this has been stated merely in terms of the remedies;

the transformative remedy (*vivartana-pratipakṣa*), the concurrent remedy (*sādhāraṇa-pratipakṣa*), the complete remedy (*paripūrṇa-pratipakṣa*), and the ultimate remedy (*paramārtha-pratipakṣa*) have not yet been discussed. These are fully explained in the original texts on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;
here, it is presented only as a general outline. Thirdly, it is to demonstrate that the factors subsumed under the aids to the path (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are all-inclusive.
This is the provisional [expedient] of the same essence (tongti) serving as an aid to the Path; only thus can it universally encompass all dharmas.

Therefore, within the main text of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, there is a brief explanation of how the various categories are subsumed to discipline the six sense faculties, including the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, up to the eighty minor marks, and all dharmas. Now, I say that if these were not of the same essence...

The primary and auxiliary practices are to be performed in conjunction. Apart from the auxiliary practices that aid the Way, there is not a single further dharma; how could [the auxiliary alone] encompass all dharmas universally?
