The answer fully provides two paths. What are they? The inherently quiescent nature of the mind is precisely the three thousand [realms]; its constant quiescence while illuminating is termed "stopping" (*śamatha*).
The inherently extinguished nature of the mind is precisely the three thousand [realms]; its constant illumination while quiescent is termed "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*). This...

This is simply the inherent nature of the fundamental virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*); it is not a matter of cultivated virtues (*bhāvanā-guṇa*). If one says that realizing the delusion is itself the *dharmatā*, then "realizing" (*tī*) is precisely "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).

Regarding the statement that *dharmatā* has no arising: "arising" (*udaya*) refers to birth. There is no arising from self, no arising from another, no arising from both, and no arising without cause.
To penetrate that delusion is fundamentally empty is the contemplation of the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Even this emptiness has no cessation. As for its marks (*lakṣaṇa*)...

This is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Although there is a sequence in their explanation, in their actual application there is no difference in time. Just as it is with the cultivation of contemplation, so it is with the cultivation of cessation (*śamatha*).

One should say: the very essence of distraction is cessation; cessation is the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*); the Dharma-nature is without distraction; distraction is fundamentally quiescent; and even quiescence is without quiescence.
One should know that the two dharmas of cessation and contemplation have nothing other than the three thousandfold Dharma-nature as their essence.

Regarding the statement that "speech" refers to the combined exposition of cultivation (*xiū*) and nature (*xìng*): the two dharmas of cessation (*zhǐ*) and contemplation (*guān*) are the two cultivations that are capable of bringing peace;
the three thousand wondrous realms are the one nature that is brought to peace. Because the two [factors] of cultivation are paired with the one [factor] of nature, it is called "combined.

If, however, cultivation and nature were explained as separate, there would be three for each of cessation and contemplation, making six cultivations, while the wondrous realms would originally remain three.
The nature [of the three] is threefold. Now, in order to clarify cultivation in contrast to nature, they are combined.

Nevertheless, as for the discourse on separation and combination, who is unable to recite the text? Yet the essential meaning of this separation and combination is rarely understood in the world; therefore, one should know it.
Though speech seems to join together, it never fails to separate; though words seem to separate, they never fail to join together.
To speak of joining and separating is because its essential nature is eternally perfect—this is the fundamental meaning.

Question 8: In the "General Placement" (*sō-an*), both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) are cultivated in a balanced manner; in the subsequent "Specific Placement" (*beku-an*), only one is cultivated.
How can it be said that the general governs the specific?
The commentary states: This question arises from common misconceptions, as well as due to heterodox masters who claim that this "General Placement" [is merely...]

This refers to the "sudden within the sudden. It means that by establishing the lower [stages] separately, one proceeds toward gradual perfection; therefore, this question is posed with the intent of providing an answer that refutes deluded attachments and establishes the correct.

The answer is as follows: What is called "partial" does not mean a permanent separation. It is merely the *śamatha* (calm abiding) of the practitioner of *vipaśyanā* (insight), and *vipaśyanā* is the [insight] of the practitioner of *śamatha*.

Contemplation: their essence is identical while their functions differ; they are temporarily adapted to what is appropriate for practice. Thus, one should know that they are collectively unified, yet distinct at the same time;
they are differentiated according to their functions and integrated in accordance with principle.
The commentary states that there are three parts to the response. First, it answers the question regarding how distinct establishments have the same essence but different functions.

Second, from the words "If its... onwards, it clarifies through a distinct sequence that distinct establishments are not partial. Third, from the words "If they are perfect... onwards, it explains how the general encompasses the particular, such that the beginning and end are non-dual.
Regarding the first response, the statement "What is called 'partial' does not mean permanent separation" refers to the nature of distinct establishment.

Although one distinguishes between *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), as well as faith and the Dharma, they always mutually support one another within the nature of the faculties, revolving back and forth.
Whether one applies oneself predominantly to *śamatha* or predominantly to *vipaśyanā*, each possesses the four *siddhāntas*.

One must understand that *śamatha* is the *śamatha* of the practitioner engaged in *vipaśyanā*, and *vipaśyanā* is the *vipaśyanā* of the practitioner engaged in *śamatha*; their essence is identical, yet their functions differ. For a time, they bring temporary satisfaction to the practitioner.

This is appropriate. Thus we know that establishing them separately is precisely the differentiation within the totality at one and the same time. They must be divided because medicine is administered according to the specific ailment;
they must always be combined because their underlying principle and essence are identical. There is no difference between them.
If one were to separate them into the distinct sequence of the three truths, then *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* could not coexist at the same time;
this is as detailed in the various teachings regarding their differentiated characteristics.
The commentary states: This constitutes the second [section], which clarifies that these distinct arrangements manifest a specific sequence, rather than being practiced in isolation. It says:

Regarding the phrase "if it were to depart" in the context of the distinctions in the sequence of the three truths: the words "if it were to" refer to the provisional application of skillful means (*upāya*).
This means that from the single reality of the perfect fusion of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one provisionally opens them up to establish the sequential *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of the three truths.
Therefore, it says: "If it were thus"—this reveals the meaning of the distinct stages found throughout the various Mahāyāna teachings, thereby clarifying this separate arrangement.
However, while their essence is identical, their functions differ; therefore, this is not a case of sequential or distinct calming and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).
As for "perfectly settled" (*yuan-an*), it is as stated in the "General Settlement": "Immovable calming is simply immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*);
immovable wisdom is simply immovable calming. Because these share the same essence while presiding over their respective functions, there is no duality between them.
The commentary states: This constitutes the third [section], wherein the general is used to crown the particular, such that the beginning and end are non-dual.

Why is this? Above, the sequential order was clarified to reveal the principle of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*). Therefore, although there is now a distinction between the general and the particular within this perfection, the intent is to have the general crown the particular.
For this reason, the initial section on settling the mind (*anxin*) states: "Immovable cessation is simply immovability."

Regarding "wisdom": Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) is precisely immovable cessation (*acala-śamatha*). Immovable cessation is the cessation of the non-duality of cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).
Immovable wisdom is the contemplation of the non-duality of cessation and contemplation.

By employing this general cessation and general contemplation as appropriate, one achieves specific stability. Thus, we know that the "specific" mentioned in the subsequent text is precisely the "specific" within the general.
The general principle mentioned above is precisely the general that is identical with the particular. Because the general subsumes the particular, there is no duality between them.
Failing to perceive this, people give rise to divergent views; this is a most grievous error.

Question Nine: In the initial section on "Settling the Mind," it says: "One simply believes in the dharma-nature (dharmatā) and does not believe in its various manifestations. Does this mean that there is only the dharma-nature and nothing else exists?

If all phenomena were entirely non-existent, they would contradict what is currently perceived; yet, it is further stated that the dharma-nature is replete with all phenomena. How is this to be understood?

The commentary states: Regarding the skillful establishment of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the beginning of the text says: "The essence of all inversions is itself the *dharmatā*; it is neither identical nor different.
Although inversions arise and cease, one should simply believe that this mind is nothing but *dharmatā*.

Its arising is the arising of *dharmatā*; its ceasing is the ceasing of *dharmatā*. In reality, its essence neither arises nor ceases; what is falsely called arising and ceasing is merely a designation for delusion."
One should conceive that all these are the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). Now, it is said that ignorance itself is pointed out as being the dharma-nature;

ignorance itself is all phenomena (*dharma*), for there are no phenomena apart from it. However, if one believes only in the dharma-nature and does not believe in those phenomena, would this mean that there is only the dharma-nature and no further phenomena?
If there were no phenomena at all, then what is currently perceived before us—?
As for [the colors] blue, yellow, red, and so forth—what are they? This is a challenge based on emotional sentiment rather than principle; the preceding text has already provided a full explanation.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the dharma-nature (dharmatā) is replete with all dharmas": "dharma" means that which provides a standard and sustains itself, while "nature" means that which does not change. This refers precisely to the dharma of the three thousandfold reality-phenomena (trisahasra-svabhāva).
Above, it serves as the standard and sustenance for the Buddhas of the ten directions; below, it serves as [the standard] for all sentient beings.

That which serves as the guiding principle and sustainer for all that is born remains unchanged from beginning to end; therefore, it is called "nature" (*prakṛti*). Thus, one should know that the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is replete with all phenomena.

The dharma-nature is precisely the three thousand realms, and the three thousand realms are precisely the dharma-nature. Non-differentiation is precisely differentiation, and differentiation is precisely non-differentiation.
One should know that the dharma-nature is replete with all phenomena, and there is nothing else capable of being replete or by which it is replete.
The compiler, in his arrogance, claims that the "inherent possession" (xingju) refers to the three thousand realms inherent in nature, rather than the three thousand realms within emptiness.

He asserts that these are merely provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*) and that within the purity of emptiness, not a single dharma exists. One should know that such a person deeply slanders the Dharma.

Answer: Because sentient beings have for many eons been attached only to various phenomena (*dharma*) and have not believed in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), [the Buddha] speaks in terms of antidotes in order to shatter their former calculations.
This causes them to see purely the nature of phenomena within all phenomena. If one sees the nature of phenomena, one sees that the nature of phenomena is purely all phenomena.
This nature of all phenomena is fundamentally without names; it is only in terms of refuting [false views] and establishing [truth] that it is called "nature" or "phenomena."
The commentary states: In this response, first the original delusion is answered; subsequently, from "next, refuting the former" onwards, the present awakening is clarified.
Since beginningless time, sentient beings have lost their fundamental true nature and undergo the cycle of rebirth, clinging only to the various phenomena of ignorance and birth-and-death.

Who is there capable of knowing that all phenomena (*dharma*) are the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)? Therefore, one now cultivates contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to dismantle former conceptualizations.
This is explained in terms of the application of remedies, so that one may perceive only the *dharmatā* within all phenomena.

If one perceives the *dharmatā*, one sees that the *dharmatā* itself is entirely composed of all phenomena. Here, the phrase "if one perceives" refers to the state when contemplation has been perfected; once contemplation is perfected, it is universal.
The four positions. The current text speaks provisionally in terms of the stage of semblance within contemplative practice (*guanxing*).
It says that the nature of these dharmas is fundamentally without names; this is spoken of in terms of refutation and establishment, where "nature" and "dharma" are designated.
Dharmatā is itself all dharmas, and all dharmas are themselves dharmatā. Dharmatā is quiescent and absolute; fundamentally, there is no name for "dharmas," nor is there a name for "dharmatā."

[This is] a term. The name "nature" (svabhāva) is established in order to dismantle all phenomena; it is spoken of in terms of their antidotes. Therefore, "all phenomena" and "dharma-nature" are merely provisional designations.
[The tenth question: All texts state that matter and mind are non-dual. If one wishes to investigate this, how should one establish the contemplation?

The commentary states: Form and mind are non-dual when spoken of in terms of their essential nature (*dharmatā*). If form and mind are considered in relation to one another, there is both form and mind.

However, if one discusses their essential nature, then apart from mind there is no form, and apart from form there is no mind. If one discusses their mutual identity (*lakṣaṇa-samāveśa*), then if they are two, they are both two;
if they are one, they are both one. The intent of the difficulty in this passage is that since form and mind are thus mutually pervasive and integrated...
Second: How is contemplation established? Is it a joint contemplation of form and mind, or a separate contemplation of form and mind?

This is because the fundamental nature of reality is inherently fused, making it difficult to establish internal and external objects based on the specific phenomena of the aggregates (skandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas).
Answer: Matter and mind are of one substance; they are neither prior nor posterior, for both are the Dharma-realm.

The commentary states that there are five parts to this answer: first, the response to the question establishes their essence and demonstrates their fusion; second, from "cultivating the contemplation" (*xiu guan*) onwards, it answers how the contemplation is established;

third, from "inner mind" (*nei xin*) onwards, it clarifies the progression through phenomena once the contemplation is perfected; fourth, from "furthermore" (*you yi*) onwards, it clarifies what must first be undertaken.
Explanation. Fifth, the citation of evidence for the two contemplations. First, the response to the question regarding the single substance of form and mind:
because form is the Middle Way, form and mind are non-dual; because mind is the Middle Way, form and mind are non-dual.
It is not that form comes first and mind follows, nor that mind comes first and form follows. To raise one includes the whole; there is nothing that is not so.
The Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The term "Dharma-realm" is a designation for that which has no exterior.

When our school speaks of the Dharma-realm, it must be said that the ten realms, the hundred realms, and the three thousand [realms] are themselves emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle; therefore, they are named the Dharma-realm.
Such an explanation is both the contemplating observation and the principle being contemplated. For this reason, form and mind are not divided into two.
The sequence for cultivating contemplation must first begin with the internal mind.

The commentary states: this constitutes the second response, which concerns setting out from the physical basis (*āśraya*) to cultivate contemplation by distinguishing between internal and external objects.
However, regarding these terms "internal" and "external," their divisions across various texts differ, each having its own specific rationale, as detailed in the *Jiyao chao* (Essential Notes).

This has been extensively analyzed within the "Gate of the Non-duality of the Internal and External" and will not be discussed further here. The intent of the present text lies precisely in *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

In observing the mind, one discards the *zhang* for the *chi*, and discards the *chi* for the *cun*. One observes only the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*) within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).

Within this sovereign mind, one further discriminates between the wholesome and the unwholesome, observing only the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Therefore, it is said that one must first attend to the internal mind. This...
This is explained according to the principle of observing the internal first. Only after internal observation is perfected does one proceed to the external; hence it is called "sequential.
This internal mind is the practitioner’s own present *skandha*-mind.

Like cauterizing a disease by finding the correct point, or felling a tree by reaching its root, this is the gateway for initiating contemplation and the locus where principle is revealed; it is the essential pivot of the entire treatise on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
This is so. Those of old did not understand this and claimed that what is observed is itself the true mind.
Some said that the inconceivable mind is taken as the object of observation. If it were already true and already inconceivable, what need would there be for observation?
One must know that the method of observing the mind is much like clarifying water; because the water is turbid, one clarifies it. If the water were already clear...
What need is there for clarification? By means of an analogy, it can be seen with radiant clarity.
Therefore, one should know that the Samādhi of Constant Sitting takes the three thousand [realms] as its very method of contemplation.

By employing these three thousand within the single thought-moment of the deluded consciousness in the inner mind, it is said that "one thought-moment is the three thousand, and the three thousand are one thought-moment. This inner mind is precisely...

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, one employs twenty-five methods as preliminary practices (*pūrvaprayoga*) to achieve composure and clarity. How could a single moment of neutral awareness (*avyākṛta-citta*) be easily attained?

The compiler, lacking a foundation in study and failing to comprehend the Way of Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), merely sees the subsequent citation of evidence regarding the two contemplations—of phenomena (*vastu*) and principle (*tattva*)—and hastily asserts that the sequence for cultivating contemplation must necessarily begin with the internal mind. This is a single [erroneous] statement.
This refers to the simultaneous designation of the two contemplations of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*). Why such delusion?

Although both the contemplation of phenomena and the contemplation of principle universally observe the consciousness-mind, since the contemplation of phenomena allows for the free engagement with the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), it does not necessarily require that one must first [contemplate] the internal mind.
As the *Sūtra of the Divination of the Auspicious and Inauspicious* states: "At all times and in all places, whatever is performed by the three karmas..."
One observes and realizes that it is merely mind. How can one definitively claim that it must first be the internal mind?

Furthermore, this term "internal mind" precisely applies to the stage of discerning the aggregates (*skandhas*) when initiating contemplation. There are deluded people in the world who pass down the tradition that the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) does not establish the objective realm of the aggregates;
how can they face the texts? How can they face the principle? [This] fully elucidates the Perfect Teaching.
Regarding the objective realm of the sense bases (*āyatana-viṣaya*): this is not cited in full here, as it appears in my *Record of the Essential Meaning of the Golden Scalpel*.
If the inner mind is pure, then by means of this pure mind, one passes through all phenomena, and they spontaneously merge and dissolve.

The commentary states: This refers to the third stage, the completion of the contemplation that traverses all phenomena (*dharmas*). Regarding the phrase "inner mind," it refers to the aggregates (*skandhas*) that are the objects of contemplation.

By means of the three thousand sublime contemplations, one settles [the mind] within the aggregates and the mind. Through continuous settling, the inner mind and the aggregates transform into the inconceivable three thousand sublime realms;
this is termed "purity" (*viśuddhi*). If the word "pure" is used, it signifies the completion of the contemplation. Contemplation...
The stage of fulfillment encompasses all four positions; the stage of traversing phenomena is restricted to three positions.

Because the ultimate Dharma-realm of wondrous enlightenment is transparently luminous and devoid of differentiation, there are no longer any mutual perceptions of self and other or of material characteristics; there exists only the solitary persistence of True Suchness-wisdom.
Therefore, there is no dharma that can be traversed. The meaning of the current text concerns only the five stages and the ten levels of faith.

Nevertheless, regarding the intent of the method of traversal: when first entering contemplation, how could one exclude the sense bases (*āyatana*) and the other four aggregates (*skandha*), but instead contemplate only the single moment of the indeterminate mind-king?
When the beginner practices contemplation, they constrain the mind to accord with principle; once the contemplation has been fully developed—

Having already transformed the mind of the aggregates (*skandha*) into the wondrous realm, one attains entry into the first stage (*ādikṣaṇa*). The single mind and the three truths (*tisraḥ satyāḥ*) suddenly open and become luminous.
With this purified mind, one proceeds through the stages of perception, feeling, and the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

Gradually and step by step, all external phenomena, such as the environment and its retribution, spontaneously merge and harmonize with the Three Thousand Worlds (*trisahasra*). As it is with the first stage, so it is with the second.
The same applies to the third, fourth, and fifth stages. If this is so for the five grades, it is likewise for the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Since even the stage of partial realization (*viśuddha-bhūmi*) still possesses the characteristics of internal and external, how could there not be a progression through the dharmas? This section of the text discusses exclusively the path of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mārga*), which is rarely understood by those of the world.
Formerly, Master Zhao engaged in discussion with Fazhi; Zhao had once annotated this passage regarding its doctrinal significance. Now...

I record this fully so that you may distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox. In the sequence of cultivating contemplation, one must first take the internal mind as the object (this refers first to contemplating the *vijñāna-skandha*).

If the internal mind is pure (meaning one has realized that a single thought-moment contains the three thousand [dharmas]), then by means of this pure mind, one traverses all phenomena (because one has already realized the three thousand within a single thought-moment, it is said "if pure";

thereafter, one universally traverses each and every phenomenon, which does not transcend the three thousand within my own mind; thus it is said "traversing all phenomena"). They spontaneously merge and dissolve (meaning the three thousand are without...).

Externally, it encompasses all external objects and spheres of experience exhaustively, leaving nothing out. Furthermore, one first realizes that the myriad dharmas are mind-only (*cittamātra*)—"realization" meaning understanding; that is to say, the three thousand [worlds] do not transcend a single thought-moment.

Only then can one contemplate the mind (meaning that based on understanding, one contemplates that the three thousand phenomena do not transcend a single thought). When one is able to comprehend all phenomena, one sees that all phenomena are merely form and merely mind.
One should know that everything arises from the mind’s discrimination; how could phenomena ever claim for themselves identity or difference?

(The section beginning with "One should know" correctly demonstrates the intent of contemplating the mind. Since all phenomena arise from the mind’s discrimination, one therefore contemplates only the mind. Although it is said they are "merely form," form is itself mind. Thus, the *Sūtra on the Examination of the Ground* [states]:...
The Sūtra says: "There are two kinds of contemplation: first, the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*); second, the contemplation of the true mark (*dharmatā*).

The contemplation of the true mark contemplates principle—that is, contemplating that the three thousand natures are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle (which is the aforementioned purity of the internal mind). The contemplation of consciousness-only traverses phenomena (that is, employing the pure mind to pervade all dharmas).

When phenomenon and principle are non-dual (that is, phenomenon is itself principle; subsuming the external within the internal, the three thousand and the three truths encompass everything without exception), the path of contemplation gradually opens (if these two contemplations support one another, phenomenon and principle are non-dual)."

Then the Way of contemplation will gradually become clear, and one may enter the stages of contemplative practice (*guanxing*). One who can understand this may be discussed regarding the Way (one should know that those who hold erroneous interpretations and deviant attachments—how could they possibly be discussed regarding the Way?
Is not Master Jingxi’s clear admonition precisely this?). Alas! Master Zhao confused it before, and Master Fazhi cleared it away after;
it has become as vast and open as space. Although the person has passed away, the volumes still remain. The compiler, through this, though knowing the internal...
If the mind is pure, this constitutes the perfection of *vipaśyanā* (contemplation). To traverse all things with this pure mind is the method for perfecting *vipaśyanā*.

Thus, it is said that the four types of samādhi involve the concurrent cultivation of both the phenomenal (*sāṃvṛta*) and the noumenal (*pāramārthika*) contemplations; how could they differ from the teachings of Master Zhao?

Yet, one must understand that the phenomenal and noumenal contemplations take divergent paths as their starting points, and that the four types of samādhi involve both restrictive (*saṃyama*) and expansive (*prasarana*) modes of practice.
There is a difference. The faculties are distinguished as sharp or dull, and their inclinations and joys differ. How can they be spoken of as being on the same day?

Why do you arbitrarily claim that the stage of the inherent virtue of the nature-realm (*dharmatā*) in the contemplation of the Initial Vehicle is the "contemplation of principle" (*li-guan*), while the stage of the cultivated virtue of the realm examined through the fourfold analysis is the "contemplation of phenomena" (*shi-guan*), and the stage of transforming others is the "function after fruition"? Furthermore, [the teaching of] permanence...

Those who practice the contemplation of the principles of the *samādhi* of sitting should trim and simplify their physical conduct, refraining from all other affairs and remaining solely in upright posture upon their meditation seat.
As for those who practice the contemplation of worldly affairs, they may indulge in the three natures, busying themselves with public and private matters, hurrying about on horseback;

how could such a lifestyle be appropriate for one practicing the contemplation of the principles of *samādhi*? Furthermore, when practicing the contemplation of the principles of the *samādhi* of sitting...
Prior to cultivation, one employs twenty-five methods as preliminary practices (*pūrvaprayoga*). After attaining samādhi, one should earnestly exhort others to practice;

this matter is no trivial one. In the case of practicing the contemplation of things, the person and the object are antithetical; yet those who disparage what they have heard fail to employ these preliminary methods and do not even see the single section on exhorting others to practice.
How could it be appropriate for those of sharp faculties to cultivate the contemplative methods of the initial vehicle alone?
Does the contemplation on the principle of inherent virtue (xingde) then transform into the dull contemplation on phenomena (shiguan)? Is it not difficult because the mind is light and restless?
Therefore, one should know that there is a difference in the way practitioners of these two types—the two contemplations of phenomenon and principle—set foot upon the path.
Now, within the formal practice of the *Mohe zhiguan*, the ten vehicles of contemplative methods (*shicheng guanfafa*) apply exclusively to those who cultivate the contemplation of principle.

For those of middling and inferior faculties, it is not possible to engage in the contemplation of phenomena (*vastu-vipaśyanā*) within this [practice]. If a practitioner cultivates the contemplation of phenomena, their initial application of effort consists solely of the free exercise of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
The analytical investigation of the four modes of activity (*catur-yoga*) naturally comprises the ten vehicles (*daśa-yāna*).

As it is said: "The present text contemplates the four modes of activity across the ten realms; in meaning, this corresponds to the *Occhaku* (Observation and Contemplation) practice of 'all is but mind' (*sarvam cittamātram*). If one proceeds according to the sequence...

Contemplating the fourteen stages of movement is termed the "realm of thought and deliberation" (*cintā-vicāra-gocara*). Reaching the realization that the nine [stages] are themselves the Buddha is termed the "inconceivable" (*acintya*).

Nevertheless, one must still give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) and proceed until detachment from craving is achieved; only then is the characteristic of entering the Path according to this specific school established.

Verifying it by this standard, there is a difference in the point of entry between the two contemplations of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*), each possessing its own ten vehicles (*daśa-yāna*). How then could the first vehicle of the *nitya-kāyotsarga-samādhi* (the Samādhi of Constant Sitting) [be the same]?

Does one then immediately practice the contemplation of phenomena (*vastu-vipaśyanā*)? Furthermore, in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), within the section explaining the purpose of the "Samādhi Following One’s Own Intent" (*svacittānugata-samādhi*), it says:
"For a body burdened by afflictions, moments free from worldly affairs are rare; thus, for the aforementioned three samādhis, it is truly difficult for the necessary conditions to be met.

If one does not apply contemplation according to the objects encountered, but rather contemplates as soon as a thought arises, how could one quickly correspond with the underlying principle? [Therefore,] one practices the contemplation of phenomena."
What is the natural state of the human body? It is said that one should cultivate both the phenomenal and the noumenal through the four kinds of samādhi.
As for the non-duality of phenomenon and noumenon, where the root and the branch mutually reflect one another, this shall be examined in the subsequent text; there is no leisure to discuss it here.

Furthermore, one must first realize that all phenomena are mind-only before one can contemplate the mind. When one is able to understand all phenomena, one sees that all phenomena are merely form and merely mind;
one should know that everything arises from the conceptualization of the mind. How could phenomena ever claim for themselves identity or difference?
The commentary states: This constitutes the fourth [section], clarifying that one must first achieve intellectual understanding.

Thus, the *Sūtra on the Examination of the Grounds* says: "There are two kinds of contemplation: first, the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*); second, the contemplation of the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

The contemplation of the true nature contemplates principle, while the contemplation of consciousness-only traverses phenomena. When the path of contemplating the non-duality of phenomenon and principle is slightly opened, one who can understand this may be discussed with."

The Commentary states: This corresponds to the fifth [section], which cites scriptural evidence for the two contemplations of phenomena and principle. The Sūtra says, "There are two kinds of contemplation," which is the heading.

"First, consciousness-only; second, the true mark" (dharmatā), which is the enumeration. Contemplating the true mark is the contemplation of principle; consciousness-only is the contemplation of phenomena.

This is the commentary on the "Matter. Regarding the phrase "observing the principle of the true aspect" (*shixiang guanli*), it means that the characteristics of the three thousand worlds within the ten realms and hundred realms are all truly real;
these very aspects are emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle Way, which is termed the "true aspect. One employs this true aspect to settle before oneself.

When one thought-moment is clarified and concentrated, the three thousand realms are fundamentally quiescent in their true aspect; therefore, this is called "contemplating the principle of the true aspect" (*shixiang guanli*). As stated in the *Zhancha jing*:
"One who practices the true contemplation of *tathatā* contemplates that the nature of the mind is neither arising nor ceasing.

This is precisely what is meant. Regarding "investigating phenomena through the perspective of Consciousness-Only" (*weishi lishi*), it means that all dharmas are merely transformations produced by the mind; therefore, one investigates them...

The ten realms, examined through the four modes of activity, reveal that the three thousand phenomena and functions are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; thus it is called "passing through phenomena.

As stated in the *Zancha jing*: "Those who practice the contemplation of mind-only consciousness should, at all times and in all places, observe every action performed by body, speech, and mind, knowing them to be nothing but the mind. This is precisely what is meant by "phenomena."

"Non-duality of principle" means to harmonize the two preceding contemplations. As cited above, it may appear as though phenomena and principle are divergent paths and that essence and function are eternally distinct;
however, one should know that those who cultivate the contemplation of principle do so by penetrating the principle of the non-duality of phenomena and principle.
This principle means that phenomenon and principle are non-dual. Those who practice the contemplation of phenomena do so by penetratingly realizing that phenomena and principle are non-dual;
this is the contemplation of phenomena as the non-duality of phenomenon and principle. Why must one wait until phenomenon and principle are blended together before it can be called non-duality?
One who is able to understand this practice has the path of contemplation slightly opened. "Slightly opened" means:

It gradually unfolds, which refers to entering the [meditative] stages (*varga*). One may then discuss with them the path of non-duality regarding the two contemplations of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*).
Otherwise, how could one possibly discuss this contemplation? Formerly, Master Zhao stated that contemplating the internal mind constitutes the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*).

Contemplating external forms is called the contemplation of phenomena (*vastu-vipaśyanā*). The Dharma-knowledge refutes this, saying: One must understand that both the internal mind and external forms possess both the contemplation of principle (*li*) and the contemplation of phenomena (*shi*).
It is not permissible to take the contemplation of the internal mind as the contemplation of principle and the contemplation of external forms as the contemplation of phenomena.

Therefore, one should know that regarding the various dharmas of the mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—both the subjective support (*niśraya*) and the objective environment (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—in terms of principle they are all principle; in terms of phenomena...
The *Shiyishu Zhiyao Chao* (Essential Extracts from the Ten Meanings Commentary) on the "Shared Practice" is widely circulated in the world.

Its compiler recklessly disparages Fazhi for dividing the two contemplations of phenomena and principle based on internal mind and external form. How can such deception toward the living and the dead be so extreme?
The compiler generally states that all four kinds of samādhi involve the cultivation of both the phenomenal and the principled contemplations (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).

For instance, in the Constant Sitting Samādhi, one contemplates the ten stages of the aggregates (*skandha*) by means of the "Ten Vehicles" and the refutation of the four modes of being (*caturvidha-svabhāva*). It is only after subjecting these to exhaustive investigation through the four modes of being that one finally attains awakening.

Is this not the contemplation of phenomena (the so-called initial vehicle’s contemplative method, which possesses both the phenomenal and the principle)? Not understanding this person, yet asking how the contemplative method is to be practiced—such is their arrogance.

Furthermore, they say: "Others claim that the contemplation of principle contemplates principle to produce the three thousand [realms], while the contemplation of phenomena contemplates phenomena to produce the three thousand.
Yet, in the first of the ten vehicles of constant sitting, one contemplates the aggregates and sense bases to manifest the fundamental nature.
Regarding the three thousand [realms] and the three truths, he then cites the passage from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* on "the mind creates" as proof for the *Fuxing*. He states:

"The 'creation by the mind' has two aspects. First, in terms of principle (*li*), 'creation' means 'endowment. Second, in terms of phenomena (*shi*), it refers to the discussion of the three periods of time, and so forth."
Furthermore, it is only through the inherent principle (*li-jù*) that phenomenal function (*shi-yòng*) can arise.

Why, then, do you suddenly divide the wondrous provisional nature inherent in the principle and treat the transformation into phenomenal function as the two contemplations of *tathatā* and *vijñapti-mātra* (the above being from his own text)?

This person, seeing the passage on "two kinds of creation" at the beginning of the *Constant Sitting* [Samādhi], claims that the initial vehicle of contemplative methods within the *Constant Sitting Samādhi* is immediately capable of manifesting phenomenal reality.
[The claim that] "Li [the principle] creates two kinds of the three thousand" shows that you do not understand Jingxi’s intent.

In this passage, he is generally demonstrating the essence of the two contemplations—of phenomena and principle—within the four kinds of samādhi. The ten vehicles of the *changzuo* (constant sitting) are exclusively the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*) and have no other path.
Therefore, after the commentary has shown the two types of creation, it immediately states: "Now, wishing to practice contemplation, one should simply..."

In contemplating the inherent nature (*li-jù*), both are simultaneously negated and simultaneously established; both are the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). One spontaneously encompasses what is manifested through the provisional and the real. Please consider the word "only" (*dàn*):
how can it be said that the three aforementioned samādhis also involve the cultivation of the contemplation of phenomena (*shì-guān*)?
Now, as for the term "only," does it not carry the meaning of "exclusive"? If one were to cultivate both phenomena and principle together, how could one say "only"?

Although within the context of cultivating virtue there are four propositions for analytical investigation, and even throughout the lower nine [stages] there are textual passages where four propositions are analytically investigated, since the ten realms and the four phases of existence are not being investigated therein, these are exclusively contemplations of principle (*li*).

One must not see the mention of "four propositions for analytical investigation" and immediately assume it to be a contemplation of phenomena (*shi*). It should be understood that when a practitioner of the contemplation of principle sets out on their path...

The principles and the nature of the practice of *tousu* (casting down the feet) are entirely different from those of the formal monastic system. One must not practice the contemplation of phenomena (*shikwan*) merely because one has practiced the contemplation of persons (*jin'gwan*).

Fazhi said: "How could it be that those who sit upright for the ninety-day retreat must all first indulge the three natures (*sangsōng*), and only then be said to have realized the non-duality of phenomenon and principle?
How could it be that those who are pressed by public and private urgency must all [first] spend ninety..."
After sitting upright for ten days, do you then claim that this is the principle of the non-duality of phenomena and reality?

You must understand that the "three thousand [realms] produced by phenomena" which are shown here is the essence of the phenomenal contemplation of the three natures, practiced freely within the "contemplation according to one's own mind.

It cannot be seen as being identical to the phenomenal functions revealed by the contemplative methods of the Initial Vehicle (Śrāvaka-yāna) at the very beginning of the practice of constant sitting and contemplating the aggregates. Furthermore,
Furthermore, it should be understood that the two modes of creation—phenomenal and principle—are the very substance upon which the two contemplations rely.

The contemplation of principle takes the creation of the three thousand realms through principle as its substance; the contemplation of phenomena takes the creation of the three thousand realms through phenomena as its substance.

One who cultivates the contemplation of principle must necessarily realize that cultivation is entirely contained within nature, for there is no cultivation apart from nature. Thus, the non-dual contemplation of principle serves as the capacity.

Contemplation. When contemplation is perfected, one immediately manifests original quiescence. Since the three thousand [realms] are themselves the non-dual original quiescence, both essence and function are attained.
Those who practice the contemplation of phenomena must realize that cultivation arises entirely from nature; there is no nature apart from cultivation.

When this contemplation is perfected, the transformation and creation of the three thousand [realms] will necessarily manifest. Since this transformation and creation is non-dual, both essence and function are attained.
The rules and measures of the path of contemplation each have their proper sequence. How could the compiler [Zhanran] have confused his explanations?

Both the contemplations of principle and phenomena reveal the inherent three thousand [realms] as well as the three thousand [realms] of phenomenal function—each being simultaneously empty and simultaneously existent.

Is this not so? Why, then, do you further claim that the two modes of creation—phenomenal and noumenal—and the two modes of contemplation—phenomenal and noumenal—cannot be spoken of as being on the same footing?
If that were the case, the two modes of creation would certainly be the objects revealed, while the two modes of contemplation would certainly be the subjects that reveal;
how would this differ from the methods of a craftsman’s construction? Fazhi rebuked Master Zhao, saying: "The two modes of creation, phenomenal and noumenal..."

Since they are not distinguished, upon what could the two contemplations of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*) be established? These words are most profound. Fazhi possessed a wondrous realization of the *zong* (the fundamental vehicle);
after Jingxi [Zhanran], he was truly the only one of his kind. I, a person of shallow learning and no discernment, have nonetheless dared to offer this critique.
"It is like an ant trying to shake a great tree; truly laughable! Now, I ask the editor:

since the two contemplations of phenomena and principle cannot be discussed as being on the same level as the two creations of phenomena and principle, and since the wondrous provisional nature of the three thousand realms cannot be discussed as being on the same level as emptiness, yet you claim that the three thousand realms definitely belong to the realm of having marks (*sanimitta*), you must..."
To negate it by means of emptiness and to reject it through the Middle Way is merely to return to the signless;
such an explanation has not yet reached the stage of differentiation, let alone that of the Perfect and Sudden. The faults are immeasurable and cannot be fully enumerated.
Question Eleven: In the *Anxin zhong* (The Stabilization of the Mind), it says: "In essence, there is neither arising nor ceasing; it is through delusion that one speaks of arising and ceasing.

Should one merely eliminate this deluded speech while still maintaining arising and ceasing as the essence? Or should one cause the deluded speech to be such that there is no longer any arising or ceasing?"
The commentary states: This question within the text consists of two sections. First, the passage on "settling the mind" (*anxin*) is cited as the basis for raising the objection.
Second, it serves as the immediate point where Jingxi raises his critique. Regarding the phrase "to realize its essence (*ti*), it neither arises nor ceases":

the single character *ti* (realize/essence) refers to the function of cessation (*śamatha*). The word *qi* (its) is a term used to point to a phenomenon (*dharma*). Thus, "realizing the delusion" refers to the emotional mind. Therefore...
Regarding the statement that the essence of words does not truly arise or cease: it is through wondrous stillness (*śamatha*) that one brings them to rest and restores them to their original state.

To speak of "arising" is a delusion based on the attachment to the existence of nature (*dharmatā*); to speak of "ceasing" is a delusion based on the attachment to the non-existence of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

When one examines this through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), existence is fundamentally non-existent, and non-existence is likewise fundamentally non-existent; it is simply that the attachment to nature is originally empty, and even emptiness cannot be apprehended.

This is what is meant by "settling the mind. Jingxi raises an objection, asking: "Does one merely eliminate the sentiment of false conceptualization while leaving intact the phenomena of arising and ceasing?
Or, once that sentiment of false conceptualization has been realized as extinguished, does one also cause all phenomena of arising and ceasing to return to non-existence?"
Answer: This, too, has no distinction; one must understand its underlying meaning. If discussed solely from the perspective of principle (*li*), it is neither arising nor nature.

If considered in terms of the merit of the fruition, then nature does not obstruct arising. If considered in terms of sentient beings, there is only the arising of delusion regarding nature. If the sage observes the ordinary person, then arising is precisely nature itself.
Now, speaking from the standpoint of returning from delusion to awakening, we cause one to leave arising and return to nature, seeing that which is neither arising nor nature.
Nevertheless, fearing that those who are deluded might abandon arising in their search for the nature, [the text] causes them to realize that while there is arising, in reality there is no arising.
Since there is no arising, there is likewise no cessation.
The commentary states: This answer consists of five parts; some are general and some are specific. The first four are general, and the last one is specific.

In other cases, they exist separately. Now, this text reverses delusion to return to awakening. When it says that "herein there is also no distinction," it means that one merely eliminates false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
This refers to the false conceptualization that still perceives arising and ceasing within the essence; it intends to cause that arising and ceasing to be non-existent.

These two phrases differ in wording but are identical in meaning. Why? Because when one merely eliminates false conceptualization while still [apparently] maintaining arising and ceasing, this very arising and ceasing is precisely non-arising.
"Extinction. Its essence is false; it is said to bring about the absence of arising and extinction. This absence of arising and extinction does not obstruct arising and extinction;
therefore, it is said that "this also has no distinction. Regarding the instruction to "skillfully understand its meaning," this refers to both the general and specific meanings.

If one is skillful in this regard, the two difficulties raised will naturally dissolve like ice. First, regarding the fourfold general [analysis]: first, discussing the principle alone, it is neither arising nor...
Regarding "nature" (*prakṛti*): the term "non-arising" implicitly contains "cessation," for the principle is neither arising nor ceasing. Regarding the term "non-nature":

since the essence of nature is realized through cultivation, it is not a cultivation of arising or ceasing; furthermore, there is no nature that is fundamentally non-arising and non-ceasing. If there is no cultivation, there is no nature.
This first point clarifies, solely from the perspective of principle, that there is neither arising nor ceasing. Second, if we consider it from the perspective of the nature of the resultant virtues:
Regarding "it does not hinder arising": although the fruit of enlightenment has already realized the principle of neither arising nor ceasing, neither cultivation nor realization, it cannot be named;

yet, for the sake of convention, we forcibly call it "realizing the nature. It is quiescent and unmoving, yet responds universally and without fixed direction, like a great mirror facing objects and universally manifesting form-bodies.
Therefore, it is said that "the nature does not hinder arising. Third, if one considers only the arising from the perspective of sentient beings:
Regarding the nature of delusion: "Only arising" means that there is only arising and ceasing. Those whose nature is deluded do not know how to return to the source;
thus, all sentient beings are submerged in arising and ceasing. How could they know that the fundamental substance returns to its original state, wherein it neither arises nor ceases?
The compiler, failing to understand that "only arising" and "the nature of delusion" refer to the same single matter, interprets it as saying: "Only giving rise to greed and anger."

How erroneous is their delusion regarding the nature! Such are the four [points]. If one holds that what arises when a sage observes an ordinary person is nothing but the nature itself, then sentient beings are using it daily without knowing it.
It is like a great wealthy blind man who, in his every movement and coming and going, is instead obstructed by precious jewels.
Since the perfect sage’s observation is entirely the wondrous nature, it is said: "What arises is nothing but [the nature]."

This is the nature. These four [points] generally discuss the rational nature as being a "double negation" (*ubhayābhāva*). It is that which all Buddhas have realized, yet sentient beings are deluded by it.

The discerning illumination of noble wisdom has not yet reached a definitive answer; for if one eliminates delusion while claiming that arising and ceasing still exist, or if one takes delusion as the essence while claiming it causes the absence of arising and ceasing, these are not the final resolution.
The subsequent text will clarify this. Fifth, now, following the reversal from delusion back toward awakening, it is taught so that one may depart from arising and return to the fundamental nature.
"Seeing that which is not of the nature of arising" is the direct answer to the underlying intent of the "settling the mind.

This means that when one realizes its essence does not arise or perish, yet falsely claims it arises and perishes—those who speak thus do so simply because they employ the wondrous stillness of the three thousand [realms] to arrest such arising and perishing;

thus, even in dispersion, there is quiescence. Therefore, it is said: "cause them to depart from arising and return to the nature. The phrase "departing from arising" means departing from both arising and perishing. (Text)

This is abbreviated. "Returning to nature" means returning to the nature of the three thousand phenomena in their quiescent illumination, which is neither arising nor ceasing; hence it is called "returning to nature.
As for the statement "seeing the nature that does not arise," it means that by returning to the fundamental, one sees that which is neither arising nor a nature.
Because arising is itself nature, it is "not arising"; because nature is itself arising, it is "not a nature. Thus it is said. Even with such wondrous cessation, there is still apprehension...
The practitioner’s mind is deluded, giving rise to the seeking of a nature that departs from it; thus, they cause the essence to arise when in fact it does not arise.
If one seeks a nature that departs from it, it is like discarding ice while seeking water—it is merely a weariness of oneself.
Therefore, the essence is made to arise, yet in reality it has never arisen. Since there is no arising, there is likewise no cessation. Suddenly, as if resting in emptiness, there is only awareness.
There is nothing at all. Is it thus that one settles the mind in its entirety? Since this is so for total cessation (*samatha*), it is likewise so for total contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Regarding the twelve questions: since you speak of "cessation and contemplation with a single mind," how can you further establish sixty-four variations?

The commentary states: Regarding this question concerning the text on "settling the mind," since the general method of settling has already established the non-dual *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of the single mind as the means of settling (*nirveśaka*), and the three thousandfold world of quiescent illumination as the object to be settled (*nirveśya*), this is sufficient in meaning.
Why is it necessary to further establish sixty-four rounds?
Answer: Regarding the sixty-four categories, these are established by considering the mutual support of the faculties (*indriya*) and the modes of practice (*caryā*) as they revolve and interrelate;
when discussed in their totality and universality, there are sixty-four modes of practice. Why must they necessarily possess every single numerical category?

Furthermore, regarding their essential nature (*svabhāva*), they are simply based upon the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) being quiescent yet illuminating, sovereign and capable of function. Therefore, it is permitted to be thus.
The commentary states: Regarding the sixty-four cycles of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, this is an exposition of the general through the specific.

Why is this? Although the general practice is general, its essence encompasses the specific; although the specific practice is specific, its essence is always general. From beginning to end, there is no duality.

As for the mention of "according to faculties" and "according to practices," "faculties" (*indriya*) refers to that which is capable of producing [realization], while "practices" (*caryā*) refers to the progressive advancement. This is truly because, throughout the accumulation of kalpas, one has heard the Dharma.

By this, the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is perfected. Through practicing meditation for many kalpas, the faculty of dharma (*dharmendriya*) is perfected. Once these faculties are perfected, they are termed "faith-practice" (*śraddhācārin*) and "dharma-practice" (*dharmacārin*).

Therefore, each of these two practices possesses four *siddhi* (universal benefits). Through the calming and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) that settle the mind, sixteen cycles are formed. Regarding what is called "turning back":
there are eight cycles of faith-practice turning into dharma-practice, and eight cycles of dharma-practice turning into faith-practice. Furthermore...

This constitutes sixteen sets. There are thirty-two sets for the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* for one's own benefit, and likewise thirty-two for transforming others, totaling sixty-four sets;
these pertain exclusively to the nature of the faculties (*indriya*). Regarding what is called "mutual support":
there are eight sets where faith supports the Dharma, and eight sets where the Dharma supports faith, totaling sixteen sets.
Furthermore, there are eight cycles in which faith is supported by the Dharma and is transformed into the practice of faith;

there are eight cycles in which the Dharma is supported by the practice of faith and is transformed into the practice of the Dharma. These together constitute sixteen cycles, totaling thirty-two cycles.

Since there are thirty-two cycles for one's own practice, there are likewise thirty-two cycles for transforming others. This is the mutual support and reciprocal transformation of the spiritual faculties.
Together with the previous ones, these constitute one hundred and twenty-eight instances of *anxin* (settling the mind).
In this present text, however, the number sixty-four is used to encompass both [sets] simultaneously; therefore, it simply says "sixty-four.

As for the statement, "Why must a practitioner necessarily possess all the numerical categories?"—the character *xing* (practice) is pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*). The *Zhíguān* (Stopping and Contemplation) states: "If the mind rests upon the Truths..."
A single phrase is sufficient. Should it not be so settled, one employs skillful means to bring the mind to rest.
This is like catching a bird, which necessarily requires many eyes; yet once the bird is caught, only a single eye is needed.

Furthermore, regarding its essential nature (*dharmatā*), it is simply because the quiescent illumination of the *dharmatā* is sovereign and functional that it is permitted as such. The meaning is that although—

One hundred and twenty-eight methods of skillful means are employed through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. As for their essential nature, they are simply the inconceivable realm of the three thousand worlds in a single thought-moment.
These non-dual *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are applied with sovereign freedom according to the capacities of sentient beings.
The reason for this is that the mental activities of sentient beings are each different:

some have many people sharing the same mental activity, while others have a single person with many types of mental activity. Therefore, a broad net of Dharma is cast to capture the birds of sentient beings' mental activities;
thus, there are many varieties of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. These many varieties are the opening up of the general to reveal the specific, yet the specific is not...
The particular and the universal: the essence of dharmas is perfect and subtle; be careful not to hold divergent views.

Thirteenth Question: Within this very text, it is sometimes said that all dharmas are themselves the dharma-nature (dharmatā), and at other times it is said that one must investigate through the four movements and the four natures.
Which of these is the essential point?
The commentary states: "In this very text" refers to the text on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

When it says within the text that "all phenomena (*dharmas*) are themselves the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*)," it means that the very engagement with objects is itself the Middle Way (*madhyama*), for there is nothing that is not true.

In essence, this simply means that by realizing that the single thought-moment of the five aggregates (*skandhas*) is itself the three thousand [realms], it is said that "all phenomena are themselves the dharma-nature. Here, "all phenomena" refers to the aggregates.

This is stated with reference to the contemplative methods of the Initial Vehicle (*śrāvakayāna*). Alternatively, it refers to directly realizing that all phenomena are themselves the essence of *dharmatā*.
As stated previously in the ninth question regarding the initial settling of the mind: "One simply believes in *dharmatā* and does not believe in those [phenomena].

This is spoken in terms of remedial application (*pratipakṣa*), intended to cause one to perceive only *dharmatā* within all phenomena. Alternatively, it is said to refer to the four movements and the four natures.

"Examination" refers to, for example, the method within the *Suizuyi* (Following One's Own Intent) of freely employing the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) to investigate the ten realms and the four phases of mental activity.
Master Jingci feared that people might not understand the Great Master’s intention in establishing this gate of practice; for phenomena consist of both the phenomenal and the noumenal.
Faculties are either sharp or dull; therefore, the question is asked: "What is the essential gateway for entering the Way? The answer is:
Now, the method of contemplating the mind has both a phenomenal aspect and a noumenal aspect. Following the noumenal aspect, one penetrates directly to the Dharma-nature without any other path.

When engaged in practice, one focuses exclusively on the arising of the mind, wherein the four natures are found to be unobtainable; this is also called "the fundamental and the derivative reflecting each other," where phenomena and principle are non-dual.

The commentary states: In this response, in order to accord with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the contemplation of the mental aggregates (*skandha*) and the mind is established as the essential gateway. Therefore...
It is said: Now, the method of contemplating the mind (*citta*) involves both the phenomenal (*dharma*) and the principle (*tattva*).

If one discusses the objects of contemplation in general, the mind, the Buddha, sentient beings, the environment (*āśraya*), and the inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—all phenomena (*dharmas*)—may serve as objects. As for the principle, they are all principle; as for the phenomenon, they are all phenomenon.

However, for the sake of a preliminary and simplified judgment, it is said: "The Buddha-dharma is too lofty and sentient beings are too vast; these are difficult for a beginner. Contemplating the mind, however, is easy. So it is taught.

Regarding what is called "easy": it is proximate and essential. Therefore, for the time being, this is also explained according to the majority of cases; thus, taking the contemplation of the mind as the essential point.
If one considers the differences in inclinations and desires: those who should contemplate the Buddha will find it easy to contemplate the Buddha, such as in the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* and others;
those who should contemplate sentient beings will find it easy to contemplate sentient beings, such as in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* contemplation.

In the "Chapter on Sentient Beings" and other sections, the present text follows the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* regarding the observation of the mind; thus, it simply says "mind" for the sake of ease.
As for the principle of realizing only the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) and no other path:

this means that one settles the originally quiescent three thousand [realms] within the single moment of the present indeterminate thought, causing one to perceive the three thousand purely within a single thought—such that the single thought is itself the three thousand, and the three thousand are themselves the single thought.

Although there are four propositions for examining the two objects—the cultivation of one's own virtue and the transformation of others—within the context of the three thousand [realms], the essence of contemplation does not depart from the original quiescence of the three thousand.
From the initial arousal of the bodhicitta until the departure from craving, it is no different from the original quiescence of the three thousand;
all of this is solely the realization of the *dharmatā*, with no other path. The compiler’s [knowledge] is shallow.

If one studies without knowing the underlying principle, yet claims that cultivating virtue and transforming others involves the fourfold analysis, such an analysis belongs to the contemplation of phenomena (*sī-guan*).

The fourfold analysis applied to the nine vehicles below are all contemplations of phenomena. Alternatively, when using the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*), one penetrates only the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
Yet [some] claim that the four kinds of samādhis and the ten vehicles both employ both the contemplations of phenomena and principle.

How can such arrogance be so extreme? The preceding passage has already refuted this. One should know that the current text merely distinguishes the ten vehicles of contemplation on principle (*li-guan*) for the practice of sitting meditation (*dhyāna*).
Although the contemplations on principle within the other three samādhis share the same ultimate aim, they differ in their specific approaches.

To recklessly propound one's own views without having mastered the study of these meanings is to bring disorder to the gates of contemplation; no sin is greater than this. As for the practice (*shi*), it consists of single-mindedly illuminating the arising of the mind.
Regarding "the four natures are unobtainable": this refers to the fourth samādhi, wherein one freely employs the three natures to examine the ten realms and the four modes of mental activity.
Since [the mind] must necessarily belong to a single realm and a single mode, it is said that one "exclusively illuminates the arising of the mind.

This is the object of observation. "The four natures are unobtainable" refers to the observing subject that performs this investigation. This is because [the mind] is neither self-arisen nor other-arisen...
Together with the "neither" and "without cause," one exhaustively pursues them; the delusory attachment to the four natures is itself the nature of no-nature.
This absence of even that [no-nature] is the nature of signlessness. Because both nature and appearance are empty, it is said they are "unobtainable.

This contemplation of the four phrases takes the great function of the three thousand realms, produced through transformation, as its essence; this is called the "contemplation of phenomena" (*shikwan*). These phenomena are...

This is an inconceivable matter. Therefore, the preceding text states: "Contemplating this single movement as being endowed with the ten realms, the hundred realms, and the three thousand [worlds], which are simultaneously empty and the Middle, is the inconceivable realm.
Nevertheless, one must still proceed from the arousal of the bodhicitta through the severance of craving to fulfill the characteristics of entering the Way according to this school;
this refers to the ten modes of contemplation within the practice of contemplation. As the compiler says:
Why then do you say that the four kinds of samādhi—the two contemplations of principle and phenomena—share these ten Dharma-methods of śamatha and vipaśyanā?
Do you perhaps not recognize the path of the contemplative way? As for "the beginning and the end reflecting one another, where phenomenon and principle are non-dual":

taking the entirety of the three thousand realms as quiescent (*śama*) constitutes the contemplation of principle; this is termed the "beginning. Taking the entirety of the three thousand realms as transformative and created constitutes...
The contemplation of phenomena (*shiguan*) is called the "branch" (*mo*). Within the root there is the branch, and within the branch there is the root; this is termed "mutual reflection.

For one who cultivates the contemplation of principle (*lixingguan*), they realize that apart from nature (*xing*) there is no cultivation, and that the substance is fully endowed with function. Thus, this branch exists within the root.

For one who cultivates the contemplation of phenomena (*shishiguan*), they realize that apart from cultivation (*xiu*) there is no nature, and that function is entirely identical to the substance. Thus, this root exists within the branch.
Only those who can comprehend this recognize that phenomena and principle are non-dual.

Why, then, would they need to blend phenomena and principle, practicing phenomena while simultaneously attending to principle, or practicing principle while simultaneously attending to phenomena? Within the Ten Vehicles, each vehicle practices by having phenomena and principle support one another;
this is called non-duality. How could such a person fail to recognize the profound subtlety of the path of contemplation?
Question fourteen: Regarding the statement in the *Fahua Xuanyan* that "the wisdom which can illuminate the object" provides a sincere proof, yet the principle remains difficult to clarify.
The commentary states: This appears in the section on the "Excellence of Wisdom" (*zhimiao*) in the second fascicle of the *Xuanyan*. There, the question is posed: "Wisdom can illuminate the object."
Question: Can the object of cognition illuminate the wisdom? Answer: If one adopts the meaning of inconceivable mutual illumination, there is no impediment to saying so.
Although [the opponent] cites authoritative proof, they quote the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which says: "It speaks of wisdom and the locus of wisdom."
All are named *prajñā*. Now, it is said that the "knower" (*jñānin*) is the one who is able to contemplate, while the "locus of wisdom" (*jñānasthāna*) is the object contemplated.
Since all are named *prajñā*, then the objective realm (*viṣaya*) is also wisdom and functions as the illuminator. Although this is cited as proof, [it remains so].
The principle is likewise difficult to clarify; therefore, I shall now provide an analysis so that its meaning may become manifest. Answer:
If one follows the teachings of expedient means, the principle cannot be fully integrated. However, if one speaks from the ultimate perspective, it is easily harmonized within the principle.

Taking the mind as the object, the mind is also able to illumine it; both subject and object are mind, and the essence of the mind is all-pervasive. When each moment of mind illumines the other, the principle is profoundly [revealed].

[The word] "Explanation" [indicates the following]. The commentary consists of five parts: first, using the partial teachings (*prādeśika-śāsana*) to reveal the perfect and ultimate, which is easily harmonized; second, from "Therefore, not...

onwards, citing the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*) to prove that the object and wisdom are non-dual; third, from "Because this... onwards, [discussing] the four [aspects] of the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-śāsana*).
The analysis of the phrases: "The four illuminations" (below) clarifies that practitioners of the partial and the perfect differ in their explanations of illumination.
"For this reason" (below) fully enumerates what is illuminated by the partial and small vehicles to reveal the objective realm and wisdom of the perfect.

Regarding the initial statement that the teachings and principles of the provisional means (*upāya*) are "not to be harmonized": within the teachings of the provisional means, the objective realm and wisdom cannot be fused; now, we follow the ultimate perfection.
That it is easy to harmonize with principle is truly because the mind is taken as the object and is momentarily made the observed;
this very mind-object is itself the capacity to illumine and the capacity to observe. As for both subject and object being mind:

the observing subject is the mind of the three thousand, and the observed object is the mind of the three thousand; it is simply that one takes the three thousand of the fundamental principle as the observing subject.
Contemplation: By means of this contemplating mind, one contemplates that which is contemplated. The substance of the mind is entirely pervasive.

To be "entirely pervasive" means that the contemplating mind is itself the wondrous object, and the wondrous object being contemplated is itself the contemplating mind; therefore, it is said to be "entirely pervasive.

Using the three thousandfold mind to illumine the three thousandfold mind, the object is identical to the contemplation, and the contemplation is identical to the object; therefore, it is said to "illumine one another. The contemplating...
Thus, the principle is understood with great clarity. Why, then, should one doubt the wisdom that illuminates the object?
Therefore, the beginning of the "Inconceivable Object" section states: "The inconceivable object is itself contemplation."

The commentary states: This corresponds to the second [section], which cites the formal exposition of the ten vehicles regarding the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*) within *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
This is the introductory chapter’s analytical summary of the text; hence it says, "The inconceivable realm is itself contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Since it is stated that the realm is itself contemplation, what prevents the realm from being able to illumine wisdom? If this were not the case, how could one perceive non-duality?
Excellent! Based on this, one may formulate a fourfold analysis: the object illuminates the object; the object illuminates wisdom; wisdom illuminates the object;
and wisdom illuminates wisdom.

The commentary states: This constitutes the third [section], which, by means of the fourfold categorization (*catuṣkoṭi*) based on the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), distinguishes and brings forth the Perfect object and wisdom.
One should know that although "object" and "wisdom" are distinct in name, their essence is not different. Therefore, the subject and object are two yet non-dual.
While the beginner’s cultivation of contemplation provisionally establishes subject and object, within the fourfold categorization, this corresponds precisely to the third: wisdom.

It illuminates the object. If one understands that the substance of both object and wisdom is all-pervasive and constitutes only a single *trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*, then what doubt could there be regarding the object being illuminated by the object?

Furthermore, it should be known that although the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are established to differentiate between object and contemplation, at the very moment of actual application of contemplation, there is only the single *trisāhasra* world-system shining forth in absolute non-relation (*atyantāpekṣā*). What subject and object could possibly be distinguished therein?

If that which illuminates were only able to illuminate, it could not be exhausted by verbal description; if that which illuminates were to be described, it could not be understood through illumination.
If that which describes were only able to describe, it could not be exhausted by illumination; if that which describes were to illuminate, it could not be understood through description.
The commentary states: This corresponds to the fourth section, clarifying the differences in the modes of illumination as taught for practitioners of the partial and the perfect.

Why is this? It means that only those who employ the wondrous contemplation of the three thousand [realms] as their mode of illumination are able to illuminate this contemplation of the non-dual realm of the three thousand;

therefore, it is not something that can be fully fathomed by those who teach the partial teachings. Regarding the phrase "the illuminator should explain that which is not to be understood through illumination," this refers to the Perfect [Teaching].

The practitioner of the Sudden Teaching internally illumines the principle of the three thousand realms as they truly are (*trisahasra-lokadhātu-tathatā-lakṣaṇa*). Being in accord with this principle, they speak in accordance with that principle;
therefore, this is not something that can be fully understood by those who merely illumine through partial teachings.

It is said that what cannot be exhausted by mere illumination can only be spoken by one who speaks according to the Perfect and Sudden Teaching; thus, it is not something that can be illumined by partial teachings.

This is not something that can be fully exhausted by those who merely speak. One who speaks should reflect; this is not something that can be understood by those who speak through partial or inferior teachings.

For one who speaks according to the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, there is internal resonance with the principle of the three thousand realms as true reality (*dharmatā*). Thus, speaking should correspond to reflection. Therefore it is said: "The speaker should reflect;
this is not something that can be understood by those who speak through biased or minor teachings. This is evident in the text and need not be explained in detail.
