Thus, one knows that the perfect [teaching’s] aggregates, bases, and elements (*skandha-āyatana-dhātu*) point to evil as being identical to nature; this is precisely the three thousand [realms].

The wondrous realm of intrinsic virtue is without subject or object; this is called the "contemplation of absolute transcendence. Only by thus discerning the ten realms, such as the five aggregates and so forth, does the substance of the Ten Vehicles come into being.
As for the statement that "if there are no Ten Vehicles, it is called a 'ruined donkey-cart,'" this means the cart is ruined and the donkey is debilitated;
it refers to using a debilitated donkey to pull a ruined cart. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Brahma-conduct," says: "Riding..."
The broken donkey-cart travels directly south. Zhan’an offers three interpretations; I maintain that one interpretation is correct, and thus I present it here now.
The south is Li (Separation); Li is fire. This refers to riding upon the vehicle of false views to head toward the fires of the three miserable realms.
Therefore, it is said that one travels toward the south; the other two directions are not essential and thus are not mentioned here.

Furthermore, the east corresponds to the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), the south to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), and the west to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). One who delights in the vehicle of afflictions proceeds toward the suffering of birth and death.
Therefore it is said, "He travels toward the south" (this is not from the *Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*).

The Ten Vehicles of Tiantai are established based on the parable of the Great Chariot in the *Lotus Sūtra* (as seen in the previous section on the classification of schools; the detailed correlation of the Great Chariot with the Ten Vehicles has already been presented and will not be repeated here).
How can one of another school, who lacks these Ten Vehicles entirely, yet wish to practice? This is like trying to catch fish by climbing a tree. Alas! Regarding the Buddha-dharma...

Since the Dharma was first transmitted to the East, prior to the guidance and conversion of the Great Master Tiantai, people had not even heard the name of the "Ten Vehicles," let alone those who practiced based upon them.
Thus, Zhanran (Zhang’an) said, "In previous generations, this was unheard of.
This is indeed true and cannot be doubted.

Thus, one should know that it is necessary to rely on these five chapters to give rise to profound understanding. Within the development of this understanding, the general meaning briefly explains the beginning and end, as well as the causes and effects for oneself and others;

thus, while the text is concise, the meaning is expansive. The subsequent four chapters focus exclusively on names and entities; thus, both the textual expression and the underlying principles are extensive.

The commentary states: This shall now explain the third general discussion within the section resolving doubts. The opening exposition of the five chapters each has its specific affiliation. Why is this?
One who cultivates these *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* must necessarily give rise to wondrous understanding through the preceding five chapters;
this is the general explanation. Within this general explanation, the chapter on the "Great Meaning" (*mahārtha*) is termed the "Five Summaries," which is as follows:
This briefly explains the beginning and end, as well as the cause and effect, of both self and others. Thus, one's own practice has its beginning, end, cause, and effect;
the transformation of others likewise has its beginning, end, cause, and effect; this applies to both self and others alike. This means that while the text is concise, its meaning is expansive.

"The text is concise" refers to it being merely a single chapter. "The meaning is expansive" means it encompasses the nine subsequent chapters. As for the statement that the next four [chapters] focus exclusively on names and substance (*nāma* and *vastu*), although...

There are the categories of "comprehensive dharmas" (*saṃgraha-dharma*) and "partial versus perfect" (*prādeśika-vipula*). The "partial versus perfect" refers to the names and the essence (*nāma-bhāva*). The "comprehensive dharmas" likewise converge upon the essence.
Expedient means (*upāya*) and correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) pertain to the fundamental principle (*mūla*). This principle encompasses both cause and effect;

since the fruition (*phala*) achieves practical utility, these four [categories] focus specifically on the names and the essence. The compiler states: "The 'next four' refers to the general enumeration of the four chapters; 'names and essence' refers to the specific [distinctions]."
This refers to citing the first two chapters. Although it cites the first two, it also encompasses the latter two; thus, [the critic’s claim] is a profound ignorance of the meaning of the text.

As for the statement that both the phrasing and the principles are extensive: "phrasing" refers to the wording of the four chapters, and "principles" refers to the principles of interpretation and discernment within those four chapters; their extensiveness is evident.
Therefore, one employs extensive exegesis to guide the commencement of practice, ensuring that the twenty-five factors are distinguished according to the teachings.

Only when these are integrated, opened up, and the coarse elements discarded can they be called the beginning of sublime practice (*miao-xing*). For this reason, none of the five chapters may be omitted.
The commentary states: This shall explain the fourth point within the resolution of doubts—the mutual support of understanding (*adhimukti*) and practice (*pratipatti*).

The text itself consists of three parts: first, clarifying how understanding guides skillful means; second, from "If one employs... onwards, clarifying the cultivation of the ten vehicles based on understanding; and third, from "But now... onwards, clarifying [the method] for those of dull faculties.
Regarding the first, concerning the practice of guiding skillful means with understanding, it says: "Therefore, by means of extensive understanding, one guides..."
Regarding "the beginning of practice" and so forth: these twenty-five dharmas constitute the commencement of cultivation.
By means of each of the wondrous understandings opened up by the five chapters, one is guided to accomplish the initial practices of the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*).

As for "distinguishing according to the teaching," this is not the former three [teachings], but rather the skillful means that open, harmonize, and discard the coarse. Only through these skillful means practices is one fit [for the ultimate].
I consider this to be a preliminary introduction to the tenfold multiplication of the Perfect Reality (*yuan-shi*).

Were it not so, then skillful means would not be the skillful means of authentic cultivation, and authentic cultivation would not be the authentic cultivation of skillful means; it would merely be like hanging a signboard over a province to delude and confuse practitioners.
Therefore, the five chapters give rise to understanding; their merit is great.
If one employs this understanding to cultivate the ten dharmas, then merely explaining the names and sequence of these ten dharmas will be sufficient for the principle itself.
The commentary states: This refers to the second stage, practicing the ten vehicles based on understanding (*adhimukti*). What is this?

If one employs the first five chapters to extensively develop sublime understanding, and further employs the twenty-five methods as skillful means (*upāya*), then within those skillful means, understanding arises in accordance with phenomena.
When understanding is clarified, practice gradually unfolds. By employing this, one cultivates the ten dharma-vehicles.
As for this, whether in exposition or practice, it merely explains the titles and tenets (*mūla*) of the Ten Vehicles. Regarding the phrase "titles and tenets":
the preceding five chapters focus exclusively on names and substance (as seen in the text above). Here, the term "tenet" refers to the fruit and retribution of correct contemplation;

these words are spoken in accordance with the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*). As for the sequence: they constitute five layers that do not become disordered. Therefore, only the ten [vehicles] are explained.
The Dharma is termed "principle" (*zong*), and its sequential logic is herein self-sufficient; there is no need for prolixity.
However, the characteristics within this text remain extensive because those of dull faculties might still fear they would not understand the sequence of the contemplation of dharmas.
Therefore, the preceding interpretation is cited to provide a detailed discussion on entering contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

The commentary states: This corresponds to the third section within the "Mutual Support of Understanding and Practice. The text itself is divided into two parts: first, leading those of dull faculties from understanding into practice;

second, clarifying the complete cultivation of the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*) through the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*). The remaining nine [sections] follow this same pattern. The first part:

It may be thought that since the preceding text already states that merely explaining the names of the ten dharmas constitutes a sequence of principles sufficient in itself, one ought instead to directly present the essentials for practicing the gates of conduct and cultivating the mind. Yet, the current text remains so extensive and detailed;

this is because the Holy Master, fearing that those of dull faculties might not understand the sequence of the contemplative methods (*vipaśyanā*), has therefore cited the previous opening [of the text].

The explanation of this text is treated in detail within the "Ten Vehicles" (daśayāna). Although the phrasing may appear extensive and each point seems to reach its logical conclusion, it is not actually prolix.

Furthermore, fearing excessive elaboration, I have fully explained the ten dharmas regarding the aggregates (skandha) and bases (āyatana), while the nine objects (viṣaya) are to be understood by analogy. Therefore, in these various texts...
"Not without the secondary and the primary. The commentary states:

This corresponds to the second [section], clarifying that within the entry into the ten objects (*daśaviṣaya*), one must fully cultivate the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*). The remaining nine [objects] follow this same principle.

Why is this? Regarding the ten objects such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, it is logically required that each one individually clarify the ten vehicles. In the present text, however, [it is only addressed] at...

The first section on the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) fully elucidates ten dharmas. The subsequent nine sections merely apply the tenfold contemplative method (*daśavidha-vipaśyanā*) by analogy to their respective objects.
Therefore, it is said that "the contemplation is accomplished through ten dharmas. One need only thoroughly understand the underlying causes and conditions regarding the objects of the aggregates.
The remaining nine [objects] can only be used for contemplation once they have been activated. Therefore, these nine objects merely involve the discernment of objective characteristics (*nimitta*).

The ten vehicles (*daśayāna*) within the section on the objects will not be discussed in detail; rather, they are treated according to their activation and application for contemplation, as this is not the occasion for an extensive exposition. Regarding the statement that there is neither the absence of the secondary nor the primary:

although practice (*caryā*) is present within the preceding section on the development of understanding (*adhimukti*), practice is secondary and understanding is primary. Although within the text on formal cultivation...
The preceding five [stages] should also be seen as proceeding primarily through correct understanding while being accompanied by secondary aspects.
For instance, the ten objects are merely the ground upon which a single thought-moment operates; each one reveals how the characteristics of the objects differ.
The seeds of practice arise one by one from the ten modes of contemplation; these are the rain for practice.
Each transforms into the inconceivable realm; this is the sprout of practice. Each aspiration is generated; this is the trunk of practice. Each mind is settled; this is the root of practice.
The leaves of practice. Each and every one of these, from the "Pervasive" stage down to the "Auxiliary" and "Principal" practices, constitutes the flowers of practice.
Each and every stage and position, up to the "Detachment from Craving," constitutes the fruit of practice. Without these six matters, the tree of the Way would not stand upright.
The commentary states: This constitutes the third section, clarifying how the practice of understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) can bring about the tree of enlightenment (*bodhivṛkṣa*).

The text is divided into three parts: first, clarifying that within each object of focus one fully cultivates the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*); second, following the sequence below, showing that for individuals it is not necessarily fixed at ten;
and third, following the subsequent text, citing scriptural evidence for the ten vehicles. The first part contains eight phrases; the first two phrases serve as the basis, while the latter...
The six phrases constitute that which is dependent. The initial statement, "For instance, as for the ten objects," uses the word "for instance" (*qie*) as a term indicating a provisional approach.
This implies that one need not necessarily contemplate all ten objects; hence, it says "for instance.

"The ground where a single thought-moment functions" refers to the thought-moment of ignorance, which is precisely the phenomenon that is identical with principle. This single thought-moment is not... [the latter part of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
A single thought of an ordinary, mundane person is precisely the single thought-mind of a practitioner of contemplation who has already opened up sublime understanding.
Therefore, it is the phenomenon that is identical with principle; the phenomenon is itself the principle. This is called the "ground of practice.
"Ground" refers to the one mind-ground where ignorance is itself the dharma-nature. Upon this ground of the mind where ignorance is itself the dharma-nature, [all things arise].
Each one reveals that the distinct characteristics of objects serve as the seeds for practice. It is like the earth in the world, which contains all seeds;
now, the Ground of Dharma is likewise endowed with all dharmas. Therefore, the distinct characteristics of objects are revealed to serve as the seeds for practice.
"Seed" carries the meaning of that which is capable of producing. Each and every characteristic of an object...

It possesses the principle of the three thousand real aspects (*trisahasra-lakṣaṇa*). These three thousand kinds arise entirely from nature (*prakṛti*) as cultivation (*bhāvanā*), constituting the essence of the ten vehicles of contemplative methods (*daśayāna-dhyāna-dharma*).
Therefore, the preceding text states: "If there were no vehicle of the ten objects (*daśaviṣaya-yāna*), there would be no essence.

Thus, the categories of the ten objects constitute the essence of the ten vehicles; they are also termed the "nature-seeds" (*prakṛti-bīja*). Jingxi said: "At the time of their arising, these seeds transform purely into..."
Regarding the phrase "How [can one] cultivate [it]? the compiler states: "If there were no ten objects (daśaviṣaya) as the vehicle (yāna), there would be no essence.

Thus it is said that because the ten objects exist, the ten contemplations (daśa-vipaśyanā) arise; because one contemplates them through contemplation, they are called the essence of the vehicle. When one realizes that the aggregates (skandha) are themselves the principle, the entire object becomes the contemplation.
How can one direct the mind in such a way? This is utterly erroneous! Utterly erroneous! To say that each [contemplation] arises from the ten vehicles—how could this be?

Regarding the rain of contemplating the practice of the dharmas: by employing the seeds of the complete realm to accomplish the tenfold contemplation, the contemplation in turn illuminates the realm, just as rain moistens the seeds.
Each of these successively transforms into the sprout of the inconceivable realm and practice.
"Teeth" (*ya*) mean "sprouts. Regarding the character *ya* in the text that does not follow the "grass" radical (*cao*), both interpretations of its meaning are valid;

the compilers [of commentaries] claim it is an error, but this is merely due to their lack of broad learning. As for what is called "transforming into the inconceivable realm," according to the sequence of the current text, this must pertain to the stage of "Profound Names";
one cannot yet point to the five grades (*wu pin*) and beyond, because the five grades and the six faculties...
This is because, as will be explained below, they reside within the fruit. Regarding "each and every resolve for enlightenment (bodhicitta) is the trunk of practice":
in the natural world, that which is substantial and large is called a "trunk. Since the resolve for bodhicitta seeks enlightenment above and transforms beings below, that which it sustains is vast;

thus, it is like a trunk. Regarding "each and every settling of the mind is the leaf of practice": this refers to the one hundred and sixty-four instances of practicing for oneself and transforming others.
The twenty-eighth [section] and so forth: because the contemplations of phenomena are numerous, they are like leaves.

Each of these—pervasive refutation, penetration and obstruction, the factors of the path, and the primary and auxiliary practices—is like a flower. This refers to these four dharmas: pervasive refutation, penetration and obstruction, the factors of the path, and the primary and auxiliary practices.
This refers to that which is delightful in its practice; because it can personally serve as the cause for attaining the fruit, it is called a "flower.

Those who are biased and delight in hearing heterodox views, slandering the Dharma and its teachers, will likewise fall into the evil realms; they are truly and deeply pitiable.

Therefore, upon reaching the section on "Correct Contemplation" (*samyag-darśana*), the sequence of arising is discussed once again; within each vehicle, the sequence of arising is further discussed. This is why...

Each section cites specific instances to support and complete the characteristics of practice; these constitute the "flesh" of the text.

"Established. This refers to the outer skin. From the marrow to the bone, from the bone to the flesh, and from the flesh to the skin—skin being the integument.

Furthermore, it should be understood that in the preceding passage, the six dharmas that can bring about the Tree of Enlightenment were explained solely in terms of practice;

Failing to perceive this intent, there have been those who repeatedly claimed that Jingxi’s terminology was fragmented or inconsistent. Such an interpretation is not what the compiler intended.

Therefore, [the following] four [chapters] clarify the names, essence, characteristics, inclusion of dharmas, partiality, and perfection. These four...

The meaning of the four chapters is the "bone" of the Dharma-body. The ultimate destination of the intent of the four chapters is the "marrow" of the Dharma-body.
If it were not so, then the understanding would not be the understanding of the True House, and the True would not be the True of the house of understanding.

Correct. Only when understanding (*pratipatti*) and practice (*caryā*) are mutually perfected can one be fit to enter the Path. As for the "Chapter on Not Speaking of the Great Meaning," it serves as a general heading for the four dharmas of understanding and practice throughout the entire treatise;
therefore, it is not mentioned [separately] here.
"If the four matters are absent, the Dharma-body is not accomplished.

Therefore, readers and practitioners must understand the relative urgency [of these points]. Do not mistakenly point to partial statements or biased interpretations that cause practice to be incomplete.
The commentary states:
This constitutes the fourth admonition and censure. It is an admonition for those currently studying or those who will study *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* in the future; do not...
Because these ten fascicles of text are considered voluminous and extensive, one should know that every passage and every sentence contains essential meaning;
this is a warning against misinterpreting partial words or biased meanings so as to cause the practice to be incomplete.

This is a refutation [of such errors]. For instance, some erroneously identify the passage on "settling the mind in general" (*anxin zong*) as the "sudden-sudden" *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, and the passage on "settling the mind specifically" (*anxin bie*) as the "gradual-sudden" *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, and so forth. Since they point to these one-sided statements, their biased intent is evident.
This is the erroneous adherence of those teachers with perverse interpretations, which will be extensively refuted in the following text.

The process of cultivation has never exceeded the gathering of understanding to give rise to skillful means. One practices the cause to attain the fruit; when the fruit is perfected, one teaches others.
When the capacities of others have been met by my response, the cycle of stimulus and resonance ceases. Self and other alike return to the principle of cessation, the true nature.
The intent of this present section is solely such as this; therefore, these ten chapters encompass everything without exception.
The commentary states: This constitutes the fifth section, which fully enumerates the ten chapters to provide a comprehensive conclusion to the practice and realization (*gamana*).

In the preceding text, only the first five chapters were used to generate understanding (*adhimukti*), while the latter two were designated for practice (*caryā*); however, they did not yet fully enumerate the ten chapters of this entire treatise to show how the beginning and end of both self and others converge in the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*).
Therefore, it is now fully enumerated as a concluding summary. For one who has engaged in spiritual cultivation, could there be anything that exceeds this collection of explanations?

"Ji" (accumulation) means to gather and accumulate. Having extensively consulted the sūtras, śāstras, and the preceding five chapters, [the Master] accumulated [these insights] within his mind to open up sublime understanding;
thus, it is called "ji. The compiler suggests that "ji" should instead be written as "xi" (to practice).

However, I maintain that the words of the Patriarch are definitive in themselves. While errors in transcription may arise from scribal mistakes and can therefore be corrected, this is not the case here. Fortunately, there is...

In principle, why should there be any alteration? Now, in this text, the character "ji" (集, *cita*) is employed; its meaning surpasses that of "xi" (習, *abhyāsa*). The meaning has been explained above.
Through speech, one initiates expedient practices; by means of causes, one attains fruits; and when the fruits are fulfilled, one transforms others—this is the establishment of the teaching.

In transforming others, there is the capacity [of the teacher] and the response [of the recipient]. When the task is completed, all return together into the secret treasury of the principle of extinction (*nirvāṇa*). This present section...
The meaning is precisely this. The text and its significance are so evident that they do not require further detailed explanation.
○ Regarding the seventh section, "Analogies for Resolving Doubts and Manifesting the Correct," the commentary states:
This is the heading of the title. To clarify and instruct is called an "analogy" (yù); to hesitate and be indecisive is called "doubt" (yí). Having doubted...
If one were to reach a definitive conclusion, the correct principle would not be communicated.

Thus, the Venerable Jingxi used his exegesis on the wondrous practice of the One Vehicle to illustrate Master Guan’s heterodox and vacillating views, enabling him to understand that the sections on *śamatha-vipaśyanā* pertain exclusively to the Perfect and Sudden teaching and have no other destination.
Therefore, it is said that this serves to resolve doubts and clarify the correct doctrine.
Those who study this school all receive its transmission from a single master; its principles and expressions have been handed down in succession without any divergent interpretations.
It was only when encountering those who were biased—who gave different answers to the same questions—that I had no choice but to seek out analogies to investigate the matter.

The commentary states: This metaphor illustrates the reason for clarifying what is correct regarding doubt. Why is this? Because those who study this school all receive its teachings from Tiantai, it is called "one master.
From Zhiyan (Zhang’an) down to Jingxi, there have been five generations of transmission.

In their texts there are no divergent tracks, and in their principles there are no different paths; they are pure, singular, and unmixed—their source and flow are clear. Within the lineage of Jingxi’s disciples...
As for Master Chengguan, he suddenly developed heterodox views within his own school. Consequently, during a session of private instruction, when the Master questioned him, he gave a contrary answer.
Since his interpretations were so confused as to muddle our true lineage, it would have been a great harm had this not been rectified.
Having no choice in the matter, I interrogated him and reached a conclusion, subsequently enlightening him; thus, this precedent was established.

This is the original text. Question: How many types of the Sudden Teaching are there? (This is Master Jingxi’s question. Answer: There are the Gradual-Sudden and the Sudden-Sudden. (This is Master Guan’s answer. Regarding the term “The Analogy Says”:

this refers to Master Jingxi’s analogy; the same applies to all subsequent instances. The Analogy says: As for the method of exegesis, one first examines the original text. When the original text establishes a name, it cannot...
They are immediately different. In seeking a divergent interpretation, one must still maintain that their essence is the same. The terms "sudden-sudden" do not appear in the sutras or treatises;
they are absent from all other works outside this particular school’s writings. If both the name and the essence are absent, upon what can one rely for practice?

If you argue that "sudden-sudden" is equivalent to the Perfect [Teaching], just as "Perfect-Peak" and so forth are, then this meaning may be acceptable. However, since two types of "sudden" have already been distinguished—wherein "gradual-sudden" is identified as the Perfect—then "sudden-sudden" must be added further.
"To what is this intended?
The commentary states: This passage uses a metaphor to establish that the name "sudden-sudden" exists nominally but lacks substantial reality.

To say it "exists nominally" is to speak from the perspective of affirmation; yet, when speaking from the perspective of negation, both name and substance are entirely absent. All of this will be seen below. (Exegesis)
"Jiang" (to lecture/discuss) means "plowing. It refers to plowing through the texts to harmonize and clarify their principles and meanings;
hence it is called "jiang. Because the One Way is without deviation, it is called "guàn" (to penetrate/permeate). Confucius said, "My Way is unified and penetrates all.

The compiler, in explaining this, cited the metaphor of "stringing flowers" and "scattering flowers" to clarify the meaning. Now, "stringing flowers" refers to verses and hymns (*gāthā*), while "scattering flowers" refers to prose.
This refers to the prose exposition. How could a lecturer explain only the verses? Regarding the instruction to "first examine the original text," this refers to the text of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
As for the titles established in the original text, they must not be arbitrarily altered or changed.
If one wishes to seek alternative names and interpret them through reasoning, one must still ensure that the essence remains the same before attempting such an interpretation. Furthermore...
The name "Sudden-Sudden" does not appear in the sutras or śāstras. Furthermore, it is absent from all the works of this particular school.

If both the name and the substance are non-existent, then there is nothing upon which practice can rely. Now, one who practices must rely on the teachings of names and words to elucidate the essence of reality;

only by relying on this essence of reality can one truly practice. Since neither the sutras, the śāstras, nor the written treatises contain the term "Sudden-Sudden," [the basis for such a practice is lacking].

[This refers to] names. If there were no names, how could one invoke the essence? If there were no names and no essence, upon what would practice depend? Therefore, it is said that "practice has no basis.
As for the statement that "the sudden is itself the perfect, like the perfect being perfect," this meaning may indeed be so;

however, such a phrase is merely concessive. The *Miaoxuan Liaojian* (Exegesis on the Profound Meaning) discusses four propositions, stating: "There is the gradual-perfect"; this refers to the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Because those who have practiced the seven preliminary stages (*saptaprayoga*) enter into the Perfect [Teaching], it is called "gradual perfection.

There is also "perfection within the gradual," which refers to those from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) onward who gradually enter subsequent positions. There is also "gradual within the gradual," which refers to those of the seven preliminary stages prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
There is also "perfect within the perfect," which refers to the state of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*). These, then, represent the partial and the perfect throughout the past and the present.

The four propositions of the *pratītyasamutpāda* are also like this. Although the "sudden-sudden" (dun-dun) is identical to the Perfect (yuan) within the Perfect, once the two types of sudden—namely, the gradual-sudden (jian-dun) and the sudden-sudden—are distinguished, the fact that the gradual-sudden is the Perfect is sufficient for the meaning.
What further purpose would there be in adding the sudden-sudden? It is simply that there is nothing further to which it can be compared.
Question: What is the difference between these two stages regarding the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*)?

Explanation: Since they are distinguished as gradual-gradual, gradual-sudden, and sudden-sudden, and since there must be individuals corresponding to each teaching, what exactly are the stages for abandoning afflictions for those who follow these two teachings?
Answer: The two stages are different. If one follows the gradual or sudden [approach], the four abodes are first eliminated prior to the first stage (*bhūmi*).

If one follows the sudden-of-the-sudden approach, the five abodes are completely suppressed prior to the first stage, and from the time one ascends to the first stage onward, the five abodes are completely destroyed.
The commentary states: This response was formulated from the master Guān’s own perspective, as can be seen in the text.
Regarding the analogy: the four [lower] abodes are eliminated prior to the first abode. The cited proofs belong to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), and this is the case throughout.

Thus, the *Four Mindfulnesses* of the Perfect Teaching says: "It is like smelting iron to make a vessel; the primary purpose is to form the vessel, not to remove impurities. As for coarse impurities..."

First, we exclude that which does not pertain to the gradual approach. Since it is said that in the sudden approach one "ascends to the stages (*bhūmi*) and completely breaks [the afflictions]," this clearly indicates that the five preliminary stages (*pūrva-bhūmi*) prior to the first stage are fully present.

One should know that this meaning pertains neither to the Separate (*pratyeka*) nor the Perfect (*yuan*) [vehicles]. In the Perfect vehicle, the first stage alone breaks ignorance (*avidyā*); thus, one should not say that one enters the [first] stage while the five stages are simultaneously severed.
In the Separate vehicle, the five preliminary stages must be fully present; the stages break the four abidings (*catvāraḥ sthitayaḥ*), and the practice (*caryā*) breaks [the remaining afflictions].

As numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Only upon ascending to the stages (bhūmi) does one break a grade of ignorance; thus, we know it is not something separate. Apart from these two, there is no other established teaching to rely upon.

The commentary states: "The delusions of the four stages prior to abiding are eliminated; upon ascending to the stages, one breaks only ignorance; therefore, one should not enter the abiding [of the first stage]. Five.

Regarding those who abide in the simultaneous severance [of afflictions], the teaching explains the process of severance and suppression through the sequence of the gates of instruction; thus, there are distinctions of depth and priority in their order.

As for the statement that the four abidings (the four *āśrayas*) are first eliminated, this refers to the fact that the power of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) becomes increasingly manifest, whereby the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within a single great trichiliocosm naturally fall away.

However, if one speaks according to the actual substance of the delusions, these pervasive afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) are [simultaneously addressed by] the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

Contemplation continues until it reaches the final thought-moment of supreme enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), where it ceases simultaneously with ignorance and delusion; only then can it be said that one has reached the ultimate teaching.
From this we know that the four abodes (*catur-vāsa*) fall away first, and [the teaching] speaks of them in sequence for the sake of expediency. Why is this?

Since the initial mind already cultivates the three contemplations in their perfection, the five grades of practice must suppress the three delusions in their entirety. Thus, when the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*) severs the views of the mundane realms, it should likewise involve the complete severance of the three delusions.
A small portion is excluded. If it were not so, how could they be called "similar" while manifesting the three truths?
If that is the case, why did Jingxi reprimand the Master Guan, saying: "Ascending to the stages (bhūmis), one completely shatters the five abodes; this is neither distinct nor round"? I reply:

The Master Guan took what is the ultimate round [vehicle]—its subduing and severing—and degraded it as "gradual-round. His meaning has already fallen into error. Furthermore, he spoke of "sudden-sudden dwelling."

The first five stages (*bhūmi*) remain entirely intact; it is only upon entering the sixth stage that they are completely shattered. Since there is no textual evidence for this in the various teachings, they are dismissed as being neither *Pratyekabuddha* (Separate) nor *Bodhisattva* (Perfect).

Thus, one should know that if one realizes the cessation of views through the first faith (*śraddhā*), one ceases the afflictions of thought (*saṃskāra*) from the second faith through the seventh faith.

If it is claimed that from the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages of faith one subdues the delusions of ignorance, and that upon entering and abiding [in the first bhūmi], one shatters the delusions of ignorance to become a Perfectly Ultimate One (*yuanji*), then one should not falsely assert that prior to abiding one "perfectly subdues" the five stages of dwelling (*wuzhu*), while upon ascending to abiding one "perfectly shatters" the five stages of dwelling.
If this were so, how could one speak of "perfectly cultivating the three contemplations" or "perfectly shattering the three delusions"? Would this not be a self-contradiction within our own school?

"Yes," he replied. "This meaning is extremely profound; it is not something that can be discerned by those who study with a coarse mind. Now, the sequential exposition of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanlun*) is presented through the provisional gates of the teachings.
It is the state where non-differentiation is itself differentiation, yet within this very differentiation, the essence remains eternally without differentiation.

Therefore, the severing of views and so forth during the first stage of faith is described as 'differentiation. This differentiation and non-differentiation are each, in their essence, all-pervasive."
All three delusions are severed. Why is this so? To trace their origin, these three delusions are in essence perfectly interfused and fundamentally lack distinct natures;

it is only through the explanatory distinctions of the various teachings that they are described as three. What are they? They are the phenomena of birth and death within the six realms and the triple world.
Its substance is the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are attached to the emptiness of nirvāṇa. Its substance is the *rajas-aṇu* (dust-like afflictions);

the bodhisattvas grasp at the two extremes. Its substance is ignorance (*avidyā*). One who practices the Perfect Teaching understands that a single thought-moment is fully endowed with the ten realms.
Furthermore, these ten are mutually endowed with the inconceivable; thus, one delusion is itself the three delusions, and the three delusions are themselves one delusion.

As each delusion arises, it obstructs the three truths. Once one understands that the substance of the three delusions is perfectly interfused, one takes this very delusion as the subject of contemplation.
Subject and object are non-dual, and the essence of illumination stands alone. From these profound names, one attains [realization].

One enters the five grades. Once the five grades are attained without difficulty, one can enter the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*). The coarse delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) are spontaneously eliminated first;
these are designated as "views and thoughts" by way of sequential exposition, yet in their actual substance, all three delusions are simultaneously severed.

If one enters the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), it is described from the perspective of what is predominant as "shattering ignorance" (*avidyā-bhañjana*), yet in its actual substance, it fully possesses [the severance of] all three delusions. If this is so...

In the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-śāstra*, the commentary explains that after passing through the pure practices of all the bodhisattvas, one leads the bodhisattva into the ninth stage of pure meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Herein, both the general and specific afflictions (*kleśa*), as well as their active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and residual habits (*vāsanā*), are completely exhausted. The *Fazhi* commentary states:

"The 'general' refers to the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vitarka-kleśa*); the 'specific' refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). The active outbursts of the general afflictions are exhausted at the seventh stage of faith in the Perfect Teaching, while the residual habits are exhausted upon reaching Buddhahood."

The separate practice is exhausted; now the meaning is explained. Why is it said that the pervasive afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) and the fundamental afflictions (*anuśaya*) are likewise severed at the final moment of mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), just like ignorance?
It is said: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is also provisionally explained according to the sequence of the scriptural teachings.
If explained from the perspective of their essence, from the beginning until the end, the three delusions are completely severed simultaneously and are truly not separate from one another.
Therefore, know that if one realizes that a single thought-moment is replete with the three delusions, the essence of these three delusions being fused is itself the three contemplations.
Upon hearing this teaching of mine, may your minds not be startled.

Question: Regarding the two types of sudden cultivation, what is the distinction between their characteristics? Answer: For those who practice the gradual-sudden contemplation, the contemplation of emptiness is established first;

for those who practice the sudden-sudden contemplation, all three contemplations are realized simultaneously. [The opponent] says: This is in direct contradiction to the doctrinal texts of our own school.

Since it is stated that "gradual perfection" refers to the *yuan* (perfect) teaching among the four teachings, one should judge this stage of perfection according to the six levels of realization (*liu ji*). Therefore, one should not say that the contemplation of emptiness is established first.

[The threefold contemplation] is accomplished. Why? The five grades [of the ten faiths] are precisely the contemplation-practice of the three contemplations; the six faculties [of the ten abidings] are the semblance of the three contemplations;
and from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward is the partial realization of the three contemplations. How can you then say that the contemplation of emptiness is accomplished first?

Furthermore, you do not understand the meaning of the "falling away" of view-delusions and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) occurring within the semblance stage. If it were accomplished beforehand, how could it be called "semblance"? Since it is said that all three [contemplations] are attained simultaneously...

Regarding the simultaneous realization through both [insight and cultivation], at what stage does this occur? If it were at the first dwelling (bhūmi), how would it differ from the gradual and sudden approaches?

If it were prior to the dwellings, there is no such principle at all. To claim that both are suppressed prior to the dwellings and both are severed upon entering the first dwelling—since there is no scriptural authority for this in any of the teachings—it constitutes nothing but a heterodox doctrine.

The commentary states: As for this illustrative passage, that which is generally intelligible need not be further explained. Regarding those points that are obscure or hidden, I shall briefly point them out.

As for the statement, "Furthermore, one does not understand the meaning of the 'seemingly attained' stage (*sāmya-avasthā*) where view-delusions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thought-delusions (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) have already fallen away":

this refers to one within the five grades of practice who encounters no obstacles; through the manifest efficacy of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), they enter the stage of semblance, wherein view-delusions and thought-delusions [are eliminated].
Coarse defilements are removed spontaneously and prior to what was originally intended; thus, one naturally attains a semblance of the three truths.

How, then, can it be said that the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is established first? As for the statement "sudden-sudden," since it is said that all three contemplations are realized simultaneously, to what stage does this refer?
If they are realized simultaneously at the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), then it is identical to the "gradual-sudden" [approach], because in the gradual-sudden... [initial stage].

Because one abides in and perfectly realizes the three [wisdoms], if one were to suppress the three delusions while still in the preparatory stages and only sever them upon ascending to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*),
then in the absence of scriptural evidence for this in the various teachings, it would be a false doctrine.

Question: On what basis is it known that there are two types of *dun* (sudden)? Answer: According to the *Xuanyiwen* (Profound Meaning), there are eight teachings, namely: *jian* (gradual), *dun* (sudden), *mimi* (esoteric), and *buding* (indeterminate).
Within *jian*, there are four: *zang* (Tripitaka), *tong* (Shared), *bie* (Distinct), and *yuan* (Perfect). These four, together with the preceding [three], constitute the eight teachings.
Since the final one among the gradual is the *yuan* (Perfect), and a further *dun* (sudden) is established outside of the gradual, we know that the former *yuan* is merely...
[The teaching] gradually becomes complete. To establish a separate "sudden" [teaching] is itself the "sudden-of-the-sudden. He frequently used this principle to challenge others;
since no one could respond, he thought, "Only I alone know [the truth]."
The commentary states: Regarding formal debate, there are two types—internal and external.
When debating with outsiders, one must not cite the scriptural authorities of one’s own school, because they do not have faith in that school. "Outsiders" refers to those belonging to other schools;
in such cases, one may only oppose them by citing their own scriptures and treatises. When debating with insiders, it is then permissible to cite the scriptural texts of one’s own school.
Regarding the "insiders": because they belong to the same school, Master Qingliang Guan was a disciple of Jingxi.
He studied the Tiantai *Zhi guan*, the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, and other texts. Since he developed eccentric interpretations, Jingxi questioned him.
He cited the *Miaoxuan* (the *Profound Meaning*) which he had studied as his response; while the wording of his answer is clear, one shall see its errors in the following analogy.
The Commentary states: According to this judgment, there are many contradictions. First is the contradiction of failing to recognize the name of the teaching.

To establish a separate "Sudden" [teaching] is precisely the initial Sudden division of the *Avataṃsaka*. When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, before traveling through the various assemblies, he did not come from the gradual;

he directly preached the Great [Vehicle]. Because this great division was at the beginning, it is called "Sudden. However, this division still encompasses other aspects and cannot [be categorized as such in isolation].

"Exquisite Name. How could one take a sutra that combines both the universal and the particular and translate it as "Sudden-Sudden," while the *Lotus Sūtra*, which alone reveals the ultimate, is instead labeled "Gradual-Round"?
The commentary states: This passage serves as an analogy for the obstacle of not knowing the names of the teachings; specifically, it refers to not knowing the name of the "Sudden Teaching.

Now, what is called "Sudden" refers to the initial Sudden division of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, [which was taught] when the Tathāgata had just attained enlightenment... [text continues]... before [the gradual teachings].
The events across various assemblies do not gradually unfold; rather, they directly expound the Great [Vehicle]. Therefore, it is called the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*).

However, within this division, there still remains the inclusion of the Separate Teaching (*bie-jiao*), and thus it cannot be termed "Wondrous" (*miao*). This is precisely why. If one looks toward the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation of the provisional to manifest the real, this [Sudden Teaching] is still a "Perfect" [teaching] that is separated from and biased by the partial.
How could a "Perfect" teaching that is separated from and biased by the partial be considered the "Sudden of the Sudden"? The Dharma...
Does the *Huayan* alone manifest as gradual or sudden?

Second, there is a failure to recognize the obstacles to the gradual opening. Regarding what is called "gradual opening," according to the *Fahua xuanyi*, after the sudden teaching of the *Huayan*, [the Buddha] separately provided for those of lesser capacity;
without moving or descending [from that state], he bestowed the gradual teachings. At the beginning of these gradual teachings, he first preached the Tripiṭaka.
After the teaching of the Tripiṭaka, it was through criticism and refinement that the four [teachings] were finally fully established; thus, they are said to have been "opened out.

Therefore, in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text), everything from the Deer Park until the Prajñā assembly is termed "gradual" (*jiàn*). How could there be a Perfect Teaching (*yuánjiào*) within this gradual category such that it would be called "gradual-perfect"?
Furthermore, in the tenth fascicle of the *Xuán*, regarding the classification of teachings into gradual and sudden, [it covers] from the *Huányán* [Avataṃsaka] down to the Prajñā assembly.

All [teachings] possess both gradual and sudden aspects. Since the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-yāna*) of the *Avataṃsaka* and the Perfect [teachings] within the *Vaipulya* and *Prajñāpāramitā* are not different in their perfection, they should both be designated as "Sudden-Sudden.

Why should the *Avataṃsaka* alone be so named? If the Perfect [teachings] within the *Vaipulya* and *Prajñāpāramitā* are called "Gradual-Perfect," then the Perfect Teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* would likewise be called "Gradual-Sudden. What does this have to do with other sections [of the canon]?
The commentary states: "Immovable" refers to the immovable site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). "Not descending" means not descending from Tuṣita.
This clarifies that the Great Vision undergoes no change from beginning to end, whereas the Small View does. His remaining for twenty-one days was the bestowing of the Tripiṭaka;
thereafter came the refutations of the Vaipulya and the purifications of the Prajñā—both of which are termed "gradual. Only then were the four [teachings] fully employed.

Therefore, it is said that they are "opened out. Since both the Vaipulya (fangděng) and Prajñāpāramitā (bōrě) contain the Perfect (yuán), how could they be called "gradual-perfect" merely because they reside within the gradual section?
Furthermore, in the tenth fascicle of the *Xuányán jì*, the classification of teachings (*jiàoxiàng*) distinguishes between the gradual and the sudden.

From the *Avataṃsaka* down to the *Prajñāpāramitā* assemblies, there are both gradual and sudden aspects. In the *Avataṃsaka*, the Perfect is taken as the Sudden, while the Separate Teaching (*biéjiào*) is taken as the Gradual.
Up to the Prajñāpāramitā section, the general and specific [teachings] are considered gradual, while the Perfect [teaching] is considered sudden.

Since the Perfection in these three locations is not different, and since the Perfection within the *Avataṃsaka* is called "Sudden-Sudden," then the Perfection within the Vaipulya and the Prajñāpāramitā should likewise both be called "Sudden-Sudden.
Why is it that only the *Avataṃsaka* is named "Sudden-Sudden"? If the Perfection of the Vaipulya and the Prajñāpāramitā is to be called...

Regarding "gradual perfection": the perfection of the *Avataṃsaka* is also called gradual perfection. Why then is it said that only the "perfection within the middle flavor" among the gradual teachings is named gradual perfection?
The remaining text clarifies this of itself; there is no need for further explanation.
Third is the obstacle of failing to recognize the essence of the teaching (*śāsana*). If one gradually unfolds [the seven] into four, it is like opening a fist to reveal the fingers:

there are only fingers and no fist. If one combines the four to form the gradual, it is like closing the fingers into a fist: there is only the fist and no fingers. If the gradual is preserved, the teaching has only four;

if the gradual is subsumed, the teaching has only seven. To preserve both would necessarily mean that one side lacks its essential substance. To establish eight, however, ensures the substance [is maintained].
"Narrowness is called 'broadness.

The commentary states: This metaphor illustrates the obstacle of failing to recognize the essence of the teaching. The text cites opening a fist to form fingers and closing the fingers to form a fist as an analogy for the meaning of the gradual unfolding and closing of the teachings;
this is clearly evident and need not be further explained. Thus it is said: "It remains."
"Regarding the statement that 'if one maintains the gradual teaching, there are only four,' the intended meaning is:

if one preserves the gradual teaching without opening it into the four [categories] such as the *pitakas*, then the teachings consist only of the four modes of conversion (*vyañjana*). Regarding the statement that 'if one omits the gradual, there are only seven':
since the gradual has been opened into the four modes of conversion and dharma (*artha*), together with the three—sudden, indefinite, and secret—there are [seven]."

Seventh: "If both were to exist, one side would necessarily lack substance. This means that if the gradual [teaching] were preserved while also preserving the four aspects of the transformative dharma (huàfǎ), then one side would necessarily lack substance.
If the gradual alone is preserved, there can be no substance for the transformative dharma; if the transformative dharma is preserved, there can be no substance for the gradual teaching.
This argument is made solely by contrasting the gradual with the transformative dharma. Thus, the eighth [point] is established.

Regarding the statement that "the substance is narrow while the name is broad": as for the substance being narrow, it consists of only seven [categories] and lacks an eighth; thus, the substance is narrow.

As for the name being broad, it refers to the broadening of the single term "gradual" (*jiàn*). Although this is but a minor path, from antiquity to the present day, few have been able to understand it.

The Compiler says: "Establishing eight [categories] means the substance is narrow while the name is broad. Regarding the name being broad, it refers to the "Transformational Rituals" (*huáyí*) and the "Transformational Teachings" (*huǎfǎ*).
Each [of these] has four teachings. "Narrow in substance" refers to the fact that while the *huayi* (modes of conversion) lack a substantial body, the *huafa* (teachings of conversion) possess one;

thus it is said that "the substance is narrow while the name is broad. This, however, fails to recognize that Jingxi [Zhiyi] distinguished between names and substance solely by contrasting the gradual teaching with the open and the unopen.
To interpret the meaning based on the literal sound [of the characters]—is this not the work of such a person?

Fourth, suppressing the obstacles to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. In recent times, many systems of doctrinal classification (*kyōhan*) have regarded the *Avataṃsaka* as the fundamental wheel of the Dharma (*mūla-dharmacakra*) and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as a secondary or derivative wheel.

Only the Great Master Tiantai, having personally received the transmission on Vulture Peak and attained wondrous awakening at Mount Dasu, authored commentaries and treatises to compare them through ten points of analysis;
even the "Trace Gate" (*jimon*) differs, while the "Origin Gate" (*honmon*) is eternally distinct. Therefore...
In the *Xuánwén*, all explanations first employ the judgment of the teachings (*jiàopàn*), wherein three are coarse and one is wondrous;

next, they employ the judgment of the flavors (*wèipàn*), wherein four are coarse and one is wondrous. How can that which is coarse be called "sudden-sudden," and how can that which is wondrous be translated as "gradual-perfect"?
The commentary states: This passage is a metaphor for suppressing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Lotus Sūtra) while exalting the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* (Huayan).

Regarding the claim that the *Avataṃsaka* is the "Root Wheel of Dharma" (*mūla-dharmacakra*) and so forth: from the Liang and Chen dynasties onward, there were many who lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

However, it was only the Venerable Master Jizang of Jiaxiang Monastery who explained the teachings of the entire lifetime of the Buddha’s ministry through the three wheels of Dharma, identifying the *Avataṃsaka* as the first, the Root Wheel.

Regarding the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*): according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, first, those who see my body and hear what I teach immediately believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Second, for those who previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna, this constitutes the Wheel of Dharma for the branches and leaves—namely, those of the three vehicles and so forth.
Third, "I now also cause them to hear this sutra and enter the wisdom of the Tathāgata" is spoken for the purpose of gathering [them].

In the end, he returned to the fundamental Dharma-wheel, turning the three vehicles into the One Vehicle. Later, meeting the Great Master Tiantai, he realized that what he had established was erroneous.
Therefore, he turned his heart toward him and abandoned his former studies. He then ascended Mount Tiantai and wrote a letter saying:

"I have long wished to submit to the Ambrosia and wear upon my head the Dharma-bridge of Wondrous Joy. He further stated: "Since I, Jiaxiang, have received the wondrous transformation, my doctrinal principles have already [been clarified]."

Regarding the "Consecration of the Deity" (Kanshin), the established precedents must first be thoroughly refuted according to principle. Alas! To know one's errors and be able to reform them is the virtue of Master Jiashang.

How could Master Guanding follow his old doctrines? Thus, in his commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he distinguished the teaching of the One Buddha Vehicle as being explained in three ways.
He stated that the "One Buddha Vehicle" refers to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* serves to bring [beings] back to it at the conclusion of the assembly.

Fundamentally, this master of contemplation picks up treasures discarded by others and regards them as supreme jewels; this is truly laughable. As for what he calls his own commentaries and treatises:
when the Great Master seeks to benefit the multitude, he ascends the high seat and, with unhindered eloquence, expounds the teachings inexhaustibly.
This does not mean he was attached to commentaries. When it says "composed by himself," this refers to what was stated after Zhāng'ān had compiled the texts.

However, even before the Great Master passed away, some had already been compiled. As for his own personal compositions, he personally took up the pen only for the *Mysterious Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra* and the *Successive Order of the Dharma Realm*, among others.
Regarding the phrase "the ten meanings compared with these" and so forth, the first is the beginning...

Regarding "the initial vision" and "the present vision": the initial vision refers to the first attainment of the Way; the present vision refers to the revelation of the reality (*dharmatā*) in the *Lotus Sūtra*. Second, regarding "opening and closing" versus "neither opening nor closing":

the *Avataṃsaka* speaks directly of the Great Vehicle without discussing opening and closing; the *Lotus Sūtra*, as the teaching of reality, opens the three vehicles and closes the three to return to the One.
Third, regarding "vertical extensiveness" and "horizontal brevity": the *Avataṃsaka* is vertically extensive because it involves entering the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). It is not... [horizontal].

Because it spans five periods, the Avataṃsaka is horizontally abbreviated; in the Lotus Sūtra, both the horizontal and vertical dimensions are extensive. In the four original manifestations and one trace, there are many traces sharing a single original;
in the Avataṃsaka, the lotus pedestal is the single original, while the thousand billion emanations are the many traces. In the Lotus Sūtra, the five periods constitute the shared traces.

Regarding the long-distant origin and the solitary [nature of the teaching], there are five points concerning whether the teaching is supplemented or not supplemented. In the *Avataṃsaka*, it is supplemented by the four bodhisattvas, such as Vairocana-vana, who expound the forty stages (*bhūmi*).
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is spoken solely by the Buddha himself; he transforms the land six times, yet in one instance the land remains untransformed.

In the *Avataṃsaka*, the site of enlightenment (Jiǎochǎng) is not said to have the land transformed. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the land and fields are transformed three times. Seventh, regarding many locations versus few locations: in the *Avataṃsaka*... [text ends].

1. The *Avataṃsaka* is solemn in its seven locations and eight assemblies; the *Lotus Sūtra* was preached at a secluded place on Mount Vaideha. 2. The *Avataṃsaka* involves both expelling and not expelling [the śrāvakas];

the *Lotus Sūtra* eliminates the "inferior city" (the *Saṃdhinirmocana*) and the "lowly hired laborer" (the *Śrīmālādevī*). The *Avataṃsaka* lacks these elements. 3. The *Avataṃsaka* directly reveals the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*) while opening up the provisional to reveal the ultimate;

the *Lotus Sūtra* does so through the mediation of the five periods of teaching. 4. The *Avataṃsaka* is easy because those of sharp faculties enter the Buddha-wisdom immediately; the *Lotus Sūtra* requires the harmonization of the five periods before one enters.

This is difficult. By comparing it through these ten points, even the *Ji-men* (Trace Gate) already surpasses all other teachings; how much more so the *Ben-men* (Origin Gate), with its remote lifespan, which is eternally distinct from all other teachings.

How can one then take this eternally distinct teaching and categorize it as "gradual" or "sudden"? Is the *Huayan* [Sūtra], which incorporates the "distinct" [teaching], to be considered "sudden-sudden"?
Can the rest of the text not be seen? Are you able to provide a complete explanation?
Fifth is the failure to recognize the obstacle posed by the name "Sudden" (dùn). If the name is established based on the practice (*xing*), then "Perfect" (*yuán*) is simply "Sudden";
for this reason, the old title was *Yuántùn Zhǐguān* (Perfect-Sudden Calming and Contemplation). If the designation is established based on the flavor (*wei*), then "Sudden" differs from "Perfect.

Thus, the initial flavor is judged as "the Sudden teaching on the High Mountain. If one uses this "Sudden" associated with the judgment of flavors to refute the "Perfect" that is uniquely revealed through the judgment of teachings, [it is a misunderstanding].
"How mistaken! How mistaken! The commentary states:
This metaphor illustrates the error of failing to recognize the term "sudden" (*tun*). The meaning of the text is so clear that it requires no further explanation.
Sixth is the obstacle of contradicting one's own school: the Founder praised [this teaching] as uniquely sublime, yet scholars disparage it as merely gradual and incomplete.
What benefit is there in suppressing the reality and exalting the provisional?
The commentary states: "The Original Teacher" refers to the Master Zhizhe of Tiantai. He is called the "Original Teacher" because he is the master of the fundamental school.

Regarding the praise that he alone is "sublime": the two gates of the original and the trace—whether in their relative or absolute aspects—and the revelation of the provisional and the trace are things not found in other sutras;

therefore, he is said to be "uniquely sublime. Yet, teachers of biased interpretations disparage this as being merely "gradual and sudden," committing the fault of rejecting and obstructing the manifestation of the provisional.
Furthermore, how could one truly escape the charge of actual guilt? The character "贊" (zan) in the *Zuǎn* (纂) edition is an error; it should follow this [correct] "贊" (zàn).
Due to a lack of broad learning, I have erroneously made some corrections.

Seventh is the obstacle of contravening the text and departing from the meaning. As the Sūtra says: "That which has been spoken, that which is being spoken, and that which is yet to be spoken"—yet within this...
"The Lotus Sūtra is the foremost. From the Avataṃsaka up to the Prajñāpāramitā, these have already been taught; the *Anantamukha-sūtra* is called 'what is being taught now';
and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is 'what will be taught. According to that classification, the foremost has already been taught—what does this have to do with the Lotus?
To claim such exclusive knowledge is to make those who hear it cover their ears."
The commentary states: "That which has been, is now being, and will be explained as the foremost" is the interpretation of the Great Master Tiantai.
Since Master Guan studied under Tiantai, he contradicted this textual meaning; instead, he took his own previously expounded *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra to be the foremost.

In the preceding passage, I erroneously established the name "sudden-sudden. I claimed that since there is already a final "perfect" [teaching] within the gradual, and yet another "sudden" is established outside of the gradual, one should know that the former perfection is merely the gradual perfection, while the separate establishment of a "sudden" constitutes the "sudden-sudden.
I repeatedly used this argument to challenge others; no one could respond, and it seemed as though I alone understood it.
Therefore, the conclusion and censure now state: "As for this 'solitary awareness,' those who hear it cover their ears;
they cannot bear to hear such words that slander the Dharma, and for this reason they cover their ears."
Question: If the gradual [teachings] are divided into four, added to the previous seven, how do they become eight teachings?
Explanation: This is precisely the question regarding the aforementioned disappearance of the "gradual" category, whereby the teachings would otherwise remain only seven.

Although this was illustrated for the sake of the contemplative masters (*guan-shi*), those within our own school who engage in formal study and exposition should also understand it well. For instance, as for the division of the gradual into...
Fourth: "The term 'gradual' (jiàn) is already submerged. Regarding Tiantai’s classification and interpretation of the *Lotus Sūtra*, all eight [categories] are employed;
how then can the name "gradual" be established? It is said: although the four [stages] have been opened up, the name "gradual" is already submerged. Even though the name "gradual" is submerged...

There is no contradiction in still calling it "gradual" even during the three periods. If one were to explain the *Lotus Sūtra* [as gradual], there would be no suddenness and so forth, and its eight aspects of conduct would be disordered;

therefore, it is necessary to employ the name of the "gradual teaching. The reason for this is that the four [teachings] beginning with the "Non-Store" (*Acintya*) cannot, within the various flavors (*rasa*), provide a perfect [teaching] equal to the perfection of the *Lotus Sūtra*, as they are neither two nor different from it. As for the four [teachings] beginning with the "No-Sudden," they do not...

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* alone is supreme, transcending the eight teachings and differing from them. Master Guanding maintained that even after the four gradual teachings had been opened, one further gradual teaching still remained;
it is for this reason that he now employs this analogy.

Answer: Having already distinguished four [teachings], there remains one further "gradual" [teaching]. The analogy is as follows: it should be evident from the previous discussion on the third obstacle that this is a delusion.
Since they do not understand that the gradual [teaching] extends from the Deer Park to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, how can they separately establish a single "gradual teaching"?
If they were aware that [the period] from the Deer Park to the *Prajñāpāramitā* is termed "gradual" in reference to time, they would never arbitrarily categorize it within the four teachings.
The term "perfect" (*yuan*) refers to "gradual perfection. How could this be judged as making the *Lotus Sūtra* inferior to the "milk-teaching"?

The commentary states: "As in the third objection mentioned previously," which refers to the objection concerning the failure to recognize the essence of the teaching (*jiaoti*). This is what was stated in the preceding text:

It gradually unfolds into four [teachings], like opening a fist to reveal the fingers and so forth. Master Guan (Jizang) maintained that after the four have been unfolded, there still remains one "gradual" teaching (*jiàojiào*).
This is because he did not realize that what is called "gradual" (*jiàn*) refers to the period beginning at the Deer Park and ending with the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras.
Regarding this gradual teaching, once it has been unfolded into four—just as a fist is opened to reveal the fingers—there are only fingers and no longer a fist. If one were to...

Why establish yet another "gradual teaching"? If you understand the three periods as being gradual, then once the four teachings have been opened up gradually, the name "gradual" should already have vanished.
How can you arbitrarily judge that among the four teachings, the *yuan* (perfect) is called "gradual-perfect"?

Since the *yuan* within each of the various flavors (*wei*) is no different from the *yuan*, how can you rashly judge the *Lotus Sūtra* to be inferior to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s *yuan*? This is merely based on...

The teaching instructs one to observe the master with critical inquiry. If considered in terms of temporal stages and flavors, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—the "ghee" (*tīmadhu*)—alone may be designated as "wondrous," yet this does not constitute a contradiction;
this is fully explained in the various passages above and below.

Question: To which category of the *Lotus Sūtra* does this belong—sudden or gradual? Answer: It is both gradual and sudden. According to the first section of the *Xuánwén*, which concludes the analysis of the doctrinal phases (*jiàoxiàng*), it states:
"The present sūtra is gradual-sudden. Thus, we know it is not a case of sudden-sudden. The analogy says:

This master not only fails to recognize the names "sudden" and "gradual," but he also does not understand the intent of the concluding passage. After the *Xuánwén* has finished explaining the teachings of the preceding four flavors, it next...

In the gradual and other [modes], he concludes and explains the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, stating that it is neither sudden, gradual, secret, nor indefinite. First, he says: "Now, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is manifest (*prakaṭa*) and not secret;
it is definitive (*niyata*) and not indefinite. This concludes that it is not secret or indefinite—whereas secret and indefinite teachings pervade the preceding four flavors (*pañcarasa*).
Next, he says: "It is sudden and gradual, not gradual-gradual. This concludes that it is not the teaching of a sudden beginning followed by a gradual end.
Regarding the terms "gradual" and "sudden": with respect to the preceding four periods, there is the sudden within the gradual and the gradual within the sudden.

The present *Lotus Sūtra*, in its Trace Gate (*jimen*) perfect teaching, does not differ in meaning from the sudden within the gradual; it merely differs from the gradual within the gradual. As for the "gradual within the gradual," these are:
first, the Deer Park [teaching]; third, the Vaipulya [teaching]; and second, the Prajñā [teaching]. The gradual within the sudden is precisely the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*). It is...

The "gradual within the gradual" does not differ in meaning [from other gradual teachings], and thus need not be separately distinguished. The "sudden within the sudden" is identical to the "sudden within the gradual," and is likewise the same as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
For this reason, the sudden teaching need not be separately distinguished. Therefore, in the later section of the *Xuanzan*, it states:

"Now, the Trace Gate (*jìmén*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* shares similarities and differences with various sūtras; the Origin Gate (*běnmén*), however, differs entirely from all sūtras. This refers to the various sections [of the Lotus Sūtra].

Regarding the difference between the "Middle" and "Complete" [teachings]: this refers to those within various schools who, while incorporating the three teachings, fail to perceive this underlying intent.

Relying on literal exegesis based on the sounds of the words, they claim that the *Lotus Sūtra* is "gradual-sudden" rather than "sudden-sudden. Yet, the text merely states that it is not "gradual-gradual";
how could it ever have said that it is not "sudden-sudden"?

The commentary states: To say that this master not only fails to recognize the terms "gradual" (*jiàn*) and "sudden" (*dùn*), as has already been refuted above, but also fails to understand the meaning of the concluding passage, is evident from his own explanation.
Having already interpreted the teachings of the previous four flavors (*wèi*), he concludes the explanation of the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Fǎhuá*) by stating:
"Now, the *Lotus Sūtra* is manifest (*xiǎnlù*) and not secret (*mìmì*); it is definitive (*dìng*) and not non-definitive (*bù dìng*)."

Generally, the "secret" and "indefinite" [teachings] pertain to the preceding four periods. Because the capacities of the people and the [Buddha’s] intent were not yet equal during those first four periods, there were secret and indefinite teachings.

At the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, since the capacities of the people and the intent were already equal—sharing the same seat and the same flavor of the Way—there were neither secret nor indefinite teachings. Next, it says: "This is neither gradual nor sudden."

Regarding the term "gradual" (*jiàn*): this concludes the explanation that the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Fǎhuá*) is neither the sudden (*dùn*) teaching of the preceding *Avataṃsaka* nor the gradual (*jiàn*) teaching of the three periods.
This is merely a provisional assessment based on the sūtras themselves, which finds it to be neither gradual nor sudden; it does not yet differentiate according to the doctrinal systems (*jiào*).

Therefore, it is said that it is "neither the sudden of the preceding [period] nor the gradual of the subsequent. As for the statement that the *Lotus Sūtra* is "gradual-sudden," this refers to its relation to the preceding four [periods].
Within the period of gradual [teaching], there is the sudden; within the sudden, there is the gradual.
The *Lotus Sūtra*’s Perfect Teaching in the Trace Gate (*jimon*) is not different in meaning from the sudden within the gradual; therefore, it is called "gradual-sudden.

Regarding the statement that its meaning is not different from the sudden within the gradual, one should have said that its meaning is not different from the sudden within the gradual; this was merely a transposition of characters during transcription.

The meaning of the phrases "gradually" (*jiàn*) and so forth can be understood from the text; they need not be further explained. Next, regarding the point that there is no separate distinction for the "sudden" (*dùn*):
the gradual within the sudden is precisely the Separate Teaching (*biéjiào*), and its meaning does not differ from the gradual within the gradual; therefore, it is not separately distinguished.
The sudden within the sudden is the Perfect [Teaching] (*yuán*) within the Sudden Section, which is termed the "sudden-of-the-sudden" (*dùndùn*), identical to the sudden within the gradual.
This is also the same as in the *Lotus Sūtra*; therefore, there is no need to distinguish [the teachings] within the Sudden Teaching (*dun jiao*).

As for the term "Sudden-Sudden" (*dun-dun*), it does not refer to the "Sudden-Sudden" established by Master Guan; rather, it refers to the Perfect (*yuan*) within the Sudden, which is thus called "Sudden-Sudden. The remaining text is clear and need not be explained in detail.
Question: Furthermore, how can it be known that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is "gradual-sudden" while the *Avataṃsaka* is "sudden-sudden"? Answer:

According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is said that the various śrāvakas, having come from the stage of the Small Vehicle and passed through the various flavors (*rasa*), only then begin to realize the sudden teaching upon reaching the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Therefore, we know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is gradual-sudden. The *Avataṃsaka* stands at the very beginning and does not pass through the various flavors; therefore, it is sudden.
"Sudden. The analogy states: "The Lotus Sūtra is now perfectly complete and sudden; this is based on the Dharma, not on the person.
It should not be that Śrāvakas come from the gradual [vehicle], and thus one judges the sūtra to be gradual based on the Śrāvakas.
Furthermore, these Śrāvakas do not exceed five hundred, twelve hundred, or two thousand. These are merely termed 'opening the provisional to reveal the real. Moreover, there are also Bodhisattvas."

It is revealed and made manifest. Why should this apply only to the śrāvakas? As it is said: "When Bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of their doubts is entirely removed," and so forth. Furthermore, the later passage states:
"Innumerable sons of the Buddha, having heard the World-Honored One’s detailed exposition, attained the benefit of the Dharma, and great joy pervaded their entire bodies.

Moreover, there is the revelation of the original [nature], as in the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits," where it speaks of the number of atoms in three thousand [great thousandfold worlds], and so on.
This extends even to those in the four-continent world-systems. Furthermore, there are those as numerous as the atoms of a world-system who have first resolved their minds on Bodhi;

how much more so for those who surged forth from below and those who came from the east with Wondrous Sound, including King Śubhavyūha and his entire retinue, all of whom were transformed by Mañjuśrī.

How could such multitudes have ever experienced the four stages of the Dharma-taste? One should therefore judge this sutra as being of the "Sudden-Sudden" category based on these very points; how much more so regarding the "Dharma Master" chapter.
If, whether in the present or after my parinirvāṇa, there is anyone who hears even a single phrase [of this teaching], I shall bestow upon them all the prediction of Buddhahood.

Although the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* does not travel through the gradual stages, it falls short of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for two reasons: first, its partiality; and second, its concealment of the fundamental.
How could that which lacks these two meanings be called "sudden-sudden"? And how could that which possesses these two meanings be called "gradual"?
