The commentary states: The meaning of this question-and-answer analogy is plain and straightforward. Since the entire analogy is drawn from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and contains no difficult or obscure passages, it is not further explained.
Question: There are also bodhisattvas who hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* all at once; why then do you judge [the case] solely based on the śrāvakas?
Answer: This is stated according to the majority of cases. To use an analogy as previously cited: one should consider the eight elements (*dhātu*) and the hearing of a single phrase as the majority.
Yet, to instead take the śrāvakas as the majority not only shows a failure to comprehend the profound principle, but also indicates a lack of familiarity with the text. This should be understood.

Śrāvakas and bodhisattvas of dull faculties—whose karmic conditions were not yet matured prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and who were incapable of hearing the sudden teaching—were further refined and disciplined by the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā teachings.
Only then were they able to arrive at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and hear the sudden teaching.

Therefore, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* should be judged as "opening the gradual and revealing the sudden," and is thus termed "gradual-sudden. People do not see this and claim it is not the "sudden-of-the-sudden."
The commentary states: "The eight realms" refers to the eight Buddha-worlds. A single Buddha-world is a trichiliocosm (a system of three thousand great thousand worlds).
Taking all eight trichiliocosms and reducing them entirely to motes of dust serves as a metaphor for the vast number of the Bodhisattva assembly;
yet even this is not considered many. Instead, [the text] points to five hundred Śrāvakas and one thousand...
Two hundred and two thousand people considered this to be many; this is because their reading of the text was not yet proficient. The rest of the text is clear. Question:

On what basis can it be known that, according to the teaching of gradual perfection, the four abidings fall away first? Answer: It is as cited from the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*: "Forever separated..."

Regarding the "Wheel of Suffering," since it is described as a distinct suffering, one knows it to be gradual and sudden. As for the citation from the *Lotus Sūtra* concerning the purification of the six faculties—mentioning the fleshly eye and so forth—one knows this to be sudden-sudden.
The commentary states: "The Benevolent Kings shall long part from [suffering]," and so forth. The *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:

"When Bodhisattvas of the ten wholesome [stages] give rise to the great mind, they long part from the ocean of the wheel of suffering of the three realms. Here, "the ten wholesome" refers to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*).

Master Tiantai cites this scriptural passage in many places to prove that the ten stages of faith of the Perfect [Teaching] constitute the Perfect-Sudden [Vehicle]. Master Guan, however, perceived that there is a distinct suffering [in the case of the Separate Teaching].
These words refer to "gradual perfection," which is proven by the fact that the four abidings (catur-vāsa) fall away first.

Furthermore, based on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding the purity of the six sense-faculties, such as the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), it is proven to be "sudden within the sudden. The intended meaning and the metaphorical phrasing of both passages from the sūtras emerge naturally [from this].
This was not previously stated. Alas! Master Guan originally maintained that the *Lotus Sūtra* is both gradual and sudden;
yet now, by citing this very passage, he uses it to prove that it is "sudden-sudden. Is this not a contradiction of one's own words?
The commentary states: This school’s doctrine consistently cites the *Ratnarāśi-paripṛcchā* (Renwang jing) to corroborate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* speaks of the "outflow-free faculty of mind" (*anāsrava-manas*), while the *Ratnarāśi-paripṛcchā* speaks of being "permanently separated from the triple world. Both sutras refer to the same stage where the four abidings (*catuḥ-vāsabhūmi*) have already fallen away;

thus, within the realm of existence, one attains the name "outflow-free. Because outflowing karma has been eliminated, it is said that one is "permanently separated. One should know that the textual meaning in both instances is identical.
The fundamental principle is the same. How can one distinguish and separate them to prove two distinct sudden teachings?

The commentary states: Regarding the teaching tradition of our school—namely, the *Xuánzàn*, the *Jùzàn*, the *Zhǐguān*, the *Sìniànchù*, and so forth—all of these cite the *Rénwáng jīng* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) to corroborate the "purity of the six sense organs" (*liùgēn qīngjìng*) in the *Fǎhuá jīng* (Lotus Sūtra).
Because their meaning is identical, they are cited [from the *Rénwáng jīng*]. The *Fǎhuá jīng*...

Regarding the statement that the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is untainted (*anāsrava*), and the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) stating that one has "permanently parted from the three realms":

the sūtra says, "Although one has not yet attained untainted wisdom, the purity of one's mental faculty is such. At first glance, the present statement that one "has attained the untainted" seems erroneous;
however, upon examining the intent of the text, it is actually not in error. Why? Because the phrase "although one has not yet attained" [in the sūtra] contains an implicit meaning.

Regarding the terms "even" (*zòng*) and "yet" (*duó*): from the perspective of "yet," because one has not yet attained the true reality (*tattva*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state within the land of skillful means, it is said that one has "not yet attained.

From the perspective of "even," because one has already attained a semblance of the outflow-free state upon the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) produced in relation to one's parents, it is said that one has "attained.
Since this is the case for the mental faculty, it is likewise for the other faculties. Therefore, Jingxi cites:
It says: "The untainted faculty of mind (anāsrava-manas) is eternally separated from the Benevolent Kings. These two passages do not differ.

One should know that attaining the untainted necessarily means being separated from the three realms, and being separated from the three realms necessarily means attaining the untainted. Both sutras refer to the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā) within the Perfect Teaching (yuanjia).
Since coarse afflictions have already fallen away, one provisionally receives the name "untainted" within the realm; because tainted karma has been eliminated, it is said to be "eternally separated."

If even that which is outside the realms (dhātu) is still termed "with outflows" (sāsrava), because it possesses the outflows of the two extremes, it is also termed "karma with outflows," and so forth.

Furthermore, because one has not yet attained the karma of the sands-of-the-Ganges of ignorance, it is also termed "not yet distinguished from the three realms. This is the meaning of being "outside the realms," as it is established in relation to the three realms.
The present text briefly clarifies the Bodhisattva of the Ten Faiths; by means of the Bodhisattva’s severance and realization, it elucidates the two sutras.

When the literal meaning and the underlying principle are both extinguished and equalized, how can one differentiate them to prove two types of suddenness? This is a failure to understand the intent of the two sutras.
The compiler states: "Furthermore, regarding the passage 'those who attain the name of the untainted (anāsrava) within the realm,' this text is likely erroneous. Why is this so?

The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Although they have not yet attained the outflow-free [state] (*anāsrava*). This refers to those in the ten stages of faith who have not yet attained the outflow-free state of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) of the noble ones;
yet their mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is pure in this manner. This refers to the mental faculty of the inner ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

I say that this person does not read the text well and hastily gives rise to affirmations and denials; is this not a mistaken interpretation? When examined through my own commentary, the jade and the stone are clearly distinguished.

Question: Among the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, what is the "sudden" nature of the Perfect-Sudden (*yuantun*) *śamatha-vipaśyanā*? Answer: It is the "gradual-sudden" (*jiandun*). How is this known?

As shown in the first fascicle, where three metaphors are used for the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, the one who possesses supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) soaring through the air is used as a metaphor for the Perfect-Sudden.

However, in the seventh fascicle, within the section on "Recognizing Penetration and Obstruction," it states that the Middle [Way]—that is, the Three Contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*)—breaks through such supernatural powers. Thus, supernatural power...
Because it has been refuted, it is not "sudden-sudden. The text states that, while separately there is a brief indication of three gates, the general intent lies in the One Sudden.
Furthermore, at the conclusion of the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, it says: "Now, based on the sutras, I shall further clarify the Perfect Sudden.

Also, in the fifth fascicle, at the end of the section on settling the mind (*anxin*), first the number of categories is summarized according to the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, and subsequently, the number is again summarized according to the single-mind *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Moreover, in the first [fascicle]...

The text for the Vow of Resolving the Mind first concludes with the three types of cessation-and-contemplation (*samatha-vipaśyanā*), followed by the statement that it is "also concluded by means of a single cessation-and-contemplation.
These are all the primary texts of a distinct, sudden, and sudden [teaching] apart from the three types of cessation-and-contemplation.

The commentary states: Regarding the various passages cited by this master as proof that the present *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) constitutes a gradual-and-sudden contemplation, at first glance they seem plausible.
However, once subjected to Jingxi’s critique, their textual meaning collapses like a rotten tree trunk; this shall be evident from the illustrative passage [cited] below.
The commentary states: At first glance, citing these proofs seems to provide some basis; yet, upon careful investigation, they are entirely without foundation.
Why? Because they contradict the text and because they give rise to many obstacles.
The commentary states: This single illustrative passage consists of ten sections. First, a general refutation by means of concession and denial. Second, from "Which [is it]?

onwards, a refutation of not knowing the time for the correct exposition and the arrangement of the sequence. Third, from "Furthermore, three... onwards, clarifying that a disciple should not refute his teacher.

Fourth, from "How much more so, two... onwards, clarifying that the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) differ in the two places. Fifth, from "Next, based on... onwards, clarifying reliance upon the sūtras.
1. The meaning of "the intention" (之). 2. If one cites the following, it is a counter-argument. 3. The words "separately below" clarify the general and specific meanings of the three gates. 4.
"Settling the mind below" clarifies the meaning of the three being distinct while the one mind is the concluding count. 5.

The words "arising below" clarify that the three—namely, the one—of cessation and contemplation have no difference in their concluding text. 6. "If both below" clarifies that the conclusion of the three as one is merely the general and the specific.

Regarding the initial passage that "alternately grants and refutes" as a general critique: on the surface, it appears to have some basis; this is the "granting. Upon investigation, it is found to lack any foundation;
this is the "refuting. The phrase "because it contradicts the text and gives rise to many obstacles" constitutes the general critique.

Why is this? As was demonstrated in the refutation of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and further clarified according to the sūtras—the text of which appears in the Preface—and since this Preface was composed by Zhang’an, it did not exist at the time the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* was being taught;
how could one preemptively use the main text to refute it?
The commentary states: This constitutes the second refutation, concerning the failure to understand the correct teaching and the establishment of its sequence. Why is this so?
When the Great Master was correctly expounding the ten chapters, there was originally no preface; it was only at the time of the compilation that Zhiyan (Zhang’an) first established it.

How could he have preemptively used the fifth section of the "Ten Vehicles" within the correct teaching—the "Understanding the Obstructions and Penetrations"—to refute the three horizontal distinctions?

The *Guān* (Contemplation) chapter states: "The 'Middle' refers to the three contemplations used to refute supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). This means it refutes the sequence [of teachings] within the context of supernatural powers, as illustrated by the Perfect and Sudden.
Such a formulation of the thesis is truly laughable. It shall be further clarified according to the sutra; one will see this in the following text.
Furthermore, Sanlun’s own biography records that he was a disciple of Nanyue. How could a disciple then go so far as to refute his master’s school?

This would constitute a *lōkāyata* treatise of perverse doctrine. Moreover, since Nanyue inherited the teachings from Huiven and Nāgārjuna, if [Sanlun] were to refute his master’s dharma, why would he need to further state in the *Guanshin lun* (Treatise on Contemplating the Mind) that he "takes refuge in the ancestral masters"?
The commentary states: This refers to the third principle, that one should not refute the teacher by means of the disciples.

Regarding the statement that the three contemplations were originally transmitted from Nanyue, it should properly be called "the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*"; however, as the text is abbreviated for brevity, it simply says "three contemplations.

Tiantai transmitted the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* from Nanyue; these are categorized according to practice into the gradual (*anupūrva*), the non-gradual (*aniyata*), and the auxiliary (*sahāya*). As for the gradual method:
The former is shallow and the latter is deep; like a flight of stairs, they are not fixed, such that one may go either forward or backward.
The Sudden and Perfect [Teaching], however, is non-dual from beginning to end, like a diamond jewel placed in the midst of the sun.

Like a master of the arts leaping into the air, three Dharma gates are taught for the sake of the three types of spiritual capacities, employing three similes. Therefore, the Perfect and Sudden *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* is the core of our Master’s tradition. —The Master.
That is, [the teaching of] Nanyue; "principle" refers to the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. How could Tiantai, on the contrary, refute Nanyue?
Could this possibly be the same as the *Lokāyata* discourse? In the *Lokāyata* system, the teacher refutes the disciple, and the disciple who follows the *Lokāyata* refutes the teacher;
this is the doctrine of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). How could such a thing be applied to Tiantai?

Regarding the statement that "Nanyue received [the teaching] from Huiwen, who in turn received it from Nāgārjuna," one should properly say that Master Si (Huisi) received it from Master Wen (Huiwen), and Master Wen received it from Nāgārjuna;
this [current phrasing] is likewise an abbreviation. Nāgārjuna was the thirteenth patriarch of India, while Master Wen was the transverse founder of the Tiantai school’s High Ancestor.
Furthermore, when Zhizhe composed the *Guanshin lun* (Treatise on Contemplating the Mind), he already stated, "I take refuge in Nāgārjuna."
This is the height of sincere devotion. How could one dare to abruptly violate the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā*?
If one were indeed to violate it, would there even be any need for taking refuge?
Moreover, the two types of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) have distinct meanings. In the introduction, the sudden practitioner is likened to one who treads upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Emptiness has no degrees of depth, whereas the treader has steps and gradations. Emptiness is a metaphor for the sudden principle; the treading is a metaphor for the ritual practice.

Although practice may involve gradual stages, it is termed "perfectly gradual" (*yuan-jian*); yet while the principle has no degrees of depth, it cannot be categorized as either partial or perfect. In the seventh fascicle, [the text speaks of] the divine horse...

This passage comprehensively illustrates the three contemplations (trivipaśyanā) as both horizontal and distinct. Since supernatural powers (abhijñā) are themselves contained within the distinct characteristics, it uses the middle [contemplation]—which is itself the three contemplations—to shatter the "middle" that is horizontal and distinct.
How can you fail to see this immediate textual meaning, rather than attempting to refute the sequence of what has not yet arisen from a remote perspective?

The commentary states: This constitutes the fourth section, clarifying the differences between the two types of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). In the introduction, the analogy for supernormal power was used to illustrate the Perfect and Sudden contemplation (*yuan-dun guan*).
For one who practices the Perfect and Sudden path, there are six stages of realization (*liu-ji*); these are called the "gradual steps" (*jie-chai*), hence the term "perfect gradualism.
In principle, however, there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority, nor of shallow or deep. Therefore, the essence of principle is neither partial nor perfect; it is like empty space.
Originally there are no cubits or feet, yet one uses cubits and feet to measure empty space. The analogies for supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) in the Preface are like this.

Regarding the analogy for supernatural powers in the seventh fascicle, within the section on "discerning penetration and obstruction," the text horizontally distinguishes between penetration and obstruction, citing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as follows:
"There are bodhisattvas who, upon first generating the mind of enlightenment, are immediately in accord with *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge); this is emptiness. There are... [text continues].
That a bodhisattva, upon first generating the mind of awakening, is immediately able to sport with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) is a provisional (*prajñapti*) case.

That there are bodhisattvas who, upon first generating the mind of awakening, immediately sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and attain Buddhahood is the intermediate case. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites three analogies; the first is that of walking on foot.
First is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Second is riding a horse, which is provisional (*prajñapti*). Third is supernormal power (*abhijñā*), which is the middle.
These three meanings are distinct yet all reside within the initial mind; therefore, they are called "horizontal. Because they are horizontal, they must be broken through.

If the three contemplations in a single mind break through the obstructions and openings of the vertical, and if the single mind in the three contemplations breaks through the obstructions and openings of the horizontal, then one first [attains] emptiness.
Next, "provisional" (jia) refers to the subsequent middle [truth]. Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) itself is penetration; abiding in emptiness is obstruction. Provisionality itself is penetration;
abiding in provisionality is obstruction. The Middle Way itself is penetration; abiding in the Middle Way is obstruction. To break through these obstructions and penetrations:

one uses the emptiness of the threefold contemplation within a single mind to break through [the attachment to] emptiness, causing it to become the "one emptiness, all emptiness. One uses the wondrousness of the threefold contemplation within a single mind...

By breaking down the provisional, one causes all provisional phenomena to become a single provisional; by breaking down the middle within the threefold contemplation of the One Mind, one causes all middle phenomena to become a single middle.
The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "While vertical progression through gradual entry belongs to a single person, the three stages of before, after, and in between are each distinct.
Because they are distinct, they are not 'one' or 'three. Now, by means of the One Mind..."
Because it possesses the three [aspects of] breaking in sequence, it is said that "the three contemplations in a single mind break the vertical obstructions and openings.

Regarding "the single mind in the three contemplations breaks the horizontal obstructions and openings": although those three horizontal contemplations belong to three different types of persons, they all reside within the initial stage of practice;
thus, the three are not unified. Now, because the three are in fact one, this breaks through that fragmented state of three. Therefore...

It is said that "three contemplations within one mind" breaks through horizontal obstructions and permeability. Now, when we speak of "supernatural powers," this refers to using "three contemplations within one mind" to break through the middle contemplation among the horizontal distinctions.

Furthermore, one should understand that although it is said that "one mind with three contemplations" breaks through the vertical and "three contemplations within one mind" breaks through the horizontal, such distinctions are made in opposition to what is being broken; as for their actual nature...

The essence is non-dual in nature. Yet, Master Guan failed to perceive this in the immediate text, and instead went so far as to refute the sequence of that which has not yet arisen. Why such excessive toil?

Next, regarding the further clarification according to the scriptural text: previously, three metaphors were used to verify the three categories of teachings; now, it further relies on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to verify the Perfect Teaching (the *yuanwen*).
Therefore, it is said to be "further clarified. This is the intent behind revising and stabilizing the text once more.
How can one see the single character "further" (*geng*) and immediately establish the name "Sudden-Sudden" (*dun-dun*) outside of the three [categories]?

The commentary states: This constitutes the fifth section, clarifying the intent of the sūtras. Regarding the phrase "clarifying further by relying on the sūtras": previously, three types of śamatha and vipaśyanā were briefly explained;

subsequently, the detailed explanation of these three types of śamatha and vipaśyanā was completed. Thereafter, it was stated that the gradual and the indeterminate methods would be set aside for the time being and not discussed.
Now, relying on the sūtras, the perfect and sudden (yuantun) methods are clarified further; this is why the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is cited once more.

Regarding the realization of the Perfect and Sudden [Vehicle], it is because this is the primary meaning of the text and because it expands upon the preceding passage. Therefore, a scripture is cited, stating:

As the Bodhisattva Profoundly Penetrating the Sublime Virtue (Liaoda Shen-shen Miaode Xian-shou) said: "When a Bodhisattva first gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment within the cycle of birth and death, they seek only Bodhi with single-minded resolve, firm and immovable.
The merit of that single thought-moment is profound and vast, without limit or boundary. As...
I shall now explain this in detail; even were one to exhaust an entire kalpa, one could not reach its end (the full text).

Having cited this passage, Zhiyi extensively expounded upon perfect hearing, perfect faith, perfect practice, perfect stages, the adornment of perfect merit, and the perfect establishment of sentient beings.
It should be understood that this text was formerly the second version, known as the *Shanglüe* (Abridged Summary); it is now being repositioned as a scriptural citation for corroboration.

The purpose of revising the meaning of the text lies herein. One should understand that since it is stated that the gradual and the indeterminate are set aside and not discussed, is this not simply the contemplation of the Perfect-Sudden (yuantun)?
How could there be a "Sudden-of-the-Sudden" established separately outside of these three?
If citing the *Avataṃsaka* is what constitutes the "Sudden of the Sudden," then the tenth fascicle of the *Xuánzàng* (the *Dàchéng Xūnǎo Lùn*) also cites the *Avataṃsaka*,

the Vaipulya (*Fāngděng*), and the *Prajñāpāramitā* to collectively testify to the Sudden as being identical in perfection. Since the *Avataṃsaka* is not merely the "gradual perfection," how could the Vaipulya and the *Prajñāpāramitā* not also be the "Sudden of the Sudden"?
The commentary states: This concerns the sixth counter-argument from the opponent. The opponent objects:

"If you claim that citing the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* establishes it as 'sudden-of-the-sudden,' then consider the tenth fascicle of the *Xuánwén*, in the section on the classification of teachings (*jiàoshàng*), which also cites the *Avataṃsaka*, the Vaipulya (*Fāngděng*), and the *Prajñāpāramitā* as being 'perfect' (*yuán*) to prove the nature of the Sudden.
If the *Avataṃsaka* were not the 'perfect of the gradual' (*jiàn-yuán'), it would have to be named 'sudden-of-the-sudden.'"
Furthermore, since the Perfect [Teaching] of the Vaipulya and the Prajñāpāramitā are cited as evidence for the Sudden, should they not also be called "Sudden-Sudden"?

Yet you do not realize that the *Avataṃsaka* is the Perfect Teaching that incorporates the Distinct; and by claiming that this inclusive [teaching] is superior to the exclusive wonder, how can you possibly understand the intent behind Tiantai’s doctrinal classifications and exegeses?
Commentary on the *Zhiguan Yili*, Scroll Five;
Commentary on the *Zhiguan Yili*, Scroll Six.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chuyuan of Yongjia.

Following the supplementary discussion on resolving doubts and clarifying the correct teaching, it is stated that if one were to distinguish them separately, they would briefly point to three gates. The general intent, however, lies in the single "sudden" approach.

In that text of critical analysis (*liaojian*), the questions briefly clarify three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight). Since the "brief indication" and the "general intent" share similar names, the question is asked again: how are they the same and how are they different?
In the response, two meanings—general and specific—are distinguished. The general meaning provides a brief indication that constitutes the broad outline;

the specific meaning, however, is slightly different from this broad outline. Because they differ, there are three types of the specific meaning, while the broad outline is contained within only one of these three.

Therefore, the text states that the gradual and the indeterminate are set aside and not discussed; yet people, failing to see this, establish a "sudden-of-the-sudden" category apart from the three [other types].

The commentary explains: this corresponds to the seventh section, which clarifies that the three gates share both commonalities and distinctions with the "General Meaning" chapter; the explanation here is brief.
Regarding the "three gates," this refers to the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) clarified in Zhiyi’s preface.

There are several passages throughout the text where the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* are concluded within the "General Exposition of the Great Meaning" (*Dàyì zhāng*), which are similar and identical to the three gates of the Dharma.
Therefore, the "Great Meaning" chapter is compared with the preface for the purpose of analysis; one should understand this analysis.

Although Emperor Jianwen did not personally state these words, they are indeed the composition of Zhi Chang’an. Therefore, he asked: "In what way do the 'Brief' (Lüe) and the 'General Meaning' (Dàyì) agree or differ?
In the response, two types of meaning—general and specific—are contained. Generally speaking, the "Brief" merely points toward the "General Meaning.
Specifically, the "Brief" and the "General Meaning" are not the same. Because they are not the same, there are three kinds of "Briefs."

This is for the purpose of clarifying the distinctions. Although the first chapter of the *Dàyì* (Outline) contains several instances where the three types of cessation-and-contemplation (*samatha-vipaśyanā*) are concluded, it pertains only to one among those three—namely, the Perfect and Sudden (*yuán-dùn*).
Master Guǎn did not understand this and consequently claimed that the *Dàyì* pertains solely to the Sudden.
To establish three external [categories] and claim there is a separate "sudden-sudden" [practice] is an extreme ignorance of the meaning of the text.
At the end of the section on "settling the mind," the text first concludes with the number of the three successive contemplations, and next concludes with the number of the single mind.

The meaning of succession corresponds to the Separate [Teaching], while the meaning of the single mind corresponds to the Perfect [Teaching]. This perfection is identical to the initial general settling of the mind, serving as its conclusion.

Because the numerical categories are thus established, the meaning is opened into three distinct parts. Next, returning to the original basis, one binds them back into a single mind (*ekacitta*). If this intention is not perceived, divergent explanations will arise.
The commentary states:

This corresponds to the eighth [section], which refutes those who do not understand the distinction between the three types of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* and the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of the single mind.
The meaning of "enumeration" (shu). Now, there are two ways of settling the mind: first, general settling; second, specific settling.
First is general settling, which is the Perfect and Sudden [teaching]. Based on this Perfect and Sudden teaching, one discusses specific settling.

Therefore, we know that general settling is the generality of specific settling, and specific settling is the particularity of general settling. To crown the specific with the general, there is no difference between them.
For the purpose of establishing the count, one first relies on the three successive contemplations to establish that count, and subsequently uses the single mind to establish that count.
It should be understood that the three successive [contemplations] are expanded according to their meaning; subsequently, one returns to the original perfection to establish the single mind.
If the contemplation master does not perceive this, he will mistakenly claim that there is a "sudden-sudden" practice existing separately outside of the three. This is not an error.
What [is meant by this]? The enumeration of the fetters has already appeared in the preceding text and will not be repeated here.

Regarding the statement that the final *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) serves as the concluding summary for the section on "arousing the mind" (*cittotpāda*): the general meaning of the five chapters is broad and comprehensive; therefore, each is concluded with *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
At times, only a single instance of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* is used as the conclusion, such as in the text concerning the "six identities" (*ṣaḍ-yathābhūta*). [The following] six passages...
All [of these] are unified. Alternatively, they may be concluded using only the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, as at the end of the *Sui-zi-i* (Following One’s Own Intent).

Or, at times, they are concluded by employing all three—unity, three, and one—as previously cited. Furthermore, there are cases where the concluding text is missing, such as in the case of the three kinds of samādhi, including the "Constant Practice" (*sādhana*) and so forth.

The commentary states: This corresponds to the ninth [section], clarifying the three types of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. The concluding phrasing regarding the "arousing of the mind" (*cittotpāda*) is no different from the others.
As for the statement that this is the conclusion on the three types of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* following the section on the arousal of the mind:

this refers back to the biased views of the Master Guan (Jizang), who relied upon this text to establish that, apart from the three types of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, there exists separately a distinct "sudden" (*tun*) *vipaśyanā*. Regarding the "General Meaning" (*Dà-yì*), the textual structure of its five chapters is broad and comprehensive.

Therefore, all [sections] are concluded with *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). This is the intention behind the concluding passages within the "Five Brief Summaries" (*pañca-saṃkṣepa*) as expounded by Jingxi.

The chapter on the "General Meaning" contains these five brief summaries; thus, it is called the "Five Chapters. These five brief summaries encompass the nine subsequent "Detailed Explanations" (*vistara*).
Because the textual structure is broad and general, there is a concern that readers seeking the meaning might have their minds distracted by external conditions. For this reason, in all the texts...
Below this, all sections are concluded with *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight); this is the general indication. What follows is the specific indication.
As for the statement, "At times, only a single *śamatha-vipaśyanā* is used for the conclusion, as in the text on the 'Six Identities,' where all six passages are unified":

beginning from the identity of principle (*li-ji*), through the identities of name (*ming-zi*), contemplative practice (*guan-xing*), up to the ultimate (*jui-jing*), they are all likewise concluded with a single *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Therefore, it is said that there are "six passages."
All are one. The compiler says: "The first four [stages] have concluding texts, while the latter two do not. This is said to be an error by Jingxi;
however, the text of the six conclusions is clearly visible. To fail to examine this closely and instead hastily misrepresent the Patriarch—is this not arrogance?
Alternatively, one might simply use the threefold *śamatha-vipaśyanā* for the conclusion, as in the *Suizuyi* (Following One’s Own Intent).

Regarding the phrase "at the end of the text": that *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation) states: "Furthermore, if one explains 'following one's own intention' (*suizuyi*) solely in reference to the final [stage], this is the sequential meaning, a gradual conclusion.
If both good and evil are explained as following one's own intention, this is the sudden meaning, a perfect and sudden conclusion.
If one reiterates the preceding [stages] to explain following one's own intention, this is the non-fixed meaning."

This method of successive application (*nirdeśa*) is virtuous, yet it is not subsumed under the former two; nor is it separate from them. Because it applies the sudden within the gradual and the gradual within the sudden, it is indeterminate.
At times, all three are employed together to conclude [the practice], as previously cited:

that is to say, the Four Truths are concluded by means of the three [aspects of] *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, while the Four Great Vows are concluded by means of a single *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Therefore, [it is so].
It says "also. Furthermore, regarding the omission of the concluding phrase "such as the three types of samādhis, namely, constant walking (*caṅkrama*) and so forth," it should have read:

"such as the three types of samādhis, namely, constant sitting (*niṣadyā*) and so forth. This is because, in the *Sui-zi-i* (Following One’s Own Intent), the concluding phrase frequently mentions "constant walking";
perhaps this was an error in the text.
Furthermore, if one employs all three—samādhi, prajñā, and vīrya—together, they merely differ in being general or specific. Why is this? One type of formulation states:

"Arousing the bodhicitta is itself contemplation (vipaśyanā), and the cessation of deviant thoughts is itself tranquility (śamatha). One should know that within these three, there is none that does not involve arousing the bodhicitta and the cessation of deviant thoughts.
The commentary states: This corresponds to the tenth section, which clarifies that the three types of "single-triple" (san-yi) knots consist only of general and specific categories.

First, it clarifies that the single knot is general. Second, from "Furthermore, the three... onwards, it clarifies that the meaning of the three knots also belongs to the general category. Third, from "This tenth...

onwards, it clarifies that the initial passage differs from the present analysis and explanation. The initial passage states: "If both employ the single-triple [method], it is the cessation-and-contemplation knot."
This reiterates the preceding text. At times, one employs all three together to perform the binding; as cited previously, this merely represents a difference between the general and the specific.
Employing a single [formula] for the binding constitutes the general, while employing all three for the binding constitutes the specific.
What follows is the explanation of the questions raised. First, regarding the conclusion on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, it says: "Arousing the bodhicitta is *vipaśyanā*;

the cessation of deviant and perverse thoughts is *śamatha*. Thus, among these three types of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, there is none that does not involve the arousal of the mind, and none that does not involve the cessation of deviance."
One should know that this one [category] is both pervasive and general. How can it be said that this is a separate "sudden-sudden" [practice] apart from the three types of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*?
Furthermore, the three kinds of fetters (*saṃyojana*) also carry the meaning of being pervasive; because they pervade all three, they are thus grouped together. Starting from these three...
From the *Zang* (the *Zongjing lu*) down to the Perfect and Sudden [teachings], all contain gradual, sudden, and indeterminate aspects,

as detailed in the third section on "Partial and Perfect" and in the tenth chapter of the *Xuanyan wen* on the "Phases of Doctrinal Classification," where it states that the four teachings are distinct while the three types are common.
The commentary states: This constitutes the second [section], clarifying the application of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), which also pertains to the "universal" (*sāmānya*).

Regarding the phrase "also pertains to the universal": the initial passage establishes them as one single fetter and names it "universal"; this is a "universal" in the sense of being comprehensive and general.

Because these three are subsumed under this one, it is called "universal. Now, while the clarification of the three fetters should properly be termed "specific" (*viśeṣa*), that they are nevertheless also called "universal" is because...
Taking the four teachings as distinct, each teaching itself possesses the gradual, the sudden, and the indeterminate; therefore, they are also called "common.

One should know that the four categories, such as the *piṭaka*s, all possess these three aspects in common. Thus, he concludes by stating, "As fully explained in the third fascicle on the partial and the perfect," which refers to the fifth chapter on the partial and the perfect in the third fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan* (*Stop and Contemplation*), as well as the tenth fascicle of the *Fahua Xuanyi* (*Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra*).

Within the classification of the teachings (panjiao), the four teachings are treated as distinct while the three types [of practitioners] are considered universal. Within these four teachings, when categorized by their respective divisions:
the stage of causes is designated as gradual, the ultimate fruit as perfect, and the indeterminate entry into the stages as indefinite.
That text is extremely extensive; fearing it would be too cumbersome, I shall not cite it here.
This first passage does not proceed through the four teachings individually, but rather uses the three *saṃyojanas* (fetters) as a general summary for each.

It takes the four teachings collectively as the three *saṃyojanas*, pairing the three with the one, and further treating the three as distinct. People fail to see this and instead rely upon the phrase "furthermore" (*yòu yǐ*).
To establish this separately here would be profoundly inadmissible.
The commentary states: This corresponds to the third point, clarifying that there is a difference between the preceding text and the current exposition.

The preceding section was based on the partial and the perfect, as well as the tenth [chapter] of the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), treating the four teachings as distinct and the three summations (*trisaṃgraha*) as common; thus, it proceeded from the *āgama* (Tripitaka) up to the Perfect.
Each and every one of these is concluded by means of the three [applications of] *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

The present text, however, relies on what is clarified in the first chapter of the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) regarding the response of the Great Mind (*mahācitta*) and the four *siddhāntas*, all of which apply universally across the four teachings. It simply employs these four within the framework of the three conclusions.

Thus, the four teachings constitute the general category, while the three conclusions constitute the specific application. This is an instance of using the general categories of the teachings to conclude the specific applications.
This constitutes a general-and-specific classification within a single section. Furthermore, the three are contrasted with the one; the three are again treated as specific.

In the preceding passage, they were distinguished by being contrasted with the teaching; in the present passage, they are again distinguished by being contrasted with the one. Thus, the one is contrasted with the three, and the three are further differentiated.
These three [categories] are merely general and specific aspects of the same thing; how could there be a "sudden-sudden" established separately outside of these three?

Master Guan (Zhanran) did not see this, and thus appended the phrase "Furthermore, by means of one *śamatha-vipaśyanā*" to conclude the section on the external [teachings], using the words "Furthermore, by means of...
to establish the "sudden-sudden. He failed to realize that this "one" is actually the universal totality, which serves as the basis for establishing [the teachings].
[The opponent] objects: "Is this not erroneous? Question:
"What are the similarities and differences between these two types of sudden stages (*tun-wei*)? Answer: "They are distinct prior to the stage of abiding (*zhu-qian*).

Commentary: The meaning of the question is self-evident. Regarding the answer, "they are distinct prior to the stage of abiding," this refers to the distinction between the gradual (*jian*) and sudden (*tun*) stages.
Those prior to the stages (bhūmi) sever the four abodes; those at the stage of sudden-sudden (dun-dun) fully subdue the five abodes prior to the stages;
and upon ascending the stages, they completely shatter the five abodes. Therefore, it is said that the state prior to the stages is distinct.
The analogy states: All those who establish ranks must do so in accordance with the teachings. Furthermore, the single school of the ancient masters established only four distinct positions.
Within the traces of the teachings throughout a single period, cause and effect are clearly manifest; from beginning to end, nothing exceeds these four.

In the Tripitaka teaching, there are the four fruits, the pratyekabuddhas, and the hundred kalpas of the asaṃkhyeya kalpa. In the Shared Teaching, there are the common stages of the three vehicles, as well as the names and distinctions of their meanings.

The *Tong* (Shared), *Bie* (Distinct), and *Yuan* (Perfect) [teachings] all establish fifty-two stages; however, they differ in that the practices may be more protracted or abbreviated, and in their respective methods of severing or suppressing afflictions.
The Perfect Teaching, based on the *Lotus Sūtra*, further adds the five grades of practitioners. This is consistent across all the scriptural divisions utilized by our school.
I have never heard of two separate sets of "sudden" stages, as has already been refuted previously.

The commentary states: Regarding the phrase "the common stage of the three vehicles," this refers to a stage where both cause and fruit are shared. This is explained here from the perspective of the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*), which speak of a beginning and an end.
However, as for the universal and particular, or the universal and perfect [teachings], there is a stage of guidance through the universal that has a beginning but no end;

this is not what is being discussed here. As for "the name is particular while the meaning is universal," this means borrowing the name of the particular teaching (*pratyekabuddha*) to designate the stages of the universal teaching (*sādhāraṇa*). Furthermore...

The ten stages of faith constitute the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*) and are termed the "Patience of Faith" (*śraddhā-kṣānti*). The three stages of Abiding, Practice, and Approaching are termed the "Patience of Subduing" (*vinaya-kṣānti*) and the "Patience of Accordance" (*anuloma-kṣānti*).

Upon attaining the first stage, one acquires the "Patience of Non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which constitutes the stage of Vision (*darśana-bhūmi*). From the second to the seventh stage, one is a *śrāvaka*. The eighth is the stage of the *pratyekabuddha*. The ninth is the stage of the *bodhisattva*.
The tenth, the Patience of Quiescent Extinction, is the stage of Buddhahood. These names are borrowed from the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna-śāsana*).

This refers to the stage of penetration (*prativedha*). These details are fully contained in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text). Regarding the sequential stages of the Separate and Perfect [vehicles], none are as comprehensive as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (or *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda*).

Therefore, it is now said that fifty-two stages are established side by side. As for the statement that there are differences in the slowness or swiftness of practice and in the sequence of subduing and severing [afflictions]:
those of the Separate [Vehicle] first realize emptiness, then the conventional, and finally the Middle; this process takes hundreds of thousands of immeasurable eons.
It takes kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to enter the stage of the ten faiths and so forth; therefore, it is said to be "distant. Those of the Perfect Teaching possess sharp faculties;

from the very first moment they take the true reality (dharmatā) as their object, the environment is immediately the Middle Way, and the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) can be attained in a single lifetime.

Even for those with heavy obstructions, it does not exceed three lifetimes; therefore, it is said to be "brief. Regarding the difference between severing [afflictions] and suppressing them: in the Separate Teaching, this occurs during the stages of abiding, practice, and orientation.
The delusions of ignorance (*avidyā*) are suppressed during the three stages of *fupo* (subduing); they are first broken at the first stage (*bhūmi*).

For those of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanren*), the delusions of ignorance are suppressed during the five grades and the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*), and are broken immediately upon the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*). Therefore, it is said that they are not the same. Furthermore, the addition of the five grades has already been discussed above.

Within the doctrinal system of this school, we have never heard of two "sudden" stages; this was erroneously established by Master Guan. The intent behind his refutation [of this view] is as previously explained.
This refers to the passage in the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra) concerning the four stages of abiding (*catur-vihāra*), which refutes [the notion of] "falling back.

Question: For what reason are two types of sudden [attainment] established through differentiation? Answer: They are established as distinct based on the sharpness or dullness of one's faculties (*indriya*). As the analogy says:

Since ancient times, we have inherited and studied the single, perfect teaching of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). We do not perceive two separate "sudden" teachings that distinguish between two types of faculties.

Throughout various texts, it is merely stated that the *Avataṃsaka* accommodates both those of sharp and dull faculties: those of sharp faculties belong to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), while those of dull faculties belong to the Separate Teaching (Biejiao).

Alternatively, within each individual teaching, one may distinguish three grades of faculties, or distinguish between sharp and dull faculties based on the two modes of practice—faith and dharma. Thus, in every teaching and every section...
There is no school that is not thus. Upon arriving at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they all enter together into the single reality (*eka-tattva*).

It is impossible that those who have been brought together and unified within the same root-nature should still be called "dull. To claim that there are those who are "sharp" and "dull" based on the concealment of provisional means and the hiding of traces is profoundly untenable.

The commentary states: Regarding the phrase "those who receive and uphold the teachings and methods of a single perfect school," this text contains the redundant character "yuan" (perfect), which renders the reading ungrammatical and further distorts the syntax.
Alternatively, it may mean that each individual teaching is divided according to the three faculties, as each teaching possesses its own superior, middling, and inferior levels.
Or, it may refer to the division of those of dull and sharp faculties based on the two modes of practice—faith and dharma—since the practice of faith relies upon hearing.

The practice of the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) is sharp because it involves internal illumination; furthermore, the practice of faith (*śraddhānusārin*) is sharp because one attains awakening immediately upon hearing the teaching once.

The practice of the Dharma is dull because it involves observing phenomena through successive stages. Alternatively, both may be either sharp or dull: for the practice of faith, hearing is sharp while cultivation is dull;

for the practice of the Dharma, cultivation is sharp while hearing is dull. This is invariably the case across every teaching and every section. This refers to the four [noble persons] prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

[The teaching] is explained in detail: [the various vehicles] come to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and enter together into the single reality (*eka-yāna*). There is neither small nor great; all return to the Buddha-realm.

Yet, those teachers of biased interpretation do not allow for the opening and unification [of the teachings] within the same root-nature, and instead continue to label them as "dull. "Not allowed" means it is not permitted.

On the contrary, they take the revelation and manifestation of the single reality to be the mark of dull faculties, while conversely regarding the concealment of provisional means and the hiding of traces as [superior].
There are those with sharp faculties who are nonetheless termed "dull"; because the *Avataṃsaka* has not yet been revealed, it conceals the provisional [teachings].

It renders the Śrāvakas like the deaf and mute, for the *Avataṃsaka* has not yet revealed the traces [of the Buddha's career], thus obscuring the fundamental [reality]. It speaks only of the initial accomplishment at the Site of Tranquility (*Śīta-vana*).
How could it be that revealing the provisional to manifest the fundamental is considered "dull," while concealing the provisional and obscuring the fundamental is instead considered "sharp"?

Question: Within the Vaipulya (fangděng) period, among the four gradual teachings, four types of "opening" are established. Regarding these two sets of four, what are the similarities and differences between them and the Perfect Teaching? Answer: It is simply this...
"Among the four teachings, the Perfect (yuan) is entirely gradual-perfect.
The commentary states: "One who poses this question is merely testing the Master's insight; yet when the answer is given, it is indeed found that [the questioner] does not understand."

The analogy says: This master does not understand the meaning of the gradual teaching (anupūrvika-deśanā). For this reason, he fails to realize that the Vaipulya (fangděng) is merely one part of the gradual teaching;
instead, he claims that the gradual teaching and the Vaipulya are distinct. Consequently, he replies: "All four teachings are collectively termed 'gradual.
If he knew they were not different, why would he have replied with the words "merely" (dànshì)? Even prior to the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*...
Among the four teachings, the Perfect (Yuan) is all termed "gradual-perfect" (jian-yuan). In the Lotus Sūtra, the provisional is opened up to uniquely reveal the single Perfect.

Why, then, is the designation "gradual-perfect" still maintained? If this is so, one merely understands the term "gradual" as applied to the four teachings, yet fails to comprehend the intent of the Lotus Sūtra regarding the opening and abolishing [of the provisional].
Consequently, the terms "gradual" and "sudden" are established in ignorance.

The commentary states: This passage refutes the error of those who fail to understand that the four [teachings] within the Vaipulya (fangděng) and the four opened up in the gradual (jiàn) system are in fact one single set of four, thereby resulting in the fault of giving false answers.
Regarding the statement "not recognizing the meaning of the gradual teaching": since phenomena are not accomplished instantaneously, it is called "gradual.
The Deer Park is the beginning of the gradual; the Vaipulya is the middle of the gradual; and the Prajñāpāramitā is the end of the gradual.
Furthermore, there are two intentions behind establishing this gradual approach. First, it is for the sake of those whose capacities correspond to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;

they enter the path through successive stages. Thus, they realize the fruit at the Deer Park, receive censure and praise at the Vaipulya stage, undergo refinement at the Prajñā stage, and finally reach the revelation and bestowal of predictions at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly.
Second, for those who are capable of entering the Way prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly, the four [teachings] are applied horizontally.
The teaching proceeds by responding to each [capacity] one by one; the true meaning of "gradual" (zhen) lies precisely here. The Vaipulya (fangděng) is merely one part within the gradual.
Those who do not understand this claim that the four [teachings] within the Vaipulya differ from the four of the gradual. To this, he immediately replies: "All are named 'gradual.
Therefore, one should know that the fourfold opening of the gradual is the general unfolding of the gradual across the three periods."
Regarding the "emergence of the four ears": how could there be a gradual opening [of these] such that beyond the four external [ears], there were yet another set of four, namely the Vaipulya?
If one understands this, how could one answer by saying that all four teachings are merely called "gradual"?

As for the statement, "Even if, prior to the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, the Perfect [teaching] within the four teachings were all called 'gradual' or 'sudden'," this is a concessive argument (an admission for the sake of argument).
The *Lotus Sūtra* opens up the provisional (*upāya*) to uniquely reveal the single, perfect [truth]. Why, then, is the designation "gradual perfection" still established?

If this were so, what would be the merit of opening up the provisional to reveal the real? If that is the case, one merely recognizes the words "opening the four from the gradual," yet fails to understand that the reason for the gradual teaching is its shallowness in traversing the Path;
nor does one understand the intent behind opening up and then setting aside [the provisional].
In the *Chao ba* (Exceeding the Eight), the names "gradual" and "sudden" were established based on a darkened mind, resulting in such errors as these.

Question: Within the *Nirvāṇa*, what further distinction is there between "perfect" (*yuan*) and [the others]? Answer: This is also "gradual-perfection. As for the analogy: if it is as you have judged.

From its beginning at the Deer Park to its conclusion at Nirvana, [the teaching] is uniformly and gradually perfected. Why, then, does the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) laboriously refute the Gāozhái school?
The Gāozhái school still maintains that the *Lotus Sūtra* differs from the earlier teachings; yet even when they cite those earlier teachings as a pretext for their sophistry, [Zhiyi] refutes them.

This Master received his transmission from the Mountain Gate (Tiantai), yet he turns out to be no better than the Gāozhái school. One should say: although there are four types of Nirvana, the first three know the perfection [of the truth], while the Vaipulya [teachings]...
Although the four and three [aspects] do not enter into the ultimate reality, the gradual opening of the four is no different from the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings;

since this is extensively taught in various texts, why should there be further doubt? According to their own arguments, the "perfect *ī*" (*yuán ī*) of *nirvāṇa* would then become useless, and the "single practice" (*yíxíng*) would likewise be established in vain.
The commentary states: The heterodox commentators take everything from the Deer Park teachings to the Nirvāṇa Sūtra as being uniformly gradual.
They do not even equal the Master Guangzhai Yun, who honored the *Lotus Sūtra* as distinct from the previous teachings;

thus, he established the *Lotus Sūtra* as broad, lofty, and long, while regarding the previous teachings as narrow, low, and short. He cited the previous teachings as general and superficial, yet failed to exercise discernment.

Among all flavors, this work is as perfect and wondrous as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; thus, it encountered twenty-four difficulties raised by Tiantai. Hence, it is said that [Tiantai] was "harmed" (kupo).
Master Guanding, who received the teachings of the Mountain Gate (Tiantai), turned out to be inferior to it; how could his study of the Way have been so fragmented?
The compiler says that the character "màn" (謾) is an error and should be read as "mán" (漫); this is merely due to a lack of broad learning.

Question: Do all four teachings enter the Perfect [Teaching] within *nirvāṇa*? Answer: There are those who do not enter it; the ten types of non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*) are precisely such cases.
The analogy says: They merely hear the words that "one enters reality through *nirvāṇa," yet they do not understand the meaning of attaining entry by gathering [the fragments].
If even the ten ṛṣis did not enter [the path], how could the three types of practitioners have heard it? Since there is nothing at the beginning or the end, how could there be entry in the middle?

As for the ten ṛṣis not entering, why did the World-Honored One preach permanence for their sake? The refutation states: "In your heterodox systems, although the cause is permanent, the fruit is impermanent;
in my Buddha-dharma, the cause is impermanent while the fruit is permanent," and so on, up to Cunda’s [realization regarding] form.
"The self is permanent; the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent. Such is the general view of other non-Buddhist teachers.
How can they erroneously judge these to be impermanent? If even such easily understood texts are misinterpreted, how much more so those that are difficult to understand?

The commentary states: Those who merely hear the words "entering reality through *saṃkocana*" (gathering/collecting) yet do not understand the meaning of how one enters through this gathering should know that it is by means of *saṃkocana* that all enter reality.
This is because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is like the great harvest of autumn, while *nirvāṇa* is like the gathering of the remaining gleanings;
therefore, all that remains enters therein. How then can one say [otherwise] regarding the ten?
"Do the sages not enter? He replied, "The ten sages are: first, Jātiśrona; second, Vāsiṣṭha; third, Śāṇḍilya;
fourth, Kāśyapa; fifth, Pūraṇa; sixth, the Brahmacārin Śuci; seventh, the Brahmacārin Vatsa; eighth, the Brahmacārin Pāṃśukūlika;
ninth, Mahāvyūha; and tenth, Subhadra. If these ten sages may not enter, how much less [can others]?"
How could one not hear the Dharma of cultivation? Having heard the three cultivations, how could one not enter them?
As for what are called the "three cultivations," there are three kinds: first, the three false cultivations, which are the permanence, bliss, and self as conceived by non-Buddhists;
second, the three inferior cultivations, which are impermanence, suffering, and non-self according to the Small Vehicle; and third, the three superior cultivations, which are the Great Nirvana.
It is the eternal, blissful, self, and pure. Regarding the "threefold cultivation" mentioned in this text, it refers specifically to the supreme threefold cultivation.
The reason why "pure" and "impure" are not mentioned is that these three alone suffice to counteract the heterodox threefold cultivation of the non-Buddhists.

As for the statement, "If there is nothing at the beginning or the end, how can there be entry into the middle?"—this clarifies the doctrine of permanence in the first assembly of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which is precisely the supreme threefold cultivation of the eternal, blissful, self, and pure.

This refers to cultivation. Later, it clarifies that the ten sages entering reality is also superior to the three types of cultivation. Since this is the case for the beginning and the end, how could those in the middle not enter into true reality?
If the ten sages did not enter [reality], why would the World-Honored One have taught them the doctrine of permanence?
For example, when Jaṭiśonaka challenged the Buddha by arguing that cause and effect are impermanent, the Buddha immediately asked:
"Is your nature permanent or is it impermanent? Jaṭiśonaka replied, "My nature is permanent.
The Buddha asked, "Can your nature act as the cause for all internal and external phenomena? He replied, "It can. The Buddha then asked, "In what way does it act?"
[The opponent] answers: "From *prakṛti* (primordial nature) arises the Great One (*mahat*); from the Great One arises ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), and so on up to the twenty-five principles.
The Buddha asks: "Are these principles, such as the Great One and the rest, eternal or impermanent? [The opponent] answers:

"In our system, *prakṛti* is eternal, while all phenomena such as the Great One and the rest are entirely impermanent. The Buddha asks: "In your doctrine, the cause is eternal while the effect is impermanent; however, in my doctrine..."
If the cause is impermanent while the fruit is permanent, what fault would there be?

As for the statement, "Even up to Cunda, form is permanent," etc., this refers to the address to Cunda within the *Cunda-varga*, which says: "Form is impermanent; by the cessation of this form, one attains permanent form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise. Now, the *Cunda-varga* is located within the [Daśottara-sūtra].
Regarding the phrase "the sages before" (*xianqian*): what is cited here in the current text first cites the ten sages and only then presents Cūḍapanthaka;

the expression "up to" (*zhìyǐ*) merely refers back from the subsequent text to the preceding section. There is a logical reason for this, so one should not let the sequence of the text serve as an obstacle.
Since it is so for even one among the ten sages, it is the same for all the sages, up to and including the tenth.
The passage concerning Subhadra’s discourse on the perception of reality and its entry into the ultimate truth is as clear as the sun and moon;
how can you darkly judge it to mean that one does not enter the ultimate truth and is therefore impermanent?

Question: Regarding the various similes found after the first fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation), such as "the voice of the kalaviṅka bird," "pounding ten thousand ingredients into a pill," "bathing in the great ocean," and "agada medicine," for what purpose are these used? Answer: They all illustrate both the gradual and the sudden.
Why is this? It is because while still within the husk, ten thousand kinds of things must be pounded; one must wait for all waters to enter the great ocean;

and one must combine various medicines to form an *agada*. Therefore, these are gradual and sudden. If one does not emerge from the husk, even if all waters were the ocean and the ten thousand kinds were already pounded and combined into medicine, it would be merely spontaneous and natural—only then would it be truly sudden and sudden.
The commentary states: In this response, the heterodox interpreters take all the illustrative passages to be metaphors for both the gradual and the sudden approaches;
therefore, they conclude by saying, "Thus it is gradual and sudden. They then produce a metaphor for the "sudden-sudden" approach, stating:
"If it does not emerge from the egg," which implies that the kalaviṅka bird is still within the egg and has not yet emerged, waiting until it emerges before [further action occurs].
It is even more excellent. Therefore, one should know that the analogy of gradual and sudden is not as good as the analogy of "not producing [grain from] a seed" as the ultimate suddenness.

It is like various waters entering the ocean; this is not as good as the analogy of various waters already possessing fragrant pellets and combined medicines, which is better than the analogy of not pounding and not mixing—this being the analogy for the ultimate suddenness.
The commentary states: There are two faults here. First, failing to understand the intent of the analogy; second, contradicting one's own words. Regarding the failure to understand the analogy:
generally speaking, an analogy is employed only by way of a partial correspondence. Thus, the Great Sūtra says: "True liberation cannot be illustrated by means of an analogy.
For example, if one compares a snow mountain to an elephant, how could one expect to find its tail or tusks? If one raises a fan as an analogy for the moon, how could one expect to...
If even its radiance is thus, how much more so the meaning of the original text? The intent is that a single dharma is fully endowed with all dharmas.
To provide a metaphor for what is directly perceived: water that has not yet entered the ocean is incomplete;

various vapors that have not yet been pounded into a pill lack sufficient potency; other birds do not chirp from within their eggs; and although other medicines may be compounded, they do not universally cure diseases. Therefore, these [examples] are employed as metaphors.

This refers to the sudden metaphor (*tun-yù*). How can one refute a metaphor and thereby establish a gradual perfection? To criticize another metaphor on the grounds that "raising a son who is unworthy is a fault"—this is precisely what that case entails.
The commentary states: This teacher of perverse interpretations, by means of challenging the analogy, incurs two faults. The first is not understanding the metaphor.

The meaning is as follows. Second, there is the contradiction of one's own words. Regarding those who do not understand the purport of an analogy: generally, when one employs an analogy, one merely takes a small portion of it.
As the Great Sūtra says: "True liberation cannot be illustrated by means of an analogy. It is like using the whiteness of the Snowy Mountains to illustrate a white elephant;
how can one demand that it possess a tail and tusks? Or, it is like using the full moon to illustrate the Buddha.
As for the face, one cannot be faulted for lacking eyes, eyebrows, mouth, nose, ears, and so forth. It is like the analogy of holding up a fan to represent the moon;
how could one possibly fault it for lacking light or a hanging [moon] and the like? In the text, the character "guà" (挂) is an error; it should follow the radical for wood (木), not the hand (手).
To speak of "light-guì" (光桂)—that is merely following worldly convention by saying that the moon has a cassia tree. The compiler says: "Holding up a fan... (The text appears to be cut off here.)
This is an error. It should read "raising the face. Various texts contain the metaphor of raising a fan to represent the moon; why must this be doubted?

Regarding the statement that the intent of the original text lies in one dharma being endowed with all dharmas, and taking what is currently perceived as a metaphor—the character "是" (shi) in "具是" (jù shì) is likely an error and should read "足" (zú), making it "具足" (jùzú). Generally, errors in characters occur either because their pronunciations are similar or...
Therefore, it is an error. Or, it is an error because their forms and characteristics are similar; this refers to the similarity of their forms and characteristics.

The intended meaning of the original text is the intended meaning of the passage on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. For example, just as the great ocean contains all waters, this analogy illustrates how a single dharma contains all dharmas.
It is like pounding ten thousand kinds of incense to form a pellet; if one burns a single particle, it possesses all the fragrances.
A single particle is likened to a single dharma that contains all dharmas. How can the waters that have not yet entered the ocean, being self-contained, serve as a metaphor for the "sudden-sudden"?
Likewise, how can incense that has not been pounded into a pellet, being self-contained, serve as a metaphor for the "sudden-sudden"? It is like the kalaviṅka bird within its egg.

It cries out from within; its sound already surpasses that of all other birds, let alone when it emerges from the egg. This is an analogy for a practitioner who has received the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā*:
although they have not yet broken through the "egg" of ignorance (*avidyā*), they have already surpassed the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*);
how much more so once they have broken through ignorance? How could one say they are still within the egg and must wait to emerge from it? It would be better not to speak thus.

The emergence of the "grain-and-egg" [metaphor] serves as an analogy for the "sudden-sudden. Regarding the fact that other medicines, though combined, do not treat all illnesses universally, the *Zhiguan* states:
"For example, a skilled physician possesses a secret formula that subsumes the efficacy of all other prescriptions and combines the power of all medicines; this is the *agada* medicine.
How can one refute this by claiming that it is an analogy for the "sudden-sudden" because it is naturally complete without being compounded into a medicine? This refers to "nurturing."

"An unworthy son" (*xiào*): *xiào* means "to resemble. Now, when people of the world receive the physical bodies bequeathed by their parents, they must necessarily resemble them in their skeletal structure and features;

their conduct is likewise so. Yet, observing that the Master received his training from Jingxi [Zhiyi], his Way does not resemble [his teacher's]. Therefore, it is said: "Raising a son who is unworthy is a transgression.

"Transgression" (*guò*) refers to committing a fault; it does not mean following principle. As for the difficulty of using other analogies, it is because one is comparing them according to the Dharma.
"Analogies are for the sake of others; 'that is the very matter' means it is just like when people in the world raise a son who is unworthy and commits transgressions.
Thus it is said. This [interpretation] does not understand the intent of the analogy.
Second, regarding the contradiction with one's own words: you yourself established the general principle that [the teachings] are "sudden within the sudden.
Since these illustrative passages all reside within that general principle, how can you now disparage them as being "gradual within the perfect"?
The commentary states: "These metaphorical passages are all within the 'General Meaning' (Mahā-artha)" is a provisional statement.
In reality, the grinding of myriad fragrances and bathing in the great ocean are mentioned in the Introduction; the kalaviṅka bird and the agada medicine are found within the General Meaning.

Since Master Guan established the "sudden within the sudden" based on this very principle, yet here he instead rejects this analogy to illustrate the "gradual within the perfect," is this not a contradiction of his own words?

Question: In the first fascicle, it was stated that they were truly not father and son, but rather two strangers. To what does this analogy refer? Answer: It refers to those who are truly not [related].
"Bones and flesh" refers to the first two teachings; "two people on the road" refers to the latter two teachings. The commentary states: "This is profound;

the intended meaning of the metaphor within the text is not apparent. The text posits that within both the internal and external realms, there is a principle (*li*) for each, and each principle is expressed by two teachings as its designator (*nengquan*).

Both take the Four Noble Truths as the basis for delusion and awakening, as is naturally integrated within the text itself. Anger is used as a metaphor for *samudaya* (the origin of suffering), while striking [others] is used to represent...

This is illustrated by the analogy of suffering. If two people are father and son, striking them with mild anger represents a direct teaching; if they are two strangers, striking them with intense anger serves as a metaphor for an indirect approach.

This refers to the difference in the realization of the knowledge of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*); consequently, the cessation and detachment of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) also differ.
If one realizes them as identical, then suffering and its origin are themselves the principle—just as strangers would become father and son. If one realizes them as distinct...

This concerns the distinct principles of suffering and its origin. It is like regarding father and son as strangers; one should know that they are truly not unrelated kin, yet are called "strangers" merely in reference to the meaning of separation according to the crude teaching.
Furthermore, what kind of crudity is this, which even lacks the discernment to distinguish between what belongs within and without the realms?
Thus, one may cross over these distinctions to establish the four modes of teaching, as explained in detail in the *Zhiguan ji*.
The commentary states: "Taking a stranger as father and son, and taking father and son as strangers—this serves as an analogy for both the internal and external realms.
Within each of the internal and external realms, there is a principle: the internal realm is the true principle (*zhēnlǐ*), while the external realm is... [the conventional principle].

This is the central principle. Because there are degrees of lightness and heaviness in the delusion regarding the one true reality, there are the two teachings of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and the *Sūtra* (Shared).

Because there are degrees of lightness and heaviness in the delusion regarding the one [middle way], there are the two teachings of the *Vaipulya* (Distinct) and the *Vimalakīrti* (Perfect). Each of these four teachings possesses its own four truths of suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the path.
In the two teachings of the *Āgama* and the *Vaipulya*, because suffering and accumulation are heavy, they are like two people who, upon meeting on the road, harbor mutual resentment.

If one strikes them, the punishment is heavy. To take a circuitous route to the City of Transformation (nirvāṇa) and to take a circuitous route to the Precious Abode (the ultimate goal) are both indirect paths;

because suffering and its origin are treated lightly in the two provisional teachings, it is like the case of two people who are father and son—the punishment for striking them is light. To go directly to the City of Transformation and to go directly to the Precious Abode are the direct paths.

These four sets of the Four Noble Truths differ only in terms of being "identical" (*ji*) or "separate" (*li*). If explained according to the principle of identity, suffering and its origin are identical to the Path and Cessation.
It is like people on a road becoming father and son. If one speaks in terms of separation and liberation, suffering (duḥkha) and its origin (samudaya) are not the path (mārga) or cessation (nirodha).
Yet, the essence of suffering and its origin is fundamentally the path and cessation. Because of a lack of skillful understanding, they are like people on a road who become father and son.

One should know that the *Zhiguan Yili* states: "In reality, they are not flesh and blood; those called 'two strangers' are merely so according to the single meaning of separation in the crude teaching."
Regarding the term "one-sidedly detached" (*ekānta-vivikta*): it is not spoken in contrast to [the other], hence it is called "one-sidedly detached.
How can the Master [Zhiyi] claim that the first two teachings are not based on actual bone and flesh, while the latter two—referring to the "wayfarers"—are the subsequent two teachings?

To say that there is also a lack of distinction between what is internal and external to the realms is how clumsy! Since the four teachings have already been distinguished, the two being "clumsy" and the two being "skillful" should likewise [be distinguished].
It can be seen. Question:
Are the Gradual (jiàn) and the Separate (bié) teachings the same or different? Answer: These two are not the same. The Gradual opens up four [stages], whereas the Separate does not open up four.
The analogy says: Since one does not recognize that the Gradual teaching opens up four stages, what benefit is there in distinguishing it from the Separate teaching?
