Regarding the preceding discussion on supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): furthermore, if the Great Meaning (*mahā-artha*) resides solely in the sudden and sudden, for what reason are the four truths, the four great vows, and the ten types of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) all listed within the four teachings?
The subsequent text belongs to the gradual (*anupūrva*). If the refutation is the same as before, since the texts are thus contradictory, upon what basis should one establish one's practice?
The commentary states: This constitutes the third section, wherein the two masters who advocate sudden realization (*tun-guan*) are interrogated by citing the preceding and following contexts.
If the general intent were solely focused on the "sudden-of-the-sudden" (*dun-dun*), why would the cultivation of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) practice cite all three vehicles?

If this were the case, it would not be merely the "sudden-of-the-sudden. If it is argued that the subsequent sections establish gradual perfection, then [the text] skillfully arranges *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* and refutes [the opposing view].

Since the Dharma is universal, why are there instances where *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are practiced together within the "opening" and "closing" [of the gates], and where the "middle" refers to the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) that break through supernatural powers?

If this were so, how could it be merely gradual or perfect? Furthermore, if the general intent lies solely in the sudden and the sudden, why are the Four Truths, the Four Great Vows, and the ten types of generating the mind all listed according to the four teachings within the context of generating the great mind? If this were so, how could it be...?

Is it exclusively sudden-sudden? The subsequent passages clearly belong to the gradual [teaching]. Since the textual characteristics of the sudden-sudden cannot be cited in full, it is said that "the refutation is also the same as before.
This refutation is composed merely to follow their own conceptualizations; in reality, this entire treatise is nothing other than perfect and sudden.
Since the established texts are already contrary [to their claims], if one takes these [gradual] practices as the standard for contemplation and cultivation, [one will fail].

Furthermore, it says: "Regarding these two contemplations, it is extremely difficult for a beginner to distinguish them when first practicing; one must enter the contemplation oneself before they can be known. The analogy states:
"Just as when first breaking through to the stage of non-arising (*anutpāda*), one must rely upon the teachings, how much more so when the six chapters generate understanding to guide practice?
Since it is said at the outset that distinguishing them is too difficult, it is clear that the mind of understanding is obscure. If understanding is already obscure..."

Obscured, there is no means by which one may enter contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). If one’s understanding is not yet clear, yet one hastily claims to have entered contemplation—how does this differ from the "dark realization" (*andhakāra-sākṣātkriyā*) of the "enhanced mouse-chirp and bird-flight in the void," proclaiming words of realization while causing others to conceive the notion that they are noble beings?

To suddenly cause them to experience what is said to be reality is to fall into the fault of claiming superhuman status (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*). Even if one has actually attained it, such a claim still incurs the transgression of false representation; thus, it constitutes a grave offense. Furthermore, if [it were] real...

I have attained it. At what stage? If it is merely a provisional name, how does it differ from others? If one at the stage of the five ranks were identical to the Great Master, I truly could not judge it;
only those who have realized it themselves would know. I pray that you do not deceive the Sages, nor contradict your own mind.
The commentary states: This refutes the erroneous establishment of two types of sudden contemplation by certain masters of meditation (*dhyāyī*).

Having encountered this censure and finding no rational way to respond, they claim that these two contemplations are too difficult for a beginner to practice; one must enter into contemplation oneself before they can be understood.
From this, it is evident that both their understanding and their practice are incorrect, and furthermore, they falsely claim to have attained superhuman states.

Regarding the Dharma: for instance, at the beginning of the "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas" (*Fapobian*), four gates are fully set forth. Among these four gates, non-arising (*anutpāda*) is primary;
thus, one must establish correct practice based upon the teachings of the gate of non-arising.

Furthermore, the general purport of this entire treatise unfolds a wondrous understanding through the first six chapters, using that understanding to guide practice. Practice begins with the discernment of the ten objects (*daśa-viṣaya*) and the ten vehicles (*daśa-yāna*).
This is clear and evident. How can you say that it is too difficult to distinguish? Is this not because your understanding is obscure?

When one’s understanding is not clear and is thus confronted with the teacher’s interrogation, one seeks to conceal one's fault by pushing the matter into meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*). Consequently, one incurs the offense of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
To falsely claim to others that one has attained superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) constitutes a transgression when the other person understands the claim.

This is a grave offense. The person previously mentioned does not understand that they have committed a *sthūlātyaya* (grave transgression). Exceptions include cases of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) or those acquired through karmic retribution (*vipākaja*).
There is no offense if one speaks while joking or if one speaks due to illness. Regarding the statement "suddenly causing them to accept [the truth]," the intention is:
"Suddenly, you shall hear what I say and accept it," meaning, "Consider what you have said to be true. To fall into such an error constitutes a fault.
"Person" (人) means to fall or descend. If one has truly attained the Noble Path and speaks of this attainment to a layperson, they incur a *pāyattika* offense;
how much more so for a statement that contradicts both principle and sentiment? Thus, it shall be a grave transgression. Furthermore, even granting the possibility:

if you have truly attained it, at what stage or rank are you? If it is merely a provisional name or title, how does it differ from others? This demonstrates that those who rely on mere names are many.

As for those who speak of the five grades of practice (*pañca-varga*), they ought to be identical to the Great Master Tiantai, who attained the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* and gave rise to the *āvartana-dhāraṇī*.
Jingxi said: "I truly do not dare to pass judgment or compare them."
Regarding the statement that "one who realizes [the truth] knows it for themselves," Jingxi cautioned: "May you not deceive the assembly of sages;

may you not contradict your own mind. Do not rashly claim to 'enter contemplation and know for yourself,' for such dark realization has already been addressed above as being like the squeaking of a rat or the chirping of a bird in the void.
Since many passages clarify this point, I shall not explain it further here.

It is further stated: "Based on Master Ding’s text on 'Contemplating the Mind' (*guanxin*) within the twelvefold division of the scriptures, one will certainly attain [realization] through the practice of contemplation.
The commentary explains: This master also relies upon the *Twelvefold Division of Scriptures for Contemplating the Mind* (*Guansin shierbu jing*) as a "sudden-sudden" contemplation (*dun-dun guan*).
From where does this textual passage originate? There is a separate small scroll circulating in the world; that text states: "The word *jing* (scripture) means 'to follow' (*you*)."
The mind is also the "basis" (yā). All phenomena are created by the mind. To directly contemplate that the mind is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle is called *sūtra* (1).
To contemplate it again is called *geya* (2). To contemplate that within the emptiness, provisionality, and middle of the mind one can give rise to the three wisdoms is called *vyākaraṇa* (3).
To contemplate that the mind is itself the provisional and that the provisional is also empty is called *gāthā* (4). [To contemplate] the mind...
That emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are not prior thought or subsequent awakening is called "Unasked Spontaneous Discourse" (5).

Contemplating that the mind arises from conditions—just as things arise and perish—is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; this is called "Parable" (6). Contemplating the beginning and end of the mind is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
The contemplation that the ten realms—from the hells up to the Buddhas—within the mind are, in their very nature, empty, provisional, and the Middle Way, is called *Itivṛttaka* (7).
The contemplation that the mind’s emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle Way prevent error and cease evil is called *Nidāna* (9).

The contemplation that the mind’s emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle Way pervade all things both horizontally and vertically is called *Vaipulya* (10). [The contemplation of] the mind’s emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle Way...
It is not something possessed by the world; this is called "the unprecedented" (eleven). One contemplates why the mind is empty:
because it arises from conditions. Why is it provisional? Because it exists only as a name. Why is it the Middle? Because it is free from the two extremes. This is called "discursive analysis.
The Master [Zhiyi] relied upon this to establish the "Sudden-Sudden" [teaching]; therefore, I have recorded it here in brief.

The analogy states: Regarding the three great contemplations (*san guān*), their meaning consists of only three types. First, that which proceeds from practice: this involves contemplating the single mind within the ten thousand objects.

Although the ten thousand objects differ, the subtle contemplation views them as equal in principle; contemplating the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth is precisely its intent. Second, that which relies on the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*):

this refers to passages concerning the Four Truths and the Five Practices, wherein one enters into a single moment of mind to constitute a perfect contemplation. Third, that which relies upon... [text fragment]

Regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*): for example, the name "Gṛdhrakūṭa" (Vulture Peak) at Rājagṛha is established based on its physical reality. One borrows such phenomena as objects of contemplation to guide and transform clinging attachments;
this is exemplified by the *Vaipulya* teachings on Samantabhadra, the meaning of which can be understood through such cases.

The commentary states: The illustrative text has two parts. First, three types of contemplation methods are presented to show the contemplator that these contemplation methods do not exceed these three.
Second, erroneous positions are refuted, as the bases for those who establish the "sudden-sudden" approach are all incorrect. Regarding the meaning of the first part:
Jingxi demonstrated these three types of threefold contemplation as the essential gateway for entering the Way within this single school and the pivotal mechanism for the four kinds of samādhi.
Since there are only these three types, how could one establish a "sudden-sudden" [contemplation] separately outside of them?
A detailed explanation of the textual meaning is found in the section on the Threefold Contemplation Methods; it will not be recorded here again.

Therefore, the contemplations of the twelve divisions of the teachings establish their names based on specific matters. Although there are names for the three types of contemplation, the ten objects (*daśaviṣaya*) and the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*) are not listed under the title of any single division;
they are merely presented as a single phrase. How could this single phrase alone suffice to expound the gates of contemplation?

If this single phrase were sufficient for practice, then the ten objects and ten vehicles would become redundant and superfluous. Thus, we know that [the text] specifically points to one [aspect] within the text.
To take two phrases as a "sudden-sudden" [teaching] is identical in meaning to treating the insentient realm as the essence and the mind as the ground;
thus, the ten-fascicle text would become useless, and furthermore, it would incur the fault of falsely fabricating the Great Master’s teachings.
The commentary states: This constitutes the second [section], refuting their erroneous establishment of the "sudden-sudden" (頓頓) based on grounds that are all invalid.

Why? For instance, consider the *Twelve Divisions of Sūtras on Contemplating the Mind* (*Guānxīn shíèr bù jīng*). Although these are contemplations based on the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), their names also involve reliance on concrete objects (*vastu*).
Why? As it is said: "A sūtra (*sūtra*) is a 'proceeding' (*yóu*); the mind is also a 'proceeding. All phenomena proceed from what the mind creates. Thus, one directly contemplates...
This mind is precisely what is termed emptiness, the provisional, and the middle within the *Sūtras* and other texts.

Since there are neither the ten objects (*daśaviṣaya*) nor the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*), how could this single phrase alone suffice to expound the gates of contemplation? If this single phrase were sufficient for practice, then the entire work of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* would become a redundant proliferation.
Thus, we know that [this phrase] specifically points to one portion within the text on "Skillfully Establishing Śamatha and Vipaśyanā" and "Pervasive Destruction."

To take a single phrase or two concerning "the cessation and contemplation of the mind" as the "Sudden-Sudden" (dun-dun) is to equate its meaning with "taking the insentient realm as the essence of the mind" (ti-ta xin).

Regarding what is called the "insentient realm" (wan-jing): it is not a realm as expounded by the Four Teachings; rather, it is simply referred to as "taking the essence" (ti-ta), and thus it is termed the "insentient realm.
According to that [view], their arbitrary establishment of the Sudden-Sudden is precisely identical to "taking the essence. If this were so, then the text of the *Ten Contemplations* would...
This renders it useless. It also reveals the fault of the Great Master’s fabrication of expedient means, namely the improper cultivation of the ten objects and ten vehicles.
The character "ran" (芿) is an error; it should be read as "fan" (繁). "Fan" (繁) describes the appearance of luxuriant vegetation, such as grasses and trees.

Question: Is the "Middle" (zhong) of the gradual perfect contemplation (*jiànyuán guān*) the true reality (*shíxiàng*)? Answer: It is not identical to the true reality; its essence is the "mere Middle" (*dànzhōng*). To illustrate:
the true reality and the mere Middle are identical in essence but differ in name. When they are real, both are real; when they are provisional, both are provisional.

The commentary states: This illustrative passage consists of three parts. First, a refutation based on essence (*tattva*). Second, "If one relies on... and below, a refutation based on teaching (*śāsana*). Third, "Only affliction...

and below, a refutation of taking what is lost as being gained. Regarding the meaning of the first part: the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and the Middle Way (*madhyamā*) differ in name but are identical in essence.
If they are real, then both the true aspect and the Middle Way are called "real"; this is stated from the perspective of their respective domains.
If "expedient" (upāya) is taken as such, then both the true aspect (lakṣaṇa) and the Middle Way are called expedient when viewed from the perspective of the Perfect [Teaching].

The compiler did not understand this and falsely claimed that the Shared Teaching possesses only the name of the Middle Way but lacks the substance of the Middle Way. If these are expedient, they are expedient in both cases;
how can this be so far removed from the meaning?

If one explains the text according to the teachings (*yàojiào*), the "mere Middle" (*dànzhōng*) resides in the Distinct Teaching (*bié*). Nevertheless, the sequence for practicing contemplation still places it in the final mind;
within the Four Teachings, it belongs to the Perfect Teaching (*yuán*). All texts consistently state that from the very first mind, one perfectly cultivates the three contemplations (*sānguān*).

Those who take this contemplation to be for those of the "sudden-sudden" capacity establish the contemplation of the mere Middle for those of the Distinct and Perfect capacities. However, a thorough search through all the various sections [of the canon] reveals that no such text exists.

The commentary states: This constitutes the second [section], which refutes [the view] by means of the teaching. The "but-only" (but) contemplation exists only within the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*).
Because its teaching is provisional, the principle of Buddha-nature does not contain all phenomena; therefore, it is called "but. "But" means "alone.
It is alone in the single Buddha-realm and does not contain the nine [realms]. When one first hears this principle, it lies outside the three delusions; therefore, it is sequential.

First one cultivates the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), next the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), and only upon reaching the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) does one begin to correctly cultivate the Middle Way.

Therefore, it is said that [the Middle] still resides in the subsequent position. However, this is generally how the contemplation of the Middle is practiced. Within the Four Teachings (*catur-yāna*), the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is not identical to this;

for in all the scriptural texts of those teachings, practitioners from the very beginning cultivate the three contemplations in a perfect manner. Yet, those teachers of biased interpretations nevertheless...

To take this "Perfect" [teaching] as "Sudden-Sudden" and to establish a "Separate" "But-Middle" (but-madhyamaka) contemplation for those of the Perfect capacity—there is no such teaching at all within the doctrinal system of our own school.
Is this not a mistaken establishment?
Regarding the passage in the *Chishi wen* (Text on Refuting Errors) that critiques the sphere of afflictions, it states: "One does not abide in discipline, nor does one abide in non-discipline.

When practicing with the initial mind, one incurs the error of achieving a "double negation" (*ubhayābhāva*). How can you attempt to rectify this error by using it to judge the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*? Alas, alas!
It is beyond salvation.
The commentary states: This constitutes the third [point], which refutes the error of mistaking loss for gain. The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* says:

"Furthermore, there are practitioners who, upon hearing that one should neither abide in discipline nor abide in indiscipline and so forth, [conclude that] if one abides in discipline, one is a śrāvaka."
If one dwells in non-subjugation, that person is a fool. Fools dwell in existence (*bhava*); Śrāvakas dwell in emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

When a practitioner hears of these two extremes, they become terrified and, maintaining themselves with great care, desire to practice the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*). Such a person does not realize that craving itself is the path;
this [text] is a refutation of such a failure. Master Qingbian (Guanshi) selected this passage on the refutation of failure to provide a judgment.
To take the Lotus Sūtra as a gradual and perfect cultivation while practicing only the "Middle of the Mean" (but-chung) is why Jingxi deeply lamented it, saying: "Alas, alas!
It is beyond salvation. If one slanders the sūtras that exclusively reveal [the ultimate truth] yet contemplates only the Middle of the Mean, then who among those who can be saved would not be saved?
Who indeed would be unsalvageable?
Question: Since that which is cultivated by the beginner’s mind is not the true mark (*dharmatā*), is it *nirvāṇa*? Answer: It is *nirvāṇa*. The analogy states:

*Nirvāṇa* and the true mark are terms that apply universally to both the Great and Small Vehicles. If that which is cultivated by the beginner’s mind is not the true mark, then if it is not the true mark, it is also not *nirvāṇa*;
if it is *nirvāṇa*, it must also be the true mark; and if it is the true mark, it has been so from the very beginning.
Regarding the contemplation of *nirvāṇa*: how can it be said that this is not the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) and yet is called *nirvāṇa*?
The commentary states: This illustrative passage consists of three parts. First, it refutes the ignorance of *nirvāṇa*;

for while the name "true mark" is common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, some claim one is correct and the other is incorrect. Second, from the words "If one follows... onwards, it specifically clarifies that *nirvāṇa*, in its general sense, is common to both [vehicles].
Regarding the universal and particular Bodhisattvas: as for the particular, even universal and particular Bodhisattvas do not yet accept the name "nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is known that [the text] below clarifies that the initial contemplation is exclusively sudden, thereby refuting those errors. The meaning of the first passage is as follows:

the names "nirvāṇa" and "true reality" (bhūtatathatā) apply universally to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Master Guan claimed that the "but-midway" (butong zhongdao) is not true reality, but is rather nirvāṇa; he did not realize this.

Nirvana is itself the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Yet, it is said that within the four teachings, when a beginner of the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*) cultivates contemplation, they cultivate only the "mere middle" (*butian zhongdao*) and not the true reality itself.
Therefore, we now refute this by saying: if it is not the true reality, it is also not nirvana; if it is nirvana, it is also the true reality.
If it is the true reality, then it is precisely as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: from the very beginning, the Bodhisattva...
One constantly contemplates *nirvāṇa*. The practice of the principle of *nirvāṇa* is precisely the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
How can you erroneously claim that what is not the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) is *nirvāṇa*?
If, from the initial mind, it is a "lesser *nirvāṇa*," this refers to the two types of Bodhisattvas—the universal and the particular—and is merely a provisional, one-sided explanation.
Speaking in general terms: if discussed specifically, when Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching reach the seventh stage, they fear falling into *nirvāṇa* as if it were one of the three evil realms.
For those of the Distinct Teaching, at the initial stage of the mind, there is only the designation "True Truth" (*satyadharma*), yet the name "*nirvāṇa*" cannot yet be established.
The commentary states: This constitutes the second section, which specifically clarifies that *nirvāṇa* generally applies to both universal and particular bodhisattvas.

Even when discussing universal and particular bodhisattvas individually, they do not yet accept the designation "nirvāṇa. What is called "lesser nirvāṇa" is not the Great Nirvāṇa of the secret treasury of the three virtues;
it is merely the grasping of emptiness that is termed nirvāṇa. [This refers to] universal and particular bodhisattvas.

The severing of the delusions of views and thoughts is the same as that of the Two Vehicles. Generally speaking, it is said that from the initial stage of the path onward, this constitutes "small nirvana.
Therefore, the statement that it is "specifically" so refers to a general, provisional description. To say it is "specifically" so means, in effect, "for the time being" it is so.
Regarding the distinct teaching (*bipartite teaching*): the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching practice emptiness as a provisional means; they do not grasp at *nirvāṇa*.

When they reach the seventh stage, the Stage of Completion (*kṛtāvibhūmi*), they fear falling into *nirvāṇa* as they would fear the three evil realms. In the distinct teaching, the Ten Abidings are merely termed "Ultimate Truth," yet one does not grasp at *nirvāṇa*;

the virtue of severed afflictions (*prahāṇaguṇa*) resides only in the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣmabodhi*). Therefore, even the Bodhisattvas of the Shared and Distinct Teachings do not [yet fully realize it].
If this is so even for those who have attained partial realization, how much more so for those who have attained perfection?

Therefore, we know that the initial contemplation pertains solely to the sudden approach. As for the statement that "that which is not the true reality is nirvana," there is no scriptural authority upon which to rely.

The commentary states: This constitutes the third section, clarifying that the initial contemplation is exclusively sudden (*tun*). It refutes those [who hold otherwise] by concluding that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is exclusively sudden among the sudden.
One should know that when the mind first gives rise to contemplation, the three truths (*triratna*) are contemplated simultaneously.

To claim that it is merely the "Middle" (*zhong*) and not the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) or *nirvāṇa* lacks any scriptural authority to rely upon; it is merely a judgment based on personal views, using one's own sentiments to evaluate the teachings. This is indeed...
To slander the Dharma—there is no sin greater than this.
Question: Is there such a thing as taking mere "mediocrity" (zhong) and calling it the "initial mind's contemplation of Nirvana"? Answer: There is. The analogy is this:

one who does not know to seek the teachings but merely follows their own words, saying "if it must be non-existent, then it is non-existent," or "if it must be existent, then it is existent. Such a person does not perceive the doctrinal characteristics (jiaoxiang) of our school.
The junior judge [concludes] that it is merely *nirvāṇa-without-remainder*.

The commentary states: This criticizes the master for failing to seek the authoritative measure of the sages' words as the foundation for establishing names and explaining meanings, but instead speaking according to his own views.
Consequently, his every action and position are entirely erroneous. Generally speaking, when employing...
"If it must be non-existent, then it is non-existent; if it must be existent, then it is existent. "Must" (*xū*) means "necessarily. The intended meaning is: if it is existent, it must be existent;

if it is non-existent, it must be non-existent. Now, the Master [Zhiyi] observes that while the "Only-Middle" (*butong zhongdao*) is termed the contemplation of the initial mind regarding *nirvāṇa*, to say it is non-existent when it is existent, or to say it is non-existent when the "Only-Middle" is not the true reality (*shixiang*), is the teaching and contemplation of this school.

I have not seen any text that briefly judges the *Lotus Sūtra* to be either gradual or perfect, nor any that claims that practicing only the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*)—rather than [the true nature of reality]—is *nirvāṇa*. Question:
If there must indeed be two kinds of sudden [teachings], why did the Great Master not explain them clearly and explicitly? Answer: As in the *Mahā-...* [text].

The phrase "intending [the teaching] for a single meal" and so forth is precisely that passage. Furthermore, in his *Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Dharma Master Ding, while explaining the fifth line concerning the non-sequential [teaching], states:
"Whether the ten stages of faith involve severance is either the gradual-sudden; whether they do not involve severance is either the sudden-sudden.

(The two instances of the character "or" in this passage are both errors. The analogy says: The general meaning of the "single-sitting sudden" has already been refuted as before. He cites the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra Commentary* directly...

Upon a joint examination, this passage was entirely absent; it must have been a mistaken thought interpolated later. One then took the "mind of conceptualization" (*saṃjñā-citta*) to prove the meaning, yet it is not recorded in the text, which is why a re-examination found no such passage.
Furthermore, since it is not recorded in any of the Master’s own writings, why bother to cite the text of Zhǎng'ān?
Moreover, having already re-examined and found it completely absent, what is the point of laboriously citing it? Furthermore, it does not even follow the proper sequence.

The practice of the Correct [Teaching] refers to the Perfect [Teaching] among the Four Teachings (the question-and-answer regarding the three metaphors is not explained here as they are already evident).
Furthermore, it is frequently stated that because there are eight teachings, there are two types of sudden [teachings] (this directly cites their own position).
As for the metaphor, the intended meaning within the eight teachings is fully as refuted previously (the text is found in the section on "Obstacles to Not Knowing the Substance of the Teachings").
It is further said: "The two types of suddenness at the initial stage are not categorically different. Though they differ, they are the same; though they are the same, they differ. As a metaphor:
do not take this distinct substance and attribute it to another. To claim that gradual perfection is itself sudden-sudden is logically untenable;
it merely conflates identity and difference without basis.
The commentary states: "There is no one who can lead this away. This means: you cannot lead this—whether it be similarity, difference, both, or neither—to deceive others.
"Qiao" (竅) means a hollow or an aperture; "zhi" (質) means existence. Thus, the confusion between existence and non-existence, or between identity and difference, deludes people.
To blend them together without a point of return is merely an expedient resort when one’s reasoning has reached its limit.
Question: If every form and every fragrance is none other than the Middle Way, what is the characteristic of this contemplation? Answer: This is neither gradual-nor-sudden nor sudden-sudden.

The analogy states: This master has already maintained that one cultivates contemplation from the very first thought; yet, upon merely hearing of the Middle Way, he claims it is immediately perfected.

He fails to understand that while the words are partial, the principle is perfect. Therefore, the *Dàyì* (Great Meaning) says: "Do not cling to the literal expression and thereby harm the perfection [of the teaching], thus falsely misrepresenting the intent of the Sage."

Therefore, whether the enumerations of names in the sutras and treatises are complete or partial, the underlying meaning beneath the words must necessarily be all-encompassing. The Great Master [Zongmi] used these complete explanations to interpret the partial statements;
thus, it is said in the *Dà yì* (Great Meaning) that "emptiness is itself non-emptiness," and so forth. That this contradicts his own words is likewise refuted as previously explained.

The commentary states: The Master [of the school] firmly maintains that one should practice contemplation based on the initial mind. If one hears of the Middle Way, they believe this constitutes gradual perfection;
yet they do not understand that although the words refer to the "Middle," it is fully endowed with the three dharmas.

This is because the Middle Way takes the dual negation as its essence and the dual illumination as its function, being inconceivable. As for the Master’s explanation of partial statements through comprehensive completeness, it is as follows:
In the *Zhiguan*, it is cited that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of "roaming the Dharma-realm with a mind like space.
This takes emptiness as its primary point. The *Beijù* explains: "Emptiness is non-emptiness, and it is also neither empty nor non-empty. It further states:
"Within a single mote of dust there is a great thousand-fold world-system scroll; the mind possesses all dharmas. This takes existence as its primary point. *Beijù*...

The *Jiushi* (Explanatory Commentary) states: "Existence is itself non-existence; it is neither existence nor non-existence. It further states: "A single form and a single fragrance are none other than the Middle Way.
This is a partial citation intended to illustrate the principle of the Middle. The *Beijuzhi* (Complete Explanation) states: "That which is the Middle is the extremes;
it is neither the extremes nor the non-extremes. All dharmas are fully present without deficiency. Therefore, the admonition says: "Do not..."

Shouyu’s [critique] harms the perfection [of the teaching] and misrepresents the Sage’s intent; it is precisely for this reason that Master Guan is subject to such reproach. Regarding the statement that his own words contradict themselves:
the principle that "not a single form or scent is not the Middle Way" is found in the Preface and the Chapter on the Great Meaning.
Since you have already designated the general meaning as "sudden-sudden," yet now state that it is "gradual-sudden," is this not a contradiction of your own words?
As the previous passage has already refuted this, it need not be restated; therefore, it says, "it is also refuted as before."

Question: When one first gives rise to contemplation, if one abandons the two extremes and contemplates only the Middle Way, how does this differ from the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching), which possesses only the name "Middle"?
Why does the beginner, upon seeing this mere principle (*li*), remain silent and not provide an answer? The analogy says: If words have a purpose, speaking is superior to silence;
if words have no destination, silence is superior to speech. One who cultivates contemplation must establish a mind of understanding (*jie*). Understanding...
Before his mind had yet reached maturity, he abruptly established these contemplations, claiming that by investigating the ultimate principle, one arrives at the state beyond words.
The commentary states: "One who cultivates contemplation must first possess clear understanding before establishing a contemplative method.

Since the Master of Contemplation lacked perfect understanding, he abruptly established two kinds of sudden contemplations; therefore, Jingxi used these words to critique him. Thus, his arguments were exhausted and his principles reached their limit.
He then remained silent and gave no answer; hence it is said, "he reached the state of wordlessness.

Furthermore, it is said: "According to the text, one must distinguish between two kinds of sudden differences. It is truly difficult for a beginner to discern [the distinction] when practicing contemplation" (this directly cites their own tenet).

The analogy states: Previously it was said that while the teaching is singular, there are two contemplations (*guan*); here again it is said that although the text is divided into two, the two contemplations are difficult to distinguish.

Based on this text, it further becomes a case where the text is two but the contemplation is one. Since the preceding and following statements contradict one another, they cannot be further discussed.

Thus we know that when studying a school of thought, one must not act recklessly. At this time, such might still be permissible; however, if it continues through many successive lifetimes, it will still cause [the practitioner] to remain [unawakened].
"Coming, one does not encounter a virtuous friend.
The commentary states: "Thus we know that the principles of study must not be established haphazardly. 'Principles' refers to contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

If one lacks a perfect and authentic understanding while practicing contemplation, yet recklessly establishes two types of 'sudden' designations, the transgression of slandering the Dharma cannot be avoided."

Furthermore, having been burdened by transgressions throughout vast kalpas, the retributions one receives are inexhaustible. As for residual retribution and false views, one does not encounter virtuous friends—should this not cause alarm?

Question: Regarding the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) in the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), it serves as a skillful means for the simultaneous negation and simultaneous illumination upon ascending to the grounds. What is the meaning of this? Answer: The grounds...

Before [entering] the stages (*bhūmi*), both [cessation and contemplation] are lost; upon entering the stages, both are simultaneously manifested. Reaching the second stage, they are again lost and again manifested. The analogy states:
"It is not only that the continuity of the gate of contemplation is lost, but also that the textual meaning becomes inconsistent.

Since it is said that the stage prior to the stages serves as the skillful means for losing and manifesting in the first stage, one should know that the actual loss and actual manifestation must coincide in the first stage. How, then, can it be said that "upon entering the stages, both are simultaneously manifested"? Regarding the stages...

The preceding pair [of masters] and their requisites for death are as described in the third fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*. This is because their reading of the text was incomplete; there is no need to refute them separately.

The commentary states: This master’s understanding of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjie*) was not clear, and he erroneously established two types of suddenness (*er dun*). Having encountered the teacher’s interrogation, he had no rational defense.
"Shen. Because [the opponent] was rendered tongue-tied and unable to respond, it is said: "Not only has the sequence of the gate of contemplation been lost. This concludes the preceding section.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the text and meaning are inconsistent," this rebukes the preparatory practices (*upāya*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). It refers to the fact that the realization attained upon entering the stages and the mutual exclusion or inclusion [of phenomena] are not uniform;

hence they are called "inconsistent. Why is this? In the Distinct Teaching (*bipartite teaching*), which is based on practice, the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) of the path of teaching employ the truth of essence (*tattva*).

The practice of "stopping" (śamatha) obstructs existence within birth and death; by employing the contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā), one contemplates the principle of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).

The practice of "acting" (caryā) employs skillful means (upāya) to follow conditions, stopping and obstructing the dust-like phenomena of emptiness; by employing the contemplation of the provisional (prajñapti-vipaśyanā), one contemplates the principle of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

In the two stages of "abiding" and "acting," there is respectively one instance of obstruction and one of illumination; therefore, these are called "single obstruction and single illumination. Upon reaching the stage of "entering toward" [the path of seeing], one integrates the previous obstructions that occurred at different times.
Illumination enters into the one mind; by cultivating the non-duality of emptiness and the provisional, the Middle Way manifests before one.

This is simply the spontaneous simultaneous negation and simultaneous illumination of the Middle Way; therefore, it is said that at the first stage (bhūmi), one realizes the simultaneous disappearance and simultaneous illumination.

How can you arbitrarily claim that "simultaneous illumination occurs upon reaching the stages" and "simultaneous disappearance occurs prior to the stages"? The third fascicle of the *Zhiguan* provides the full details of these characteristics; a brief summary is as follows:

What was previously stated is also spoken from the perspective of the provisional teaching (*śāsana-mārga*) for the time being; it does not yet discuss the self-realization of those who have ascended the stages through perfect cultivation.
I have once composed the "Chapter on the Contemplation of the Exclusive Middle" (*But-chung-kuan chang-men*) in a separate work, wherein this matter is fully elucidated.

There are those of shallow learning in the world who, upon hearing that there are people who practice the Contemplation of the Exclusive Middle, and further hearing that the Exclusive Middle involves both simultaneous negation and simultaneous illumination, become confused and their hearts are startled. Furthermore...

There are those who clap their hands and laugh loudly; these individuals have clearly never read the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) along with its *Fuxing* (Supplementary Commentary).

For even in that text, it is stated that within the two teachings of the Tripitaka and the Shared [Vehicle], there is both the negation of both extremes and the simultaneous illumination of both. How much more so must this be true for the principle of the Buddha-nature of the Distinct and the Unique Middle Way?

Question: What is meant by the statement that the four samādhis are universal cultivation (*sāmānya-bhāvanā*), whereas mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) is specific cultivation (*viśeṣa-bhāvanā*)?

Explanation: This question refers to what is stated in the first section on the cultivation of the Great Practice (*mahācaryā-bhāvanā*) within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*: "The four samādhis are universal cultivation."
"Reciting the Buddha's name (nien-fo) is a distinct practice.
Answer: "Master Ding was mistaken; it should be said that the four samādhis are the distinct practices, while reciting the Buddha's name is a universal practice.
Explanation: The meaning of the answer is that Master Zhāng'ān made an error during the compilation [of the texts]; it should be corrected according to the text of the answer.

The commentator says: This master has erred on his own part, shifting the blame onto others. To claim that the practice is "universal" (tong) because the four samādhis encompass all practices is correct;

to interpret it as "particular" (bie) is the opposite. To argue that the mindfulness of the Buddha (nianfo) does not universally include all practices, but is merely one among those universal practices—and thus should be called "particular"—only to then mislabel it as "universal," is utterly unacceptable.
The commentary states: Master Fu Xing says that the four samādhis encompass all practices; therefore, they are called "universal" (tong).

The Buddha-remembrance samādhi (nien-fo san-mei) is but one among these various practices; therefore, it is called "particular" (bie). Furthermore, since all four samādhis universally include the remembrance of the Buddha, they are called "universal.

However, when speaking of the remembrance of the Buddha, one specifically cites a single practice; therefore, it is called "particular. Thus, the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* (*Sishenianchu*) says:
Because all four involve mindfulness of the Buddha, they are called "universal" (tong); yet because they differ according to their respective teachings, they are called "distinct" (bie).

In the Tripitaka [teaching], one is mindful of the birth-body; in the Shared [teaching], one is mindful of the response-body; in the Distinct [teaching], one is mindful of the reward-body; and in the Perfect [teaching], one is mindful of the dharma-body, wherein all bodies are fully perfected. It is further said:
Because the four samādhis pervade the four teachings, they are further termed "universal" (tong). Whenever various texts are cited, they all take the four samādhis as universal;

Master Guan alone altered this, which thus contradicts the texts. Furthermore, it is said: "Some have changed it to say that the four samādhis are distinct while mindfulness of the Buddha is universal;
this does not lose the general meaning, so why bother to alter the text? This is a case of both concession and refutation.
Regarding the phrase "The master who refutes deviant interpretations has not lost the general meaning," this is a concessive statement.

It means that even if one were to make such textual emendations, one would still not lose the general meaning of the *Zongcheng* (the Great Vehicle); however, since Tiantai already possesses the original text, why rely on emendation?
This is a refutation. The compiler, failing to understand this, instead claims that Zhanran did not lose the Great Master’s intent—how can this be so?
This is erroneous.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the Three Sages and Ten Saints dwell in the retribution-fruit" (*vipākaphala*), this combines the two teachings [the Separate and the Perfect].

The "Three Sages" refer to those of the Perfect Teaching, while the "Ten Saints" refer to those of the Separate Teaching (this is merely citing the attachments of biased interpretations). The analogy states: as for the term "retribution-fruit," it refers to the Land of True Retribution (*bhūtaviṣaya-vipāka-kṣetra*). Since one has already been born into the retribution-fruit...

These are the persons of the four stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). This master merely sees these as names for the worthy and sage (*xian-sheng*), and thus divides them into the designations for the worthy and sage of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings;
this is simply borrowing the names of the Distinct to describe the Perfect. "Innate birth" (*jusheng*) and "true retribution" (*shibao*) are precisely what clarify the stages of the Perfect.

If one were to say they are the stages of the worthy and sage of the Distinct Teaching, it would be inappropriate for them to be born there, yet [the text] judges them as being in the ten stages (*shidi*).

Regarding the attribution [of the stages] to specific individuals: since all forty positions of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) equally destroy ignorance, for what reason are they divided into ten stages and attributed to specific individuals?

Furthermore, from the perspective of the Path of Realization (zhengdao), the "stages" (di) are themselves the "abodes" (zhu); why then is it necessary to differentiate them? Even if one were to maintain the Path of Teaching (jiaodao), the ten stages already encompass both teachings, and thus there would still be no basis for such a division.

The commentary states: "The three sages and ten saints dwell in the retribution fruit. This passage is from the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*. Our school cites this solely as proof for the Perfect [Teaching].
This is because it borrows the name of a distinct [teaching] to designate the stages of the Perfect. Why is this so?

"Dwelling in the retribution fruit" refers precisely to the Real Reward Unobstructed Land (*sambhoga-kṣetra*), where only the sages of the Perfect [Teaching] are born, and others cannot reach it. Thus, it borrows the name of a distinct [teaching]. The Perfect...

There are no Three Worthies (the stages of abiding, practice, and orientation). Because those in the stages of abiding, practice, and orientation have all shattered ignorance (*avidyā*) and have all realized the three virtues, they are all categorized as sages.

There is no separate stage of abiding that constitutes a fruition; this is because those in the stages of abiding, practice, and orientation merely shatter the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vicikitsā*) and the dust-and-sand-like afflictions (*rajas-kaṣāya*), and thus do not take birth in that land.
Therefore, it is only those in the ten stages of the sages who have shattered ignorance and are born in that land; these are the ranks of the Perfect Sages (*pariniṣpanna-ārya*).
Furthermore, there are eccentric commentators who claim that the Three Sages belong to the Perfect [Teaching] (yuan) while the Ten Sages belong to the Separate [Teaching] (bie).
Now, since all forty stages of the Perfect Teaching involve the destruction of ignorance, why would the Ten Grounds not be able to produce them?

Why then do they assign the Ten Sages to the Ten Grounds of the Separate Teaching? Those teachers merely see the words "Sages" and "Sages-and-Sages" in the scriptural text and immediately divide the sages and the worthies accordingly.
The two teachings do not realize that the titles "Worthy" (xian) and "Sage" (sheng) are actually used as provisional designations for the Perfect [Teaching].

Furthermore, if one were to claim that the Worthy and Sages of the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* belong to the Distinct Teaching, then it would follow that neither Worthy nor Sages could arise [in this teaching]. Since they are "Worthy," they do not arise;

and as for the ten Sages, being merely provisional establishments, how could they possibly arise? Since neither Worthy nor Sages can arise, why do you insist on making such a distinction regarding the ten?

If the stages (*bhūmi*) belong to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*), then why are the forty stages of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-śāsana*) all said to simultaneously destroy ignorance? For what reason are the ten stages specifically assigned to the Separate Teaching?

Furthermore, if we consider the arising of the ten stages in terms of the path of realization (*adhigama-mārga*), then since the path of realization is identical to that of the Perfect Teaching, these stages are simply "abodes" (*vihāra*);
why then must one distinguish them as separate stages? Moreover, even if one were to maintain the path of teaching (*deśanā-mārga*), the ten stages [of the Separate Teaching] have already...

It encompasses both teachings and likewise possesses no sense of differentiation; why then specifically say it is "distinct from the ten stages"? This is because the character "encompassing" (含) is an error;
it should instead be the character "this" (此).

Question: That questioner asks: "If it is said that the Śrāvaka sūtras are 'gradual' and 'gradually perfected,' yet the arousal of the mind in the eight realms does not come from a gradual process, then by what teaching should this be categorized?"
The commentary states: This Master Jingxi once had this question posed by a teacher of deviant interpretations, which he then directed at others.

His intention was that since Śrāvakas undergo gradual realization and, upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other such texts, receive awakening—coming from a gradual path—he judged the *Lotus Sūtra* to be "gradual-perfection" (*jiànyuán*).
If [it were so] for bodhisattvas numbering as many as the atoms of the eight realms...
The arousal of the mind for unsurpassed bodhi does not come through gradual stages. From this perspective, how should it be categorized as a teaching?
Answer: It is the person of "sudden-sudden" (a response given by a biased interpreter). To illustrate: the difficulty has already been stated as before;
why not categorize it as "sudden-sudden" based on the number of realms and sense-objects, rather than naming it "gradual-perfect"?

The commentary states: This analogy has three parts. First, it refers back to the previous counter-argument. Second, it briefly clarifies the faults of contemplation and concludes the preceding section.

Third, it takes refuge and seeks realization. Regarding the first part, it says: "The objection is as before. In the preceding text, it was already refuted that those who come gradually are judged as gradual and complete;
yet now, the arousal of the mind through the eight elements is again treated as sudden and sudden. Now, this is a counter-argument.
He said: "Why do you not simply judge that [the teaching] arising from the eight realms is 'sudden-sudden' (dun-dun), rather than calling it 'gradual-perfect' (jian-yuan)?

Furthermore, this results in a contradiction with your own words. Since you have already judged the *Lotus Sūtra* (Fahua) as gradual-sudden and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (Huayan) as sudden-sudden, why now treat the *Lotus Sūtra* as sudden-sudden? How can your standards be so inconsistent?"
From this point forward, the errors of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) are briefly clarified; the errors of the teachings (*śāsana*) are not discussed. The commentary states:
This constitutes the second section, which briefly clarifies the errors of contemplation.

In order to support the Perfect and Sudden Buddha Vehicle of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, forty-six points are earnestly explained and illustrated. The intention is that those with deviant understandings may return to the correct path. However, the gold...

The *Bianzhi* (Discrimination of the Subtle) also states that there are forty-six for the "guests from the wilds. It correlates these with the six levels of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanwei*), which is why they reach that number.

Is it not the same in the present case? That is to say: the forty stages of Abiding, Practice, Direction, and Ground constitute the "partial realization" (*fenzhen*) aspect of the Immediate (*lijie*).
Together with the Immediate, the Name (*mingzi*), the Contemplative Practice (*guanxing*), the Similar (*xiangsi*), and the Equal and Wondrous (*dengmiao*), they total forty-six. That [text]...

This is for the sake of rescuing the insentient Buddha-nature; it serves to support the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Through his interpretation and this practice, [the truth] can be understood.

Nevertheless, I shall briefly clarify the errors in contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Since errors in contemplation arise from errors in the teachings (*dharma*), I shall briefly elucidate them in order to rescue the gate of contemplation.
Therefore, I shall set aside the errors in the teachings and not discuss them here. This concludes the "Metaphor for Dispelling Doubts and Revealing the Correct."
Is this not the very point? Alas! Master Guan was no ordinary man. He stood nine feet tall, with hands that reached below his knees;
his eyes possessed a divine radiance, and he had forty teeth in his mouth. His talent could manage two brushes at once, and his vision could take in nine lines of text simultaneously.
Though he studied the Tiantai school, he did not reach the ultimate Way—was this not because his karmic conditions belonged elsewhere?
I take refuge in all the worthy sages. May you set aside thoughts of right and wrong, so as to plant the causes for nirvana; this is not intended as a disparaging assessment.
The commentary states: Since the discussion has concluded, I request the worthy sages to serve as clear witnesses.

What has been explained above begins with the distinctions between the transmitted schools and culminates in the resolution of doubts to reveal the correct teaching, thereby establishing the aspiration for the Dharma and constructing the foundation for nirvana.
On this path, for this reason, I do not dare to arbitrarily judge gain or loss by asserting "this is right" or "that is wrong. My own mind is naturally empty;
right and wrong are like echoes. I universally pray that the minds of all beings shall likewise be so, and that they all return to the ocean of the harmonious integration of the three virtues.
*Jìguān yìlì suíshì*, Scroll Six (End).
I have spent a full year composing this work from beginning to end. The reason for this is due to many circumstances.
First, as my body has grown frail and I am pressed by the twilight of old age, I dare not abruptly abandon my daily recitations for the Western Paradise. Only after completing these daily duties...
Regarding my approach to the brush and inkstone: first, because my mountain retreat is not secluded, guests frequently visit to extend invitations for conversation that lasts for several days;

second, because I occasionally fall ill, I do not write a single character for ten days or more. Now, fortunately, I have set aside my pen and compiled these into six volumes. The language is coarse and rustic;
what is valued here is merely the direct manifestation of the essential meaning. May future worthies who read this not [be offended].
I have been requested to write this without formal literary embellishment; I shall simply keep the correct principle in mind.
Whether seen or heard, whether criticized or praised, all serve as conditions for seeing the Buddha in the Pure Land. Beyond this, what further can one hope for?

Written on a day of rest during the first ten days of the middle month of the second summer in the year of Yiyou (1655), by Yuan, the sixteenth-generation successor of the Tiantai Chan school and abbot of Guanchu Monastery.

The "Pointing to the Root of Non-Abiding" (Wuzhuben) addresses the guest’s question regarding delusion; the "Discrimination of the Root of Non-Abiding" (Wuzhuben Liaojian) provides a definitive response;

the "Discourse on the Universal Characteristics" (Jiajia Bianzheng) explains the general aspects; the "Ten Questions on the Threefold Contemplation" (Sanguan Shiwen) concerns the three methods of contemplation;
the "Ten Meanings of the Letter" (Sanyuanguanfa Shiyi Shu) points out errors.
The Essential Record of the *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra* on the Separate Teaching’s “Only Middle” (*butong zhongguan*);
the *Record of the Meaning of the Fourfold Constantness in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*; the *Explanatory Examples for the Meaning of Calm Abiding and Contemplation*;
and the *Brief Notes on the Three Prefaces of the *Myōhokke Genron* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra).
I have recently heard that there exists a record titled *The Meaning of the Four Teachings* (*Shikyōgiroku*), in which my name was privately attributed to me;

it was not written by my own hand. On the fifteenth day of the fifth month of the summer in the year of Jia-shen (the first year of the Bōei era), the śramaṇa Shūun of Tōkei on the Western Pagoda of Hieizan has revised this.
